p.note: : so [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 8, 1, Vitellius ortus familia nobili; contrast Eutrop. vii 18, 1, Vitellius . . familia honorata magis quam nobili.

: two classes who distort the truth; cf. the words of Tacitus (H. i 1) describing how the history of the early emperors was biassed by partizan views: Simul veritas pluribus modis infracta, primum inscitia rei publicae ut alienae, mox libidine adsentandi aut rursus odio adversus dominantes: ita neutris cura posteritatis inter offensos vel obnoxios. Sed ambitionem ("servility'') scriptoris facile averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur: quippe adulationi foedum crimen servitutis, malignitati falsa species libertatis inest.

: other examples of the use of the impersonal passive by Suetonius are Aug. 56, 2, assurrectum ab universis in theatro et a stantibus plausum: Claud. 11, 1, de mutando rei p. statu haesitatum erat: Ner. 26, 2, cum lapidibus et subselliorum fragminibus decerneretur: ib. 38, 2, ea clade saevitum est: Oth. 9, 1, plurimum profligari posse.

div.p: §2. extat Q. Elogi.. libellus: the correct reading is quite uncertain. The MSS. give extatq. elogi (-ii, -ium) and M. Hertz would write this as extatque elogi (Bentley, extaretque elogi), presumably understanding elogi libellus to be a genealogical monograph such as was written for the family of the Junii by Atticus (Nep. Attic. 18, 3; see also on Suet. Galb. 3, 1). It seems more probable that some proper name should be read: Muretus suggested "Q. Clodii"; Lipsius "Q. Longini"; Casaubon "Q. Eulogii (or Eclogii)"; Roth kept to the letters of the MSS. and read "Q. Elogi" (so Preud'homme; Ihm prints "Q. † Elogi'"). Casaubon's conjecture "Q. Eulogii" is perhaps more satisfactory than any other; he assumes that Eulogius was a freedman of Quintus Vitellius and after his manumission took the name of Q. Vitellius Eulogius; to please his patronus, he drew up a stemma or family-tree of the Vitellian gens and dedicated the work to him; in the same way Julius Marathus, a freedman of Augustus, published records of Augustus (Aug. 79, 2:94, 3). There is no evidence for "Elogius'' as a name; there are a few instances of "Eulogius" (see Pauly-Wissowa).

p.note: : uncle of the emperor; see c. 2, 2.

: he was probably one of the special quaestors assigned to the emperor in virtue of his proconsular power; they were known as quaestores principis, quaestores Caesaris, quaestores Augusti. These imperial quaestors were employed to read to the senate the letters and the orationes of the emperor; cf. Tit. 6, 1. Sometimes they are referred to as quaestores candidati principis, being chosen from, and usually coextensive with, the candidates for the quaestorship who were recommended by the emperor and elected as a matter of course. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 529. The younger Pliny was an imperial quaestor, as he mentions in Ep. vii 16, simul quaestores Caesaris (i.e. Domitian) fuimus. See

: Faunus was an old rural divinity, in whose honour the Faunalia were celebrated by the country people on Dec. 5 (cf. Hor. C. iii 18). His worship was introduced into the city of Rome in 196 в.с. The Roman annalists seem to have invented the legend that he was a Rex Aboriginum (Dion. Hal. i 31, ἐτύγχανε δὲ τότε τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν ᾿Αβοριγίνων παρειληφὼς Φαῦνος), the third amongst the mythical kings of Latium (viz. Saturnus, Picus, Faunus, Latinus). He was also identified with the Greek Pan, whose cult was said to have been brought to Rome by the Arcadian Evander, and Wissowa (Relig. u. Kult. Röm. p. 174) holds that the multiplication of Fauni was due to assimilation to the Pans and Satyrs. As a prophetic god he was believed to reveal the future by oracles (in Saturnian verse), dreams, and voices of unknown origin (Aen. vii 81 sqq., Cic. N.D. ii 2, iii 6, etc.); hence the name Faunus was explained as the "speaker, foreteller (fari)" by Isidorus, and Nettleship (Essays in Lat. Lit. p. 52) says "Once imagine Faunus as a 'speaker,' and all becomes clear. He is not only the composer and reciter of verses, but generally the seer or wise man, whose superior knowledge entitles him to the admiration and dread of the country folk who consult him. But as his real nature and functions are superseded, his character is misconceived: he becomes a divinity, the earliest king of Latium, the god of prophecy, the god of agriculture." (Quoted by Warde Fowler, Rom. Fest. p. 259, who examines critically the various theories with regard to Faunus and his cult.)

: the Aborigines (in Gr., with long penult., ᾿Αβοριγίνες) who are connected in legend with Aeneas, Latinus, and Evander, were said to have been the oldest inhabitants of Latium, having been driven down by the Sabines from the mountain country about Reate. They are first mentioned in Lycophron's Alexandra (v. 1253) where Cassandra prophesies that Aeneas will colonize χώραν ἐν τόποις Βορειγόνων (cf. Sall. Cat. 6, Urbem Romam condidere atque habuere initio Troiani . cumque eis Aborigines). The traditional derivation of their name is “ab origine,” i.e. original inhabitants, αὐτόχθονες; some regarded it as a corruption of “aberrigines” i.e. nomads (Fest. p. 266, Dion. Hal. i 10); others explained it as "mountain dwellers," connecting it with ὄpos (Dion. Hal. i 13).

: the worship of a goddess Vitellia is not mentioned elsewhere. The name Vitellia, like Italia, is from ἰταλός vitulus (Tusc. vitlu = bos), and would mean "the goddess of calves." Servius (on Aen. viii 328) gives ‘“Vitalia'' as the old name of Italy, the land of cattle. A female head, representing the personified Italia, with the inscription “Italia” or “viteliu" is found on several coins; see Roscher, Lex. Myth. iii 558 sqq., Eckhel i 103 sqq.

: it is doubtful whether toto Latio is dat. or abl.; in Ner. 12, 3 all the better MSS. give magistros toto certamini praeposuit consulares, and the dat. toto occurs in Caes. B.G. vii 89, Hirt. B.G. viii 34, Prop. iii 11, 57, Ov. Am. iii 3, 41, and other passages collected by Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre ii 529.

: see on Oth. i, 3. The Vitellii were patricii at Rome at the time of the last Tarquin. Livy (ii 4) mentions two of the Vitellii as leaders of the "nobiles adulescentes” who conspired to restore Tarquin; the plot failed, and they paid the penalty. Livy also mentions a sister of these Vitellii who was married to the consul Brutus; two of their sons were implicated in the conspiracy and were executed by order of their father Brutus. Plutarch (Poplic. 3), in his account of this plot, describes the Οὐιτέλλιοι as patricians (καλοὶ κἀγαθοί) and senators (βουλευταί). The patrician family of the Vitellii may have become extinct at that time, as we do not hear of them again under the Republic.

div.p: §3. viam Vitelliam: there is no other reference to this road. Witzschel would identify it with the via Ianiculensis as a name for the beginning of the via Aurelia (see Galb. 20, 2) which ran from the Porta Ianiculensis.

p.note: : a long and almost continuous hill on the right bank of the Tiber, east of Rome and outside the limits of the city.

: Vitellia was a town on the borders of Latium and the territory of the Aequi. Its name occurs in Liv. ii 39 among the towns captured by Coriolanus (c. 490 в.с.). In Liv. v 29 it is mentioned as a colonia Romana founded in the territory of the Aequi, which was taken in a surprise night attack by the Aequi in 393 в.с.; we are not told whether the Romans recovered it. Livy does not state directly when it was founded, but in v 24 he mentions the foundation of a colony of 3000 Roman citizens in the territory of the Volsci in 395 B.с., which (if "Volsci" is used in its broader sense including "Aequi'") may be Vitellia, as Niebuhr and Mommsen conjectured; see Weissenborn ad loc. Pliny (N.H. iii 69) includes Vitellia among the cities of Latium which were utterly extinct in his time.

: there is no historical evidence of the truth of this family tradition. The most famous example of a family furnishing a military force is that of the Fabii who asked the senate to be allowed to conduct the war against Veii (Liv. ii 48). In 479 B.c. the Fabii marched from Rome and founded a fortified post on the Cremera, but two years later the whole Fabian gens (save one survivor) were slaughtered by the Veientes.

: the Aequiculi, or Aequi, were mountain dwellers in central Italy between the Latins, Marsi, and Hernici, in the valley of the upper Anio and on the western shore of the Fucine lake. Their rugged land bred hardy warriors; cf. Aen. vii 746 (describing the warrior Ufens), Horrida praecipue cui gens adsuetaque multo | venatu nemorum, duris Aequicula glebis: Ov. F. iii 93, Aequiculus asper ("rugged''): Sil. Ital. viii 368, quique Anienis habent ripas, gelidoque rigantur | Simbruvio, rastrisque domant Aequicula rura. The Aequi (and Volsci) were constantly at war with Rome, their power being greatest in the first half of the fifth cent. B.C. In 389 they were defeated by Camillus, and in 304 they were completely subjugated, forty of their towns being captured in fifty days (Diod. Sic. xx 101, Liv. ix 45); the vanquished were granted the civitas sine suffragio (Cic. Off. i 35).
: this was the second of Rome's three Samnite wars: (1) 343-341 в.с., (2) 327-304, (3) 298-290.
: 'settled at"; cf. Vesp. 1, 4, subsedisse in oppido Reatino: Cic. Fam. vi 8, in Sicilia ut subsidas.

: one of the principal cities of Apulia. It is better known as Luceria, and is to be distinguished from the cities in Campania and Umbria which bore the name of Nuceria. In Ptol. iii 1 it is called Νουκερία ᾿Απουλῶν, and in App. B.C. ii 38 simply Νουκερία; Livy, Strabo, and Diodorus call it Luceria, Λουκερία (mod. Lucera); cf. Tac. H. iii 86, Patria illi (i.e. the emperor Vitellius) Luceria. In the second Samnite war, while the other Apulian cities broke the alliance which they had made with Rome in 326, Luceria remained loyal and was besieged by the Samnites. In the attempt to relieve it the Roman army suffered humiliation at the Caudine Forks (321), and Luceria fell, but was recovered by the Romans in the following year (Liv. ix 12-15). In 314 it was betrayed into the hands of the Samnites, but once again the Romans made themselves masters of it, slaughtering most of the inhabitants and replacing them by 2500 Roman colonists (Liv. ix 26, Vell. Pat. i 14, Diod. Sic. xix 72).

: notorious as a defamatory writer under Augustus and Tiberius. Tacitus (A. iv 21) describes him as “sordidae originis, maleficae vitae, sed orandi validus.” He was banished to Crete by Augustus "commotus Cassii Severi libidine, qua viros feminasque inlustres procacibus scriptis diffamaverat” (Tac. A. i 72); later, under Tiberius, as he continued his attacks, he was removed to Seriphos where he died in 34 A.D. after 25 years of exile. His writings were suppressed by decree of the senate, but Caligula allowed them to be circulated again (Suet. Calig. 16). He introduced a new style of oratory, bitter and abusive (Tac. Dial. 26); Quintilian (x 1, 116) says of him: ingenii plurimum est in eo et acerbitas mira et urbanitas ("wit") et fervor; sed plus stomacho quam consilio dedit. sutorem veteramentarium: a cobbler, repairer of old shoes. The adj. veteramentarius seems to occur only here; it corresponds to the Gr. παλαιουργός “cobbler” (Poll. vii 82); "sutor cerdo" was also used in this sense (Mart. iii 16 and 59). These cobblers were distinct from the various classes of shoemakers (e.g. calcearius, solearius, sandaliarius, crepidarius, caligarius); see Marquardt, Privatl.2 596 sq. =

: auctionibus bonorum publicatorum, auction sales of confiscated goods; cf. Tac. H. i 90, Neronianae sectiones: id. A. xiii 23 (quoted below on “cognituris''): Cic. Phil. ii '64, illud scelus sectionis: Caes. B.G. ii 33, sectionem eius oppidi universam Caesar vendidit. So "sector'" was used for a purchaser at such sales; cf. Gaius iv 146, sectores vocantur qui publica bona mercantur. The derivation from secare (not sequi) is confirmed by Cicero's jest in Rosc. Amer. 80, sectores bonorum et collorum. Rejecting the theory that sectores were so called from "cutting up" the property to resell it, Mommsen explains their name as "cutters off," referring to the deduction (sometimes very large) from the price of a property in consideration of the debts and liabilities attaching to it. See Halm, Introd. to Cic. Rosc. Amer. p. 4; Mayor on Cic. Phil. ii 39. =

: cognitor was used of one who appeared in place of another or represented his interests in court, and so cognitura munus defensoris in iudicio (cf. Gaius iv 124). In relation to the State a cognitor was one who represented and defended the interests of the State, especially the Treasury, not merely by informing about debts due to the Treasury, but also by buying such debts from the Treasury as a speculation, and then recovering them from the debtors. The conjunction of sectiones and cogniturae in our passage is illustrated by Tac. A. xiii 23, where Paetus “exercendis apud aerarium sectionibus famosus” is sentenced to exile, and the records, by which he was reviving forgotten debts due to the Treasury, were burnt (tabulae exustae sunt, quibus oblitterata aerarii nomina retrahebat). Cf. also Manil. v 319, non illo coram digitos (i.e. "bidders'") quaesiverit hasta ("auction"), | defueritque bonis sector, poenamque lucretur | noxius, et patriam fraudarit debitor aeris; | cognitor est urbis. =

: meretrice; cf. Ov. F. iv 865, numina vulgares Veneris celebrate puellae: Suet. Dom. 22, inter vulgatissimas meretrices (where Baumg.-Cr. would read vulgarissimas); in Cic. Phil. ii 18, 44 Antonius is called "vulgare scortum.”
: not mentioned elsewhere.

: furnaria (post-class.) sc. ars et negotiatio; cf. Plin. N.H. vii 135, castrensis furnaria "a camp bakery." The word furnus denoted especially a baker's oven (see Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1420); hence panis furnaceus, bread baked in an oven, as distinct from panis subcinericius, p. testicius, p. clibanicius. Wolf (followed by Baumg.-Cr.) strangely explains furnariam exercere as meaning “ex furnis vulgo locandis quaestum facere, ut moris erat Romae"; but, as Hofstee points out, this view rests apparently on a doubtful inference from Juv. vii 4, balneolum Gabiis, Romae conducere furnos. The enemies of Augustus, like those of Vitellius, gave a disparaging account of his ancestors, and said that his great-grandfather had carried on a bakery (pistrinum exercuisse) at Aricia; see Aug. 4.

: cf. Liv. ix 46 id, quod haud discrepat: Claudius' speech "de iure honorum,” col. i 1. 16, nam et hoc inter auctores discrepat. The impers. use of "discrepat" (opp. "convenit") also occurs in Suet. Claud. 44, 2, veneno occisum convenit; ubi autem et per quem dato, discrepat; this is frequent in Livy, e.g. iii 31, cum de legibus conveniret, de latore tantum discreparet.

: cf. in medio relinquere, "to leave it to every man's judgment, leave it an open question," Cic. Cael. 20, 48, Sall. Cat. 19, 8. Tacitus has in medium relinquere (cf. θεῖναι εἰς μέσον), Germ. 46, quod ego ut incompertum in medium (medio, Halm) relinquam.
: Dessau (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 453) suggests that there may be a mistake in the praenomen (“Publius'' instead of "Aulus") as his eldest son was called "Aulus" and only his third son "Publius."

: abl. of origin, "whose home was Nuceria," Nuceria being in app. with domo; cf. Aen. x 183, Qui Caerete (abl. of Caere) domo sunt. A common phrase in asking a person's native place was "unde domo?" lit. "whence from home?” “from what home?" e.g. Aen. viii 114, Qui genus? unde domo? (Conington, however, citing Plaut. Cist. iv 1, 6, haec cistella numnam hinc ab nobis domo est?, says the abl. means “in respect of domicile'"). For Nuceria see on c. 1, 3.
: cf. Hor. C. ii 4, 20, crede non illam potuisse nasci Matre pudenda.

: Hirschfeld (Kais. Verwaltungsb., 3 sqq.) shows that apparently under the early Empire the official expression for the emperor's income was res Caesaris or res familiaris Caesaris; it is from the time of Claudius that we find the term fiscus or fiscus Caesaris definitely used in contrast to aerarium (see on Vesp. 16, 3); the imperial revenues previously grouped as res or res familiaris (-es) of the emperor were now divided into fiscus and patrimonium, the emperor's public and private income, and a procurator patrimonii was appointed; under Septimius Severus the patrimonium as crown property was divided from the patrimonium privatum (called res privata), the emperor's personal property, and a procuratio rerum privatarum was established as distinct from the procuratio patrimonii principis. See Mattingly, Imp. Civ. Serv. p. 14 sqq.

: though the father was only an eques, the sons filled curule offices (which are called “amplissimi honores,” Iul. 72, Ner. 3, 2, etc.) and so gained admission to the senate ("amplissimus ordo,” Calig. 49, 1: Oth. 8, 1: Vesp. 2, 3).
: bearing the same nomen (gentilicium) of "Vitellius." See on Oth. 1, 3. The cognomen is not found in the case of the Vitellii, only the praenomen and nomen.
: in 32 A.D. he was consul suffectus from the Kalends of July (C.I.L. i² p. 71, x 1233).
: i.e. Domitius Ahenobarbus (see on Oth. 2, 1). ..

: strictly speaking, the expression ‘“consulatum cum Domitio inierat could only be used of Camillus Scribonianus (Oth. 2, 1) who was consul for the first half of the year 32 A.D. along with Domitius; cf. Tac. A. vi 1, Cn. Domitius et Camillus Scribonianus consulatum inierant. Suetonius (if not guilty of an inaccuracy) uses it loosely of A. Vitellius, meaning that when he entered on office as consul suffectus his colleague (the existing consul) was Domitius. Being related to the house of Caesar, Domitius was allowed to hold the consulship for the whole year, and so was an exception to Tiberius' practice of appointing as many successive consuls as he pleased each year (Dio lviii 20).

: the MSS. have praelatus, but praelautus was correctly read in the Basle ed. of 1533. Cf. Ner. 30, 1, sordidos ac deparcos esse putabat quibus ratio impensarum constaret ("who could balance their accounts''); praelautos, vereque magnificos, qui abuterentur ac perderent. This compound is not cited from any other author. For other adjs. strengthened by prae- which are used by Suetonius see on Galb. 21.

: "in other respects” (τὰ μὲν ἄλλα); cf. Tib. 71, sermone Graeco quamquam alioqui promptus et facilis, non tamen usque quaque usus est abstinuitque maxime in senatu. It is a post-Aug. word and is used also in the sense of "besides" (praeterea), and "otherwise" "in the opposite case"; see Peterson, Introd. to Quintil. x, p. li. Cicero uses ceteroqui “in other respects."

: see c. 1, 2, where he is described as “Divi Augusti quaestor.” If Hirschfeld is right in his ingenious restoration of Q. Vitellii in Tac. A. i 10 († que tedii † et Vedii Pollionis luxus), Augustus was censured by some for having such a luxurious spendthrift as a friend. He is mentioned among the senators impoverished by extravagance, whom Tiberius in virtue of his censorial powers expelled from the senate or allowed to resign; Tac. A. ii 48, prodigos et ob flagitia egentes, Vibidium Varronem, Marium Nepotem, Appium Appianum, Cornelium Sullam, Q. Vitellium movit senatu aut sponte cedere passus est. Dio (li 22) refers to a certain Quintus Vitellius who, though a senator, fought as a gladiator at games given by Augustus in 29 B.c.; he was probably an uncle of the Q. Vitellius mentioned here.

: this unusual phrase, instead of motus est ordine senatorio or senatu, suggests that Q. Vitellius may have been one of those whom Tiberius allowed “sponte cedere senatu.” The simple ordo is used in the sense of ordo senatorius; cf. Tac. A. xiii 11, Lateranum ordine demotum reddidit senatui.
: cf. Vesp. 11, auctor senatui fuit decernendi (where see note): Oth. 8, 1, auctor senatui fuit mittendae legationis: Dom. 8, 2, auctor tribunis plebis fuit aedilem .. accusandi.

div.p: §3. Publius: P. Vitellius served as legatus of Germanicus in Germany and in 15 A.D. amid great difficulties succeeded in leading back in safety the 2nd and 14th legions from the attack on the Chatti and other German tribes (Tac. A. i 70). In the next year he was sent to take the census of the Gauls (A. ii 6). He accompanied Germanicus to the East and was proconsul of Bithynia in 18 A.D. On the death (attributed to poison) of Germanicus in Syria in 19, Vitellius was one of those who aided in the prosecution of Cn. Piso as the author of his death. Tacitus (A. iii 13) says that Vitellius spoke "multa eloquentia.” Piso slew himself before the investigation by the senate was finished; some maintained that he was slain by an emissary of Tiberius, who feared the revelations which Piso might make of the emperor's machinations against Germanicus. The accusers of Piso, including Vitellius, were rewarded with a sacerdotium by the senate on the proposal of Tiberius (A. iii 19).

p.note: : Germanicus was son of Nero Claudius Drusus and brother of the emperor Claudius. He was adopted by his uncle Tiberius, who afterwards became madly jealous of his popularity and military success. Among his children were the emperor Gaius Caligula and Agrippina the mother of the emperor Nero.

: consul in 7 B.C., along with Tiberius the future emperor; sent by Augustus as legatus to Hispania Tarraconensis, where he incurred the hatred of the provincials; appointed by Tiberius as governor of Syria. in 18 A.D. with secret instructions to thwart in every way the plans of Germanicus who had been given the command of all the eastern provinces (Tac. A. ii 43 sqq.).

: the bitter relations between Piso and Germanicus are described by Tacitus. When Germanicus suspected that Piso was slowly poisoning him, he sent him a letter in which he formally renounced his friendship (amicitiam ei renuntiabat, Tac. ii 70).

: it is doubtful whether Piso did poison Germanicus: Tacitus (iii 14) admits that the evidence was in no way conclusive; but, rightly or wrongly, the people were convinced of his guilt (cf. Suet. Tib. 52,. Calig. 2 sq.; Dio lvii 18; Joseph. Ant. Iud. xviii 2, 5). condemnavit: "secured the condemnation of." For condemnare used. of a prosecutor cf. Tib. 8, Caepionem. reum maiestatis apud iudices fecit et condemnavit: Plaut. Most. 1098, apud iudicem hunc argenti condemnabo: Cic. Div. in Caec. 10, 30; id. Verr. ii 5, 69, 177, etc.

: Suetonius is inaccurate here in saying that the arrest of P. Vitellius in 31 A.D. followed his praetorship, for he must have been praetor before 14 A.D., as he is mentioned as proconsul of Bithynia (18 A.D.) on a coin of Germanicus (Eckhel, ii p. 400). See Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 453.

: in 31 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. v 8 where we are told the precise charge that was made against him: Relatum inde de P. Vitellio illum indices ("informers'') arguebant claustra (“keys'") aerarii (sc. militaris), cui praefectus erat, et militarem pecuniam rebus novis obtulisse. The notorious Aelius Sejanus succeeded his father as prefect of the praetorian guard in the reign of Tiberius with whom he became all-powerful. Ambitious of empire, he contrived to remove the members of the imperial house who stood in his path. At length Tiberius became suspicious of his designs and sent a letter from Capreae (where he was living in seclusion) to the senate denouncing Sejanus as a danger to the State. The senate decreed his death, which was carried out at once, his body being dragged through the streets and flung into the Tiber. Juvenal (x 56 sqq.) cites Sejanus as an instance of the vanity of human ambitions.

: as was done also in the case of Pomponius Secundus who was accused along with P. Vitellius; Tac. (l.c.), neque aliud periclitantibus auxilii quam in fratrum constantia fuit, qui vades exstitere (i.e. gave surety and undertook their custody, till their appeal should be heard by Caesar; see Furneaux ad loc.). The custodia mentioned by Suetonius is that known as libera custodia by which accused persons instead of being kept in prison were held by the consuls or other magistrates in their own houses, or consigned to relatives or others who became responsible as securities for their safe-keeping; cf. Sall. Cat. 47; Cic. Verr. v 29, 73; Liv. xxiv 45; Vell. Pat. i 11; Ulp. Dig. xlviii 3, 1; Dio lviii 3, 5. The brother to whose safe-keeping Publius Vitellius was entrusted was probably Aulus.

: cf. Tac. (l.c.): mox crebris prolationibus ("postponements") spem ac metum iuxta gravatus Vitellius petito per speciem studiorum scalpro levem ictum venis intulit vitamque aegritudine animi finivit (these words of Tac. seem naturally to imply that the self-inflicted wound caused his death; if so, Tac. differs from Suet.). The scalprum librarium was a pen-knife used by writers in cutting and shaping the calamus. P. Vitellius edited his speech against Piso (cf. Plin. N.H. xi 187; Teuffel-Schwabe, Röm. Lit. 276, 4).

div.p: § 4. Lucius Syriae praepositus: Lucius Vitellius was consul in 34 A.D., and in the following year Tiberius appointed him proconsul of Syria and gave to him the general control of the campaign against the Parthians (Tac. A. vi 32, cunctis quae apud orientem parabantur L. Vitellium praefecit). For such extraordinary commands (imperia) which raised the holder over the governors of other provinces see Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 853. Tacitus (l.c.) praises L. Vitellius highly as a provincial governor: regendis provinciis prisca virtute egit; cf. Dio lix 27, ὁ δ᾽ οὖν Οὐιτέλλιος ὁ Λούκιος οὔτ᾽ ἀγεννὴς οὔτ᾽ ἄφρων ὤν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐν τῇ Συρίᾳ ἀρχῆς ὀνομαστὸς γενόμενος, τά τε γὰρ ἄλλα λαμπρῶς ἡγεμόνευσε, καὶ τὸν ᾿Αρτάβανον . . κατέπληξε ἀπαντήσας αὐτῷ ἐξαπιναίως περὶ τὸν Εὐφράτην ἤδη ὄντι, κ.τ.λ. in

p.note: : Artabanus III was a descendant of the Arsacidae on his mother's side, and in 16 A.D. he supplanted Vonones as king of Parthia. In 35 A.D. Artabanus tried to make his son king of Armenia, and sent insulting letters to Tiberius at Rome. Tiberius thereupon appointed Mithridates to be king of Armenia, and Tiridates to be king of Parthia. To enforce these arrangements, Tiberius conferred on L. Vitellius, governor of Syria, the same large powers in the East as he had previously conferred on Germanicus. Vitellius established Tiridates, but in the following year when Vitellius had withdrawn his forces, the Parthians recalled Artabanus, and Tiridates had to flee into Syria. Vitellius again advanced against Artabanus, but an agreement was entered into by which Artabanus recognised Mithridates as king of Armenia, while the Romans discontinued their support of Tiridates. Artabanus also paid homage as Suetonius describes, and sent his son Darius as a hostage to Rome (Tac. A. vi 31-37, 41-44; Dio lviii 26; Joseph. Ant. Iud. xviii 4, 5).

: Dio (lix 27) and Suetonius (Calig. 14) say that this conference took place in the reign of Caligula, but Josephus (l.c.) puts it in the reign of Tiberius. Schiller (Gesch. röm. Kaiserz. i 278, n. 2) proposes to reconcile these statements by assuming that negotiations began in the last months of Tiberius (ob. 37 A.D.) and were concluded at the beginning of the reign of his successor Caligula.

: in the principia (see Oth. 1, 2, n.) of a Roman camp there was a portable shrine in which were kept the standards and the images of the emperors; medallion portraits of the emperors were also affixed to the standards. For the sanctity of the standards cf. Tac. A. i 39, illic signa et aquilam amplexus religione sese tutabatur: A. xv 16, iure iurando Paeti cautum apud signa: Liv. xxvi 48, obstringere periurio non se solum suumque caput, sed signa militaria et aquilas sacramentique religionem. Dio (l.c.) says that Artabanus made offerings to the images of Augustus and Caligula: ἔς τε λόγους (conloquium) αὐτὸν ὑπηγάγετο (pellexit) καὶ θῦσαι ταῖς τοῦ Αὐγούστου τοῦ τε Γαΐου εἰκόσιν ἠνάγκασε, σπονδάς τε αὐτῷ πρὸς τὸ τῶν Ῥωμαίων σύμφορον δοὺς καὶ προσέτι καὶ παῖδας αὐτοῦ ὁμήρους λαβών. ..

: in 43 and 47 A.D.; he had been consul earlier under Tiberius in 34. Eutropius (vii 18) says of the emperor Vitellius: pater eius non admodum clare natus tres tamen ordinarios gesserat consulatus. For “ordinarios” see on Dom. 2, 1. censuram: L. Vitellius was censor along with the emperor Claudius in 47-48 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. xii 4, Silanus repente per edictum Vitellii ordine senatorio movetur: A. xi 13, Claudius munia censoria usurpans theatralem populi lasciviam severis edictis increpuit: Suet. Claud. 16, 1, gessit et censuram intermissam diu post Plancum Paulumque censores (in 22 B.C.). For the censorship under the Empire see Mommsen Staatsr. ii³ 336 sqq. Vespasian and Titus held it in 73-74 (Tit. 6, 1), and Domitian assumed it for life in 84 (Dom. 8, 3).

: cf. Plut. Galb. 22, where L. Vitellius is described as τιμητής (censor) καὶ τρὶς ὕπατος (consul) γενόμενος καὶ Κλαυδίῳ Καίσαρι τρόπον τινα συνάρξας (consors imperii). Mommsen (op. cit. ii³ 1114) gives other examples of persons entrusted with the “cura imperii" during the absence of the emperor from Rome, viz. Maecenas under Augustus, Seneca under Nero, Mucianus under Vespasian. These all occupied a position for which there is no official title and no formal recognition under the constitution of the principate; it was a personal appointment of the emperor. Mommsen also corrects the statement in Dio lx 21 (of the events in 43 A.D.), ὁ Κλαύδιος τὰ μὲν οἴκοι τῷ Οὐιτελλίῳ τῷ συνάρχοντι (i.e. joint consul) τά τε ἄλλα καὶ τοὺς στρατιώτας ἐνεχείρισε· καὶ γὰρ ἐξ ἴσου αὐτὸν ἑαυτῷ ἑξάμηνον ὅλον ὑπατεῦσαι ἐποίησεν. Dio's attempt to connect the appointment of Vitellius as deputy of Claudius with his position as consul breaks down because both Claudius and Vitellius had laid down their consulships before March 1, 43 A.D., and the emperor did not leave Rome for Britain till the latter part of that year.
: for the expedition sent under A. Plautius to Britain see notes on Vesp. 4, 1.

: honest" "disinterested"; cf. Sall. Cat. 54, cum strenuo virtute, cum modesto pudore, cum innocente abstinentia certabat: Cic. .. Verr. i 4, 12, Sicilia, quam iste per triennium ita vastavit vexavit ac perdidit, ut vix per multos annos innocentesque praetores aliqua ex parte recreari aliquando posse videatur: Plin. Pan. 28, 3, quodque (sc. congiarium) antea principes, ad odium sui leniendum, tumentibus plebis animis obiectabant, id tu tam innocens populo dedisti, quam populus accepit. The subst. innocentia is used in the same way for probity in money matters in c. 5 infr.; the “iustitia et aequitas et innocentia” of Aristides are mentioned in Nep. Arist. 2.

: Tacitus (A. vi 32) refers to the unsavoury reputation of L. Vitellius at Rome: eo de homine haud sum ignarus sinistram in urbe famam, pleraque foeda memorari, ceterum <in > regendis provinciis prisca virtute egit. The compound perinfamis occurs again in Apul. Met. iii 16 where it takes the 'gen.: publicitus maleficae disciplinae perinfames sumus. Other adjs. with intensive per- in Suet. are percivilis, peridoneus, permodicus, perparvus, perpauci, persenex; also the advs. perindigne, persaepe, persancte.

: arteria meant the "windpipe," and as this divides at the base into the two bronchial tubes, the pl. arteriae was also used (so in Gr., ἀρτηρία and ἀρτηρίαι): cf. Ner. 25, 3, ut conservandae vocis gratia neque milites umquam, nisi absens aut alio verba pronuntiante, appellaret neque quicquam serio iocoque egerit, nisi astante phonasco (“a voicetrainer'') qui moneret parceret arteriis ac sudarium ("handkerchief'') ad os applicaret.
: 'throat"; often joined with arteria (-ae), e.g. Pallad. ii 15, 19, ut ex eo (melle) facta potio arterias curet et fauces.
: cf. Ner. 35, 5, Burro praefecto remedium ad fauces pollicitus toxicum misit.

: fovere, which is used very freely of medical applications, here means to gargle or to soothe an irritated throat; cf. Novius, Atell. 109, fauces fovi (= gargarissavi): Fronto, p. 69, 14 N., aqua mulsa sorbenda usque ad gulam et reiectanda fauces fovi potius quam dicerem gargarissavi: Verg. G. ii 135, animas (“breath'") et olentia Medi | ora fovent illo (flore) et senibus medicantur anhelis. The disgusting practice of Vitellius, which Suetonius describes here, may be referred to in Tac. A. xi 3 where Asiaticus, accused by Vitellius, speaks of the "os impudicum” of his accuser.

div.p: §5. miri in adulando ingenii: cf. Tac. A. vi 32, unde (i.e. from Syria) regressus et formidine Gai Caesaris (i.e. Caligula), familiaritate Claudii turpe in servitium mutatus exemplar apud posteros adulatorii dedecoris habetur, cesseruntque prima postremis et bona iuventae senectus flagitiosa oblitteravit: Dio lix 27, Οὐιτέλλιος .. πάντας . . τοὺς ἄλλους κολακείᾳ ὑπερεβάλετο. Dio tells how on one occasion Caligula claimed to be enjoying converse with the Moon, and asked Vitellius if he could see the goddess with him; Vitellius with downcast eyes replied in awe-struck accents: "Only you gods, master, may behold one another."

p.note: : Caligula, jealous of the success of L. Vitellius against Artabanus, and fearing that he might aspire to empire, recalled him in 40 A.D. to put him to death. Vitellius managed to save his life by throwing himself at the emperor's feet with tears and lamentations, calling him by many divine titles and paying him worship, and by promising that if he were spared he would offer sacrifice to him. Caligula not merely granted him his life, but admitted him among his most intimate friends (Dio l.c.).

: the Greeks worshipped "capite aperto," but the Romans (except at the rites of Saturn) "capite velato (operto)," a custom said to be derived from Aeneas; cf. Aen. iii 405, purpureo velare (imper.) comas adopertus amictu, | ne qua inter sanctos ignes in honore deorum | hostilis facies occurrat et omina turbet. Plutarch (Quaest. Rom. x sq.) suggests various explanations: (1) it is a sign of humility, (2) it prevents the hearing of ill-omened words, (3) it signifies that the soul which worships is covered and concealed in the body. See the discussion in Daremberg-Saglio, iv 977; Rose on Plut. l.c. circumvertens se, deinde procumbens: the Roman worshipper did not approach the image of the god directly, but advanced to the left of it and after prayer turned to the right and fell down before it in adoration; see Munro on Lucr. v 1198, nec pietas ullast velatum saepe videri | vertier ad lapidem atque omnes accedere ad aras, | nec procumbere humi prostratum, etc. The custom is often referred to; e.g. Plaut. Curc. 69, quo me vortam nescio. Si deos salutas, dextrovorsum censeo: Liv. v 21, convertentem se inter hanc venerationem traditur memoriae prolapsum cecidisse, idque ómen pertinuisse postea eventu rem coniectantibus visum ad damnationem ipsius Camilli: Plin. N.H. xxviii 25, in adorando totum corpus circumagimus, quod in laevum fecisse Galliae religiosius credunt (in the temple of Aesculapius at Rome they also turned to the left, C. I. G. 5980); Val. Fl. Arg. viii 246, precari Incipiunt . . dextrum pariter vertuntur in orbem. Plutarch (Num. 14) attempts several explanations of Numa's religious ordinance “ τὸ προσκυνεῖν περιστρεφομένους.”

: cf. Claud. 29, His (libertis) uxoribusque addictus non principem sed ministrum egit, compendio ("according to the interest of'") cuiusque horum vel etiam studio aut libidine honores exercitus impunitates supplicia largitus est, et quidem insciens plerumque et ignarus: ib. 25, Sed et haec et cetera totumque adeo ex parte magna principatum non tam suo quam uxorum libertorumque arbitrio administravit, talis ubique plerumque qualem esse eum aut expediret illis aut liberet. Claudius, who had previously divorced two wives (Plautia Urgulanilla and Aelia Paetina), was at the time of his accession (41 A.D.) married to the infamous Valeria Messalina. She was put to death in 48 for publicly marrying a handsome Roman youth C. Silius while Claudius was away at Ostia (Tac. A. xi 26-38). After her downfall he married his niece Agrippina (see on Galb. 5, 1), who poisoned him in 54. For the influence of Messalina cf. [Sen.] Octavia 950, rexit principis aulam cara marito partuque (her son Britannicus) potens. Tacitus (A. xii 7) describes the domination of Agrippina: Versa ex eo civitas, et cuncta feminae oboediebant, non per lasciviam, ut Messalina, rebus Romanis illudenti; adductum (‘stringent") et quasi virile servitium: palam severitas ac saepius superbia; nihil domi inpudicum, nisi dominationi expediret. Suetonius (Claud. 28) enumerates the freedmen who controlled the emperor: the eunuch Posides, Felix, Harpocras, Polybius his literary adviser (a studiis), and especially Narcissus his secretary (ab epistulis) and Pallas his treasurer (a rationibus). For ‘addictus" "a slave to" (properly of a bondsman debtor) cf. Prop. iii 11, 1, Quid mirare, meam si versat femina vitam | Et trahit addictum sub sua iura virum?: Amm. Marc. xxi 16, 16, addictus uxoribus et palatinis: Suet. Calig. 55, 2, prasinae factioni ita addictus et deditus: Tib. 69, addictus mathematicae ("astrology'').
: cf. Vesp. 2, 3, Gaium ne quo non genere

: Oth. 4, 2, alium alia via militem demerebatur: Claud. 40, 3, nihil habere se, quare eos demereatur. Suetonius also uses the form "demereo," Aug. 8, 1, avunculum magno opere demeruit. In this sense (= aliquem sibi obligare, devincire) the verb is not found earlier than Ovid and Livy.
: "as a supreme favour." Ihm adopts the reading proximo munere (MGLP), but this yields no satisfactory sense ("at the next gladiatorial spectacle''?). Iac. Gronovius proposed pro suтто.

: the intimacy of Messalina and Vitellius is seen in Tac. A. xi 2 sq., where she uses her influence with him to secure the condemnation of Asiaticus in 47 A.D., when Vitellius (who was consul and censor with Claudius in that year) was sitting as assessor with the emperor at that trial. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1.

: see on Vesp. 8, 3. Ovid (A.A. ii 211) describes the lover, like a slave, removing or putting on the shoes of his mistress: Nec dubita tereti scamnum producere lecto, | et tenero soleam deme, vel adde, pedi.

: a shoe or slipper worn by women, which fitted the heel but left the instep open; it was often adorned with gold and pearls (Sen. Ben. ii 12, Plin. N.H. ix 114). The soccus muliebris affected by Caligula (Calig. 52) was a socculus of this kind. See Daremberg-Saglio iv 1366 for probable illustrations of socculi. tunicas: two tunicae were regularly worn, the inner shirt being called tunica interior or subucula; cf. Varr. ap. Non. 542, 24, Posteaquam binas tunicas habere coeperunt, instituerunt vocare subuculam et indusium. Augustus in winter wore four tunicae besides a subucula and a thorax laneus or “chest protector” (Aug. 82). See Marquardt, Privatl.2 552.
: this expression shows the way in which so-called "frequentative" verbs like gestare had lost their special meaning. See App. I. § 7. b.

: a verbal adj. found first here and later in Apul. Met. xi 6, Apol. 94, where it takes the acc. (cf. Suet. Tib. 65, 2, speculabundus signa; Draeger, Hist. Synt. i² 357). Similar adjs. used by Suetonius are errabundus (Iul. 31, 2), gratulabundus (Galb. 19, 2), indignabundus (Aug. 40, 5, Calig. 35, 3), ludibundus (Ner. 26, 1), venerabundus (Calig. 15, 1).
: for this freedman and secretary of Claudius see on Vesp. 4, 1, Tit. 2.

: another freedman, who was treasurer of Claudius and exercised an immense influence during his reign, especially when Agrippina, aided by his support, became the wife of the emperor in 50 A.D. He was deposed from office by Nero in 55 and died in 62, having been poisoned by order of Nero who was covetous of his enormous wealth. His intolerable arrogance is described in Tac. A. xii 53; Plin. Εp. vii 29.
: see on Dom. 17, 2.

: the same expression occurs in a birthday wish in Censorin. De die natali c. 2, Nunc quoniam liber de die natali inscribitur, a votis auspicia sumantur. Itaque “hunc diem,” quod ait Persius, “numera meliore lapillo,” idque quam saepissime facias exopto.
: celebrated by Claudius in 47 A.D. An interval of 100 or 110 years was supposed to elapse between successive celebrations. See on Dom. 4, 3. ؟

: cf. Celsus iii 27, Resolutio (= παράλυσις) nervorum frequens ubique morbus est. Sed interdum tota corpora, interdum partes infestat. Veteres auctores illud ἀποπληξίαν, hoc παράλυσιν nominaverunt. utrumque παράλυσιν appellari video. Nunc

: for the omission of post before quam cf. Liv. xxxi 14, altero die quam a Brundusio soluit in Macedoniam traiecit: Suet. Claud. 17, 2, sexto quam profectus erat mense: Iul. 35, 2, intra quintum quam affuerat diem: Tib. 60, in paucis diebus quam Capreas attigit. See KühnerStegmann, i 405. ..
: Aulus (the emperor) and Lucius (see on c. 15, 2).

: praised by Tacitus also, H. ii 64, Galéria imperatoris (i.e. Vitellius) uxor.. et pari probitate mater Vitelliorum Sextilia, antiqui moris. She was spared and cared for by Otho at Rome, even after her son had revolted against him (Plut. Oth. 5, 16). When he entered Rome in triumph, Vitellius honoured her with the title of Augusta (Тас. Н. ii 89). She died, old and feeble, a few days before the overthrow of Vitellius, having gained nothing from his imperial dignity but sorrow and a good repute (H. iii 67). For the rumour that she was poisoned by the emperor see c. 14, 5. Ihm retains the form Sestilia, which is given by M. ..

: in 48 A.D., a year in which the emperor Claudius and their father L. Vitellius were censors (see c. 2, 4). Aulus Vitellius, the subsequent emperor, was consul ordinarius at the beginning of the year along with L. Vipstanus Poplicola, their names being used to mark the year (Tac. A. xi 23, A. Vitellio L. Vipstano consulibus). The younger brother Lucius was consul suffectus in the latter part of the year. For the tenure of the consulship under the empire see on Dom. 2, 1. Lucius also succeeded his brother Aulus as proconsul of Africa (c. 5 infr.).

: a funus publicum or funeral at the expense of the State was first given to Sulla, and always had to be authorised by a decree of the senate; cf. Tac. A. vi 11, Piso publico funere ex decreto senatus celebratus est: A. iii 48, ut mors Sulpicii Quirini publicis exsequiis frequentaretur, petivit a senatu. The senate might also instruct a particular magistrate to deliver the panegyric on the dead (laudatio funebris), e.g. Tacitus as consul was directed to pronounce the panegyric on Verginius Rufus; cf. Quintil. iii 7, 2, funebres laudationes pendent frequenter ex aliquo publico officio atque ex senatus consulto magistratibus saepe mandantur. See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 1187.
: the erection of a statue at Rome required the authorisation of the senate: see on Galb. 23.
: "on the front of the Rostra"; see on Vesp. 7, 2, pro tribunali. For statues on the Rostra cf. Cic. Phil. ix 2; Vell. ii 61; Plin. N.H. xxxiv 6; Dio xlii 18, xliii 49.

: allegiance, devotion to the emperor as a divine being and father of his country (pater patriae); cf. Dom. 11, 3; Aug. 66, 2, laudavit pietatem tanto opere pro se indignantium. In this sense pietas is frequent in Tacitus; e.g. A. iii 51, Tiberius cum extolleret pietatem quamvis modicas principis iniurias acriter ulciscentium. So impietas = maiestas "treason," see on Dom. 10, 1. •

div.p: § 2. A. Vitellius natus est: for the difficulty in reconciling the date given here for the birth of Vitellius with his age at death as given in c. 18 see note there.

p.note: : Sept. 24.
: Sept. 7.
: son of the emperor Tiberius; consul with Norbanus Flaccus in 15 A.D.; cf. Tac. A. i 55, Druso Caesare C. Norbano consulibus decernitur Germanico triumphus. He was poisoned by Sejanus in 23 A.D.

: Gaius Norbanus Flaccus was praetor (urbanus) in 11 A.D. and consul (ordinarius) in 15 A.D. Either he or his brother Lucius (cons. 19 A.D.) was slain by the German body-guard of Caligula when that emperor was murdered in 41 A.D. See Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 416.
: see on c. 14, 4; Tit. 9, 2; Dom. 14, 1.
: the legions in Lower Germany; see c. 7 infr. and Oth. 8, 1.

: “mourned him as stricken"; cf. Dom. 2, 3, pro mortuo deseri iussit: Claud. 37, 1, pro deprenso ("as if caught in the act'") ad poenas raptus est: Tib. 52, 2, ut et praeclara facta eius pro supervacuis elevarit: ib. 73, 1, pro contempto se habitum. Tacitus (H. ii 64) mentions the reply that his mother Sextilia sent to the first letter of Vitellius from Germany, in the superscription of which he had apparently described himself as “Germanicus”: Dixisse quin etiam ad primas filii sui epistulas ferebatur non Germanicum a se, sed Vitellium genitum. Nec ullis postea fortunae inlecebris aut ambitu (‘‘interested homage") civitatis in gaudium evicta ("won over to joy'") domus suae tantum adversa sensit.

: Capreae, mod. Capri, an island off Campania, was a favourite haunt of Augustus, who acquired it from the people of Naples in exchange for Aenaria (Aug. 92). In 27 A.D. the emperor Tiberius withdrew there permanently and spent the last ten years of his life on the island, being attracted by its solitude and inaccessibility (Tac. A. iv 67). He built twelve villas, and is said to have given himself over to the most bestial debauchery which is described in Suet. Tib. 40-43.

: cf. Dio lxiv 4, ὅτι γε παιδικὰ τοῦ Τιβερίου ἐγεγόνει (Οὐιτέλλιος) καὶ ὅτι ἀκολούθως τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ ταύτῃ ἔζη οὐκ ἐνενόησαν (οἱ στρατιῶται). For scortum used "de viro" cf. Cic. Phil. ii 18 where Antonius is called “vulgare scortum"; id. Sest. 17; Plaut. Curc. 472. =

: qui muliebria patitur; cf. Tib. 43, 1: Calig. 16, 1. Tacitus (A. vi 1) mentions spintria among the new terms of sensuality introduced by Tiberius at Capreae: tunc primum ignota antea vocabula reperta sunt sellariorum et spintriarum ex foeditate loci ac multiplici patientia. Cratinus (ap. Hesych.) has σφίγκτης = κίναιδος. See L. and S. Gr. Lex. s.v. σφιγκτήρ.

: cf. c. 17, 2, cum auriganti Gaio ministratorem (se) exhiberet. Caligula gave many exhibitions of his skill as a charioteer: Calig. 54, 1, aurigabat exstructo plurifariam circo. He was so passionately devoted to the "Greens'' (prasina factio, c. 7, 1, n.) in the Circus that he constantly supped and lodged in the stable where their horses were kept. He made presents worth two million sesterces to their charioteer Eutychus. On the day before the Circensian games he used to send soldiers to enjoin silence in the neighbourhood, that the horse Incitatus ("Speedy'") might not be disturbed. Not merely did he give this horse a stall of marble, purple blankets, and a jewelled frontlet, but he also provided him with a furnished house and a retinue of slaves for the reception of those invited in the horse's name; it was said that he even intended to make him consul (Calig. 55).

: Claudius was a confirmed gambler, playing even while taking carriage-exercise; cf. Claud. 33, 2, aleam studiosissime lusit, de cuius arte librum quoque emisit, solitus etiam in gestatione ludere, ita essedo (“carriage") alveoque (“dice-board'') adaptatis ne lusus confunderetur. Seneca (Apoc. 14) describes Claudius being sentenced by Aeacus in the underworld to gamble with a bottomless dice-box: Aeacus iubet illum alea ludere pertuso fritillo. For the gaming propensities of other emperors see on Dom. 21.

: Tacitus (H. ii 71) is very severe on the admiration and imitation of the debauchee Nero by the debauchee Vitellius: Quantoque magis propinquabat (Romam Vitellius), tanto corruptius iter inmixtis histrionibus et spadonum gregibus et cetero Neronianae aulae ingenio ("characteristics'"); namque et Neronem ipsum Vitellius admiratione celebrabat, sectari cantantem solitus non necessitate, qua honestissimus quisque, sed luxu et saginae mancipatus emptusque.

: Nero was an enthusiastic devotee of the Circus and also drove a team himself; cf. Ner. 22, 1, equorum studio vel praecipue ab ineunte aetate flagravit: ib. 24, 2, aurigavit quoque plurifariam, Olympiis vero etiam decemiugem: ib. 53, quia Apollinem cantu, Solem aurigando aequiperare existimaretur. He played at dice for 400,000 sesterces a point, i.e. for each pip of the winning throw (ib. 30, 3, quadringenis in punctum sestertiis aleam lusit). Dio (lxv 2) describes Vitellius as a frequenter of pothouses and gaming dens and an associate of dancers and charioteers.

: the only other example cited of peculiaris in the sense of "praecipuus, insignis, singularis" is Just. xxxvi 4, 3, Omissa deinde regni administratione, hortos fodiebat, gramina seminabat, et noxia innoxiis permiscebat, eaque omnia veneni succo infecta, velut peculiare munus, amicis mittebat. For another meaning of peculiaris see Galb. 12, 3.

: Vitellius was one of the ex-consuls (consulares) whom Nero chose by lot to preside over the new quinquennial contest called Neronia or Neroneus agon (Ner. 21, 1) which he established in 60 A.D.; cf. Ner. 12, 3, Instituit et quinquennale certamen primus omnium Romae more Graeco triplex, musicum gymnicum equestre, quod appellavit Neronia .. Magistros toto certamini praeposuit consulares sorte, sede praetorum: Tac. A. xiv 20, quinquennale ludicrum Romae institutum est ad morem Graeci certaminis, varia fama, ut cuncta ferme nova. The second lustrale certamen in 65 A.D. is mentioned in Tac. A. xvi 4. The contest was discontinued after Nero's death (68 A.D.), but Domitian's agon Capitolinus (see Dom. 4, 4) was a revival of it in another form. We find mention of a celebration of Nero's lustrale certamen under Gordianus Nepos; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 27, Eoque anno (242 A.D.) lustri certamine, quod Nero Romam invexerat, aucto firmatoque, in Persas profectus est. See Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 149 sqq.

: see on Dom. 4, 4. Nero, who had previously performed in the theatre at Neapolis (Naples), gave his first performance at Rome in 65 A.D. in the great theatre of Pompeius. The demand of the people to hear his 'divine voice," a demand to which he gladly yielded, is described in Ner. 21, 1: Cum magni aestimaret cantare etiam Romae, Neroneum agona ante praestitutum diem revocavit flagitantibusque cunctis caelestem vocem respondit quidem in hortis se copiam volentibus facturum, sed adiuvante vulgi preces etiam statione militum, quae tunc excubabat, repraesentaturum ("would perform forthwith") se pollicitus est libens; ac sine mora nomen suum in albo profitentium citharoedorum ("the list of competing lyre-players") iussit ascribi sorticulaque in urnam cum ceteris demissa intravit ordine suo, simul praefecti praetorii citharam sustinentes, post tribuni militum iuxtaque amicorum intimi. He then sang the part of Niobe, and postponed the award of the prize and the rest of the contest to the following year, that he might appear again. He made his professional tour of all the competitions in Greece in 66-67 (see Vesp. 4, 4). At the outbreak of the revolt in Gaul against him nothing irritated him so much as a proclamation of Vindex in which he was called a bad citharoedus. Among his last utterances was the famous “Qualis artifex pereo!” "What an artist I am to perish!"

: quamvis c. ptc. is not class. but is frequent in post-Aug. writers; e.g. Tac. A. xv 38, quamvis patente effugio: xv 71 quamvis absolutus. Suetonius has it in Iul. 26, 2; 48 (abl. abs.); 70: Calig. 13; Claud. 20, 2 (abl. abs.); 27, 1: Vesp. 15. See KühnerStegmann, ii 445.
: Becher would read prodire.

: Tacitus, in the account which he gives in A. xvi 4, does not mention that Nero left the theatre and did not return till Vitellius had prevailed upon him to appear. According to Tac. Nero appeared first as a poet and then as a musician, his second performance being given in response to the insistent demand of the people that he would make public property of all his accomplishments: primo carmen in scaena recitat; mox flagitante vulgo ut omnia studia publicaret (haec enim verba dixere) ingreditur theatrum, cunctis citharae legibus obtemperans, ne fessus resideret, ne sudorem nisi ea quam indutui gerebat veste detergeret, ut nulla oris aut narium excrementa viserentur. Postremo flexus genu et coetum illum manu veneratus sententias iudicum opperiebatur ficto pavore.

: for quasi c. abl. abs. cf. Aug. 16, quasi occasione ultionis oblata: ib. 19, quasi debita sibi fato dominatione: Cic. Sen. 83, nec vero velim quasi decurso spatio ad carceres a calce revocari. See Kühner-Stegmann, i 790 sq.
: = praestiterat ut exoraretur. Corrections have been proposed (e.g. exoratumque Ernesti, exorabilemque Bentley), but no change seems necessary.
: Caligula, Claudius, and Nero.

: including the consulship in 48 A.D., see c. 3, 1. Tacitus (H. iii 86) says that Vitellius owed all his distinctions, including his consulship and his priesthoods, to the renown of his father: consulatum, sacerdotia, nomen locumque inter primores nulla sua industria, sed cuncta patris claritudine adeptus.

: Vitellius is mentioned as one of the Fratres Arvales during Nero's reign in 57–60, 62 (?), 63, 66 (?) A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2039-2044, 2046: Henzen Acta Fr. Arv. p. lxiv sqq.). He appears on coins as quindecimvir sacris faciundis (Eckhel, vi p. 316: Cohen, i² p. 365), but it is not certain that this was before he became emperor; see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 449. Other examples of priesthoods conferred as honours were those given to Galba (Galb. 8, 1) and Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 2).

: Vitellius held this in 60 or 61 A.D. Cf. Tac. H. i 70, pro consule Vitellium Siliani in Africa habuerant (‘Siliani" were a famous cavalry corps called after C. Silius, legatus of Tiberius in Upper Germany; this "ala Siliana" had served in Africa when Vitellius was proconsul, and supported him afterwards against Otho). The proconsulship of Africa was also held by Galba (Galb. 7, 1), by Otho's father (Oth. 1, 2), and by Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 3). curam operum publicorum: this was one of the new offices established at Rome by Augustus; cf. Aug. 37, Quo plures partem administrandae rei publicae caperent, nova officia excogitavit: curam operum publicorum, viarum, aquarum, alvei Tiberis, frumenti populo dividundi, praefecturam urbis, etc. The first four of these departments had previously been under the control of the censors. The curatores operum publicorum were two in number. Their full official title seems to have been "curatores aedium sacrarum, locorum et operum publicorum,” which in inscriptions is abbreviated in various ways. The occupant of the position must be of senatorial rank and have held the office of praetor; nearly all those who are mentioned were ex-consuls. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 1022 sq. Mommsen, Staatstr. ii³ 450, 1147 sqq.

: see on 'innocens” c. 2, 4. Cf. Cic. Manil. 13, where “innocentia imperatorum” is contrasted with "avaritia imperatorum.” Tacitus (H. ii 97) records the integrity of Vitellius' administration of Africa and contrasts it with that of Vespasian: Quippe integrum illic (i.e. in Africa) ac favorabilem ("popular'") proconsulatum Vitellius, famosum invisumque Vespasianus egerat: proinde socii de imperio utriusque coniectabant, sed experimentum contra fuit. Suetonius gives quite a different account of Vespasian's administration of Africa; see Vesp. 4, 3.
: abl. of duration of time; see on Galb. 6, 1.
: his brother Lucius succeeded him as proconsul in Africa; he had previously succeeded him as consul in the latter part of 48 A.D. (see с. 3, 1).

: under the Empire, as under the Republic, a certain number of legati were attached to the governors of provinces, to whom the governors could delegate certain of their functions. Three were assigned to the consular proconsuls in Asia and Africa and one to the praetorian proconsuls in the inferior provinces like Sicily and Baetica. Nominally they were chosen by the proconsul, but his choice had to be approved by the emperor. They must be senators of a rank equal or inferior to the governor but not superior (cf. Dio liii 14, where they are called πάρεδροι "assessors"). As a rule the legati were of a lower rank. Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 248) says that consular legati of a consular proconsul are exceptional and perhaps only found in the case of relatives. Besides this example of the two Vitellii in Africa, Mommsen cites C.I.L. viii 7059; Lucian, Demonax 30; vit. Gordiani 7, 18. See also Greenidge, Rom. Public Life, p. 433.

: = remansisset in provincia (Baumg.-Cr., who points out that fratri depends on legatus). The variant substitutus esset (X) yields no satisfactory sense though read by some of the older editors, e.g. Burman, who says: "Posset tamen ‘fratri substitutus esset' ita explicari ut frater non venerit in provinciam sibi datam, sed absentis eius vices noster Vitellius, ut legatus, gessisset." Graevius, reading substitutus esset, would alter succedenti to decedenti (Heinsius secedenti).

: i.e. his position as curator aedium sacrarum, locorum et operum publicorum. surripuisse: used of sacrilegious pilfering also in Plaut. Men. 922, At ego te sacram coronam surrupuisse Iovi scio: id. Trin. 83: Cic. Div. i 54, cum ex aede Herculis patera aurea subrepta esset.

: cf. Plin. N.H. xxxiv 159, Plumbi nigri origo duplex est; aut enim sua provenit vena nec quidquam aliud ex sese parit, aut cum argento nascitur mixtisque venis conflatur. Huius qui primus fluit in fornacibus liquor stannum appellatur; qui secundus, argentum. The forms in the Romance languages, Ital. stagno, Fr. étain, Span. estaño, support stagnum (so Ihm with the better MSS.) against stannum, which is the spelling generally adopted. Walde (op. cit.) suggests a connexion with σταφύλη "the plummet of a level," but prefers to regard stagnum as a word which came from the Celtic, since Pliny mentions "tinning" as a Gallic discovery.

: this form of the word is due to a false assimilation to (and derivation from) aurum, the more correct form being orichalcum from ὀρείχαλκος, “mountain (ὄρος) copper” or “brass." Plato (Crit. 114 E) describes ὀρείχαλκος, as a precious metal no longer existent; cf. Plin. N.H. xxxiv 2, aurichalco, quod praecipuam bonitatem admirationemque diu obtinuit, nec reperitur longo iam tempore effeta tellure. In Plautus it is a precious metal and aurichalcum and aurum are used in similar phrases; e.g. Epid. 407, non carust auro contra (‘he is worth his weight in gold''): Pseud. 692, aurichalco contra non carum fuit. Cicero (Off. iii 23,92) speaks of it as an existing metal of little worth: Si quis aurum vendens orichalcum ("brass'") se putet vendere, indicetne ei vir bonus aurum illud esse an emat denario, quod sit mille denarium? See Conington on Aen. xii 87, auro squalentem alboque orichalco | circumdat toricam umeris; Wilkins on Hor. A.P. 202, tibia non ut nunc orichalco vincta tubaeque | aemula.
: a similar fraud is alleged of Julius Caesar in Iul. 54: in primo consulatu tria milia pondo auri furatus e Capitolio, tantumdem inaurati aeris reposuit.

: daughter of P. Petronius who was consul suffectus in 19 A.D., proconsul of Asia for six years (prob. 29-35), and legatus pro praetore of Syria in 39-42; he is mentioned as an intimate of the emperor Claudius in Sen. Apoc. 14, P. Petronius, vetus convictor Claudii, homo Claudiana lingua disertus; he himself had married into the house of the Vitellii, his mother-in-law's name being Vitellia (Tac. A. iii 49). Petronia was divorced by Vitellius and she then married Cn. Cornelius Dolabella (see Galb. 12, 2), a marriage which roused the animosity and suspicion of Vitellius who ordered the death of Dolabella. This murder at the beginning of his reign greatly damaged the reputation of Vitellius; cf. Tac. H. ii 64, magna cum invidia novi principatus, cuius hoc primum specimen noscebatur.

: luscum “blind of one eye." The abl. of respect or limitation was used with captus in the sense of "seized" by a malady (Lucr. v 929, genus humanum multo fuit durius nec facile ex aestu nec frigore quod caperetur); cf. Liv. xxii '2, Hannibal altero oculo capitur; id. xliii 7, princeps pedibus captus: Cic. Div. ii 3, 9, si captus oculis sit, ut Tiresias fuit: Verg. G. i 183, oculis capti talpae ("moles"). See Kühner-Stegmann, i 392. =

: cf. Iul. 68, 1, concessam sibi sub condicione vitam si: Claud. 24, 1: Plin. Ep. viii 18, 4; so sub condicione, ut (or ne), Suet. Tib. 13, 2:42, 2: Plin. Ep. iv 13, 10: Phaedr. iv 5, 8, matrem fecit heredem senex Sub condicione, ut. Suetonius uses indifferently sub condicione (not in Cic.) and ea condicione (with ut in Galb. 15, 1: Vitell. 15, 1: Dom. 9,2; with ne in Tib. 26, 1). ..

: two similar instances of children being emancipated from the patria potestas, in order that they might take inheritances, are mentioned in Pliny's Letters: iv 2, filium Regulus emancipavit, ut heres matris exsisteret (where see Merrill's note): viii 18, Curtilius Mancia, perosus generum suum sub ea condicione filiam eius, neptem suam, instituerat heredem, si esset manu patris emissa. The right of a Roman father to sell his children came to be used as a means whereby children could be made independent of the patria potestas and so become capable of inheriting property in their own right. The law of the Twelve Tables laid down "Si pater filium ter venumduit ('sells'), liber esto.” The father sold the son to a fictitious purchaser who at once manumitted him (as he might manumit a slave he had purchased) and then the son reverted into his father's power; this process was repeated a second time, but by a third sale the son ceased to be in the power of the father, and was in the “mancipium” of the fictitious purchaser, who could either manumit him himself (thus acquiring the right of a patronus over a freedman to succeed to half his estate at death), or, as was more usual, remancipated or resold him to the father who himself manumitted him and became his patronus. One sale was sufficient in the case of a daughter. Justinian substituted for this cumbrous process a simple declaration before a magistrate (Inst. i 12, 6). See Roby, Rom. Private Law i 74, and Poste on Gaius i 132 sqq.

: insimulare is used here, as generally, of a false accusation (Festus defines it as "crimen in aliquem confingere"); but the verb was also used in the wider sense of accusare, whether the charge was false or true. It does not occur elsewhere in Suet.

: "(attempted) parricide"; cf. Calig. 12, 3, etsi non de perfecto, at certe de cogitato quondam parricidio professus. Suetonius uses parricidium for the murder (1) of a father: (2) of a mother, Ner. 34, 5: (3) of other relatives, Tib. 66; Ner. 33, 1: (4) of one who was "pater patriae,” Claud. 12, 3; so the Ides of March when Caesar was murdered were called “Parricidium” (Iul. 88, 1): (5) of any freeman, Iul. 42, 3. The wide sense in which parricidium was used from a very early period is seen from Fest. p. 221 Müll: parricidii quaestores appellabantur, qui solebant creari causa rerum capitalium quaerendarum. Nam parricida non utique is, qui parentem cecidisset, dicebatur, sed qualemcumque hominem indemnatum. Ita fuisse indicat lex Numae Pompilii regis, his composita verbis: “Si qui hominem liberum dolo sciens morti duit, paricidas esto.” Philologists usually reject the derivation from pater and caedo which is accepted by Quintilian (viii 6, 34), who cites as an example of κατάχρησις or abusio the extended use of parricida for matris aut fratris interfector. See Walde, op. cit.

: highly praised by Tacitus (H. ii 64) for her exemplary modesty and for keeping aloof from the horrors (tristia) with which her husband was associated: Et Triariae (wife of Lucius Vitellius, brother of the emperor) licentiam modestum e proximo exemplum onerabat ("made more invidious"), Galeria imperatoris uxor, non inmixta tristibus. She is also mentioned (ib. 60) as protecting Galerius Trachalus, a relative of her own and a leading Othonian, on the accession of her husband to the throne. On the other hand, Dio (lxv 4) speaks of her extravagant requirements and says that she derided even the sumptuous appointments of Nero's Aurea Domus as absurdly inadequate for her needs: ἡ γυνὴ δὲ αὐτοῦ Γαλερία, ὡς ὀλίγου ἐν τῷ βασιλικῷ κόσμου εὑρεθέντος, κατεγέλα. In this (according to Dio) she shared the sentiments of her husband Vitellius who, though in general an ardent admirer of Nero (see c. 11, 2), blamed him for having been badly housed and poorly provided with furniture. For the splendours of the Aurea Domus see on Oth. 7, 1.

: for this expression see on Vesp. 3. Vitellius, when at Lugdunum on his way from Germany to Rome to assume the empire, assembled his army to greet his infant son; he brought him out, wrapped in a military cloak (paludamentum), and holding him in his arms conferred on him the title of "Germanicus" with all the insignia of imperial rank (Tac. H. ii 59; in Zon. xi 16 the boy is said to have been six years old at the time). This “parvulus filius” was borne in a litter in the sorrowful procession when Vitellius left the Palace to surrender the empire (Tac. iii 67). He was put to death by order of Mucianus in the following year (see c. 18 infr.). The daughter was of marriageable age (nubilis, Tac. iii 78) on her father's accession in 69 A.D., and had been betrothed by him to D. Valerius Asiaticus (Tac. i 59) who seems to have died before the wedding, and, according to popular report, Vitellius tried to detach Antonius Primus from the Flavians by offering him her hand in marriage (Tac. iii 78). Suetonius (Vesp. 14) tells us that Vespasian arranged a splendid match for her and gave her a handsome dowry, but we are not told the name of the bridegroom. Both children appear on coins of Vitellius with the superscription Liberi Imp. German. or Imp. German. Aug. (Eckhel, vi 315; Cohen, i² 366; Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 454).

: "stammering” “stuttering"; cf. Claud. 30, linguae titubantia. The form titubantia is not cited from any other author; linguae titubatio occurs in Macrob. Sat. vii 6, 10. Cf. the use of titubare in Ov. A.A. i 598, Fac titubet blaeso subdola lingua sono; Cic. dom. 54, mente ac lingua titubante.

: tongueless” “tongue-tied"; cf. Liv. x 19, ex muto atque elingui facundum etiam consulem haberent: Cic. post redit. 3, 7, mutum forum, elinguem curiam, tacitam et fractam civitatem videbatis: Tac. Dial. 36, mutum et elinguem videri deforme habebatur. The Gr. ἄγλωσσος is used in the same way: e.g. Pind. Nem. viii 24, ἢ τιν᾿ ἄγλωσσον μέν, ἦτορ δ᾽ ἄλκιμον, λάθα κατέχει | ἐν λυγρῷ νείκει. ..

: the legions stationed in Lower Germany (i Germanica, v Alaudae, xv Primigenia, xvi Gallica) were left without a legatus of consular rank from the time that Fonteius Capito was put to death by Galba in 68 A.D. (see Galb. 11) till Vitellius was sent there about Dec. 1 in the same year. According to Tacitus (H. i 9) Galba thought that by appointing a commander of noble birth, son of one who had been three times consul and censor, the disaffected German legions would be reconciled to the new régime, or would at least remain quiet: Inferioris Germaniae legiones diutius sine consulari fuere, donec missu Galbae A. Vitellius aderat, censoris Vitellii ac ter consulis filius: id satis videbatur.

: the two Germanies were not provinces in the same sense as the other imperial provinces; they were merely two frontier districts along the left (or Gallic) bank of the Rhine, each occupied by four legions under a legatus of consular rank. Upper Germany extended from Lake Constance to Brohl, midway between Bonn and Coblenz, and Lower Germany from Brohl to the sea. The most important military station in Upper Germany was Moguntiacum (Mainz). In Lower Germany the civil capital was Colonia Agrippinensis (Cologne) and the military capital was Vetera or Castra Vetera (Xanten). For the purposes of civil administration the two Germanies formed part of Gallia Belgica and their taxes were gathered by the procurator of that province. It was probably after the revolt of L. Antonius Saturninus (Dom. 6, 2) that governors of the two Germanies were first appointed with full civil as well as military authority. See Henderson, Five Roman Emperors p. 114.

: see on Galb. 14, 2. Vinius, together with Laco and Icelus, completely dominated Galba. The reading Vini was restored by Torrentius for iuni or iunii of the MSS.; in Galb. 14, 2, iunius and lunius are variants for uinius (Vinius).

: the Blue was one of the four racing companies (factiones) in the Circus; see on Dom. 7, 1. The devotion of Vitellius (like Caracalla, Dio lxxvii 10) to the Blue is mentioned again in c. 14, quosdam de plebe, quod Venetae factioni male dixerant, interemit. Dio (lxv 5) says that Vitellius riding in state and wearing the imperial purple seemed a ridiculous sight to those who remembered him wearing the dress of the Blues and rubbing down the chariot-horses in the Circus (τοὺς ·ἀγωνιστὰς ἵππους ἐν τῇ οὐενετίῳ ἐσθῆτι ψήχοντα). The Green (prasina, viridis) being the factio favoured by Domitian (as by Caligula and Nero), the Blue is ridiculed by Martial, vi 46, Vapulat adsidue veneti quadriga flagello, | nec currit : magnam rem, Catiane, facit. See also Mart. x 48, 23; xiv 131. Walde (op. cit.) connects venetus “sea-blue” with unda. ..

: i.e. the general opinion that Vitellius owed his appointment to the influence of Vinius is shown to be false by Galba's own statement of his reasons for his selection. Hand (Tursellinus, iv 235) discusses various explanations given of the elliptical use of nisi quod .. His own theory, which seems the simplest, is that nisi quod is a compressed way of saying non est, si est quod, or non est, si in considerationem venit quod. He explains nisi quia similarly. Suetonius uses nisi quod in three other passages: Vesp. 4, 3; Dom. 4, 4; Iul. 45, 1, fuisse traditur valitudine prospera, nisi quod tempore extremo repente animo linqui atque etiam per somnum exterreri solebat. For instances in Plaut., Cic., Tac., etc., see Kühner-Stegmann ii 416.

: Dio (lxv 2) says that Vitellius cared for nothing "divine or human" except self-indulgence: τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ προσκείμενος, οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων οὔτε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων οὔτε τῶν θείων ἐφρόντιζεν.

: cf. Curt. x 2, пес pudet profundo ventre devictarum gentium spolia circumferentes, etc. In Plaut. Capt. 182 a greedy parasite's stomach is described as a bottomless abyss (profundum). For gula ("gullet'') in the sense of gluttony cf. c. 13, 3, homo non profundae modo sed intempestivae gulae: Juv. 1, 140, quanta est gula, quae sibi totos | ponit apros? ..

div.p: § 2. exituro viaticum defuisse: cf. Curt. x 2 (Alexander upbraids his troops): In Europam ire properatis, rege deserto, cum pluribus vestrum defuturum viaticum fuerit, ni aes alienum luissem.

p.note: : so Tacitus (H. ii 59) describes Vitellius on his march to Rome "nullo principali paratu, sed vetere egestate con- -spicuus"; cf. Plut. Galb. 22, (Οὐϊτέλλιος) τὴν λοιδορουμένην ὑπ᾽ ἐνίων πενίαν δεῖγμα λαμπρὸν ἔχων χρηστότητος καὶ μεγαλοφροσύνης. The objective gen. "rei familiaris'' is added as in Sall. Iug. 44, egestas pabuli; Tac. A. vi 23, eg. cibi; Lucr. v 1211, eg. rationis; there is no example in Cic.

: Galeria Fundana and her children, see c. 6. Tacitus- (H. i 75) says that Vitellius sent letters from Germany to Titianus, brother of Otho, threatening that he would make him answerable with his life for the safety of his (Vitellius') mother and children at Rome.

: under the Republic provincial governors could not bring their wives to the provinces, but under the early empire this rule was frequently broken; in 21 A.D. the senate rejected a motion “ne quem magistratum, cui provincia obvenisset, uxor comitaretur” (Tac. A. iii 33); in 24 A.D. they decreed that a governor should be held accountable for any misconduct of his wife in the province, such as is described in Juv. viii 128, where see Mayor's note.

: “hired"; cf. Iul. 57, meritoria raeda: Calig. 39, 1, meritoria vehicula: Claud. 15, 4, meritoria scorta. The neut. pl. as a subst. means "lodgings"; e.g. Juv. iii 234, quae meritoria somnum | admittunt?

: "attic” or “garret"; cf. Juv. x 18, rarus venit in cenacula miles: Quintil. vi 3, 64, cum cenaculum eius perplueret: Apul. Met. ix 40. Varro (L.L. v 162) explains how the word got this meaning: ubi cenabant cenaculum vocitabant posteaquam in superiore parte cenitare coeperunt, superioris domus universa cenacula dicta. Suetonius uses cenaculum in two other passages: Aug. 45, 1, Ipse circenses ex amicorum libertorumque cenaculis (“upper rooms”) spectabat; ib. 78, 2, in proximo cuiuscumque domesticorum cenaculo manebat. Petronius, Satyr. 38, describes a nouveau riche letting his garret, having purchased a house: C. Pompeius Diogenes ex kalendis Iuliis cenaculum locat; ipse enim domum emit.

: abdere with the abl. of place occurs also in Oth. 6, 3, abditus sella muliebri: Iul. 20, 1: Tib. 12, 2, etc. Cicero (Arch. 12) has qui se litteris abdiderunt (where Reid would insert in), but before the Silver Age this constr. is almost entirely poetical, e.g. Verg. G. iii 96, abde domo. Another constr. is used by Suetonius in Galb. 20, 2, in gremium abdidit. Cicero elsewhere uses in c. abl., in c. acc., or acc. (Att. ix 6, 1, neque me Arpinum hoc tempore abdam).

: "let out,” alii habitandam locaret. This compound (= ἀπομισθόω) is peculiar to Suetonius, who uses it also in Iul. 26, 2, ea quae ad epulum pertinerent, quamvis macellariis ablocata (“though contracts had been given to the market-vendors''), etiam domesticatim . apparabat.
: Sextilia (c. 3, 1).

: uniones were the largest, most beautiful, and most highly valued of all pearls. Pliny (N.H. xii 2) says that they were got from the mare rubrum (Red Sea or Persian Gulf), and that they received their name from each of them being unique, no two alike: N.H. ix 112, nulli duo reperiuntur indiscreti, unde nomen unionum Romanae scilicet imposuere deliciae. The two finest uniones ever seen were those worn as earrings by Cleopatra (see on Galb. 18, 2). The number, weight, and value of the uniones worn in the ears by Roman matrons are denounced by Seneca. (Ben. vii 9, 4; Vit. Beat. 17, 2).

: "pawned," pignori dederit; cf. Juv. vii 73, alveolos et laenam pignerat. The deponent pignerari means "to establish a lien on" (pignoribus obstringere et devincire sibi), e.g. Suet. Claud. 10, 4 (of Claudius' largess to the soldiers), primus Caesarum fidem militum etiam praemio pigneratus: cf. Cic. Rep. i 8, Phil. xiv 32. For the perf. pigneraverit coupled with the imperf. ablocaret see on Galb. 3, 1; Bentley's conjecture ablocarit is needless.

: Dio (lxv 3 and 5) says that Vitellius spent incalculable sums (ἀμύθητα ἀνήλισκε) on gluttony, gambling, actors, and charioteers; and he was in debt to so many that no one could see him in the Forum on account of the multitude of his creditors (ὃν οὐδεὶς οὐδὲ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ πρότερον διὰ τὸ τῶν δανειστῶν πλῆθος ἰδεῖν ἐδύνατο). His creditors would not let him start for Germany till he had given security (ἐξορμῶντος αὐτοῦ .. ἐπελάβοντο, καὶ μόλις ποτὲ κατεγγυηθέντα ἀπέλυσαν). Sinuessanos Formianosque: Sinuessa was a town on the Tyrrhenian sea, on the borders of Latium and Campania, now ruins at the foot of Monte Dragone. Formiae was 18 miles from Sinuessa, where the town of Mola di Gaeta now stands. Both Sinuessa and Formiae were on the Appia Via. "diverted to his own use” “embezzled"; cf. Cic. Verr. ii 4, 68, interverso hoc regali dono: id. Phil. ii 79, promissum et receptum intervertit, ad seque transtulit. Plautus, who first uses the verb, has not merely intervortere aliquid, but also intervortere aliquem ("to defraud'") and intervortere aliquem aliquo. We have no information as to how Vitellius came to handle the revenues of these two towns. Even if we assume that he could have been a redemptor vectigalium, the towns would normally have been secured against loss by his sureties (praedes).

: calumnia (from O. Lat. calvi "to deceive") was used in two senses: (1) as here, a false action or prosecution brought by one who "intelligit non recte se agere sed vexandi adversarii gratia actionem instituit” (Gaius iv 178); cf. Suet. Dom. 9, 3; (2) an action or conviction for dishonest litigation; cf. Cic. dom. 19, 49, accusare propter calumniae metum non ausus est. See Poste on Gaius l.c.

: on the iniuriarum actio see Roby, Rom. Private Law ii 220. The offence is defined generally in ad Herenn. iv 25, 35, Iniuriae sunt, quae aut pulsatione corpus aut convicio aures aut aliqua turpitudine vitam cuiuspiam violant. Proceedings might be either civil or criminal; cf. Just. Inst. iv 4, 10, In summa sciendum est de omni iniuria eum qui passus est posse vel criminaliter agere vel civiliter. Et si quidem civiliter agatur, aestimatione facta, secundum quod dictum est, poena imponitur; sin autem criminaliter, officio iudicis extraordinaria poena reo irrogatur.

: a technical expression in the procedure per formulas, i.e. by issues stated by the praetor. The word “formulae” expressed the different forms in which the directions of the praetor were given to the iudex or arbiter or reciperatores to whom he sent the case for trial. The praetor could vary the formula to meet the requirements of justice in each case. The phrase “formulam intendere’” (cf. actionem intendere, Cic.) was used of the plaintiff; “formulam accipere” of the defendant. In Suet. Claud. 14 “formula excidere” means "to fail in an action"; cf. “formula cadere" (Sen.) and the common “causa cadere" (= ''litem perdere"). Sandars (Institutes of Justinian p. 69) collects and analyzes a specimen formula from Gaius: "Iudex esto: Quod Aulus Agerius Numerio Negidio hominem vendidit; si paret Numerium Negidium Aulo Agerio sestertium x. milia dare oportere, iudex Numerium Negidium Aulo Agerio sestertium x. milia condemnato, si non paret, absolvito.''. The words "Iudex esto” are the order for the appointment of the judge (whose name would be inserted); from “quod” to “vendidit” is the demonstratio or statement of the facts on which the plaintiff bases his case viz. that he has sold the slave to N.N.; from “si paret” to “dare oportere is the intentio or precise statement of the demand which the plaintiff made against (tendebat in) his adversary. The iudex has to determine whether A.A. has sold the slave to N.N. at the price he alleges, and whether the debt is still owing; if the judge is satisfied on these points (si paret), he is instructed to pronounce judgment against N.N., if not, he is to be acquitted; the words from "iudex Numerium” to the end form what was known as the condemnatio.
: about £425.

div.p: §3. male animatus exercitus: Tacitus (H. i 8) mentions the reasons for their disaffection, including the execution of their legatus Fonteius Capito (see Galb. 11) by Galba's orders: Germanici exercitus, quod periculosissimum in tantis viribus, solliciti et irati, superbia recentis victoriae (over Vindex, see Galb. 9, 2) et metu tanquam alias partes fovissent. Tarde a Nerone desciverant; nec statim pro Galba Verginius: an imperare noluisset dubium: delatum ei a milite imperium conveniebat. Fonteium Capitonem occisum etiam qui queri non poterant, tamen indignabantur. Dux deerat, abducto Verginio per simulationem amicitiae; quem non remitti atque etiam reum esse tanquam suum crimen accipiebant.

p.note: : with hands uplifted and upturned to heaven; cf. Verg. A. iii 176, tendoque supinas | ad caelum cum voce manus (= ὑπτίας χεῖρας ἀνατείνω). Hor. C. iii 23, 1, Caelo supinas si tuleris manus. If this is the meaning here, the soldiers are represented as returning thanks to the gods for the coming of Vitellius; but it is possible also to explain “supinis manibus excepit" by the Gr. ὑπτίαις ταῖς χερσὶν ὑποδέχεσθαί τι (Philostr. 771), the soldiers holding up their hands as if to catch a gift dropping from the sky.

: for the three consulships held by his father Lucius Vitellius seé c. 2, 4. Cf. Tac. H. i 9, A. Vitellius censoris Vitellii ac ter consulis filius: ib. 52, Vitellio tres patris consulatus, censuram, collegium Caesaris et imponere iam pridem imperatoris dignationem et auferre privati securitatem: Plut.
