Galb. 22 (quoted on c. 2, 4). For the attributive use of ter see on “olim” c. 17, 2.

: cf. Calig. 25, Caesoniam neque facie insigni neque aetate integra amavit: Tib. 10, integra aetate ac valitudine. Suetonius also uses integer aetate (Aug. 19, neque aetate neque corpore integer). Vitellius was 53 years old at the time and hardly to be described as "aetate integra''; Servius on Aen. ix 255 (integer aevi Ascanius) says "Integer aevi, id est adolescens cui aetas integra superést.” ..
: cf. Auson. Carm. 259, 9, prodiga sceptra Vitelli.

: = fidem, firmam opinionem; cf. Tib. 69, persuasionis plenus cuncta fato agi: Plin. N.H. xxv 2, durat tamen tradita persuasio in magna parte vulgi, veneficiis et herbis id cogi: Quintil. i 1, qui paulum aliquid ultra primas litteras progressi, falsam sibi scientiae persuasionem induerunt. In Cicero persuasio is used in an active sense for the act of persuading: Inv. i 5, dicere apposite ad persuasionem.

: = .... manipularium, gregariorum, "common. soldiers'" "privates"; cf. Aug. 25, 3, vallares ac murales coronas saepe etiam caligatis dabat: [Quintil.] decl. iii 15, cui parere caligatum lex iubet: ib. 19, commendem tibi ordinem caligati militis. The caliga, or boot of the rank and file, was of leather with soles thickly studded with iron nails; see Mayor on Juv. xvi 24, offendere tot caligas, tot | milia clavorum. The emperor Gaius got his nickname "Caligula" from being brought up in the camp and wearing the private's uniform; Calig. 9, Caligulae cognomen castrensi ioco traxit, quia manipulario habitu inter milites educabatur.
: "even"; see App. I. § 13.

: cf. Plin. Ep. vi 19, urbem Italiamque non pro patria sed pro hospitio (= deversorio, caupona) aut stabulo quasi peregrinantes habere. The stabulum provided accommodation primarily for the horses or mules of the viatores, and there Vitellius would meet the muliones; but the word is also found (e.g. in Mart. vi 94) in the general sense of an inn. Ulpian, Dig. iv 9, 5, differentiates between cauponae, for travellers only, and stabula, for beasts of burden: Caupo (mercedem accipit), ut viatores manere in caupona patiatur; stabularius, ut permittat iumenta apud eum stabulari. Lafaye (Daremberg-Saglio iv 1448) says: "Il est probable que les clients du stabulum se contentaient souvent d'y remiser leurs bêtes et leurs voitures les jours de marché, comme on le fait encore dans toutes les petites villes; eux-mêmes n'y couchaient pas; le soir venu, ayant terminé leurs affaires, ils reprenaient avec leurs bêtes le chemin de la campagne. Il y avait à côté de l'écurie un cabaret et aussi quelques chambres pouvant servir en cas de nécessité; en un mot, le stabulum, c'est par excellence l'auberge des rouliers, l'osteria qu'on rencontre au bord des grandes routes, à l'entrée des villes." Suetonius elsewhere uses stabulum for "stable" (Calig. 55, 2) and "brothel" (Iul. 49, 1).

: Tacitus (H. i 52) states that comitas was one of the virtues falsely attributed to Vitellius by his supporters, while sterner judges pronounced him a man of low tastes: Et ut Vitellius apud severos humilis, ita comitatem bonitatemque faventes vocabant, quod sine modo, sine iudicio donaret sua, largiretur aliena; simul aviditate imperi dandi ipsa vitia pro virtutibus interpretabantur.

: "breakfasted"; cf. Mart. viii '67, 10, Ut iantes, sero, Caeciliane, venis: Isidor. or. xx 2, 10, Iantaculum est primus cibus quo ieiunium solvitur, unde et nuncupatum. Nigidius: Nos ipsi ieiunia iantaculis levibus solvimus. On the forms iento, ianto, from *ieiunto, *iaiunto see Lindsay, Lat. Lang. p. 17; in the MSS. of Plautus iaiunus is the best attested form. The iantaculum was usually taken during the third or, at the latest, the fourth hour, and consisted of bread dipped in wine or eaten with honey, dates, olives, or salt: sometimes fried cakes. and cheese were used. (Marquardt, Privatl.2 265.)

: the careful inspection of the winter-quarters of the legions in Lower Germany by Vitellius, the newly arrived legatus, is described in Tac. H. i 52: Sub ipsas superioris anni (i.e. 68 A.D.) kalendas Decembres Aulus Vitellius inferiorem Germaniam ingressus hiberna legionum cum cura adierat. The winter-quarters of the First legion were at Bonna (Bonn), of the Sixteenth at Novaesium (Neuss), and of the Fifth and Fifteenth at Castra Vetera (Xanten, below Wesel), which was the chief military centre of the province (see on c. 7, 1).

: cf. Tac. (l.c.): Redditi plerisque ordines, remissa ignominia, adlevatae notae; plura ambitione, quaedam iudicio, in quibus sordes et avaritiam Fontei Capitonis (the late commander, see Galb. 11) adimendis adsignandisve militiae ordinibus integre mutaverat. The centurions who had openly declared their adhesion to the cause of Nero and Verginius Rufus, and thus compromised themselves in relation to Galba, had been degraded and were now reinstated.

: = ignominia notatis. Some of the ignominiae or notae, i.e. degrading punishments inflicted for military offences, are described in Aug. 24, 2, Centuriones statione deserta, itidem ut manipulares, capitali animadversione puniit, pro cetero delictorum genere variis ignominiis adfecit, ut stare per totum diem iuberet ante praetorium (the general's quarters), interdum tunicatos discinctosque, nonnumquam cum decempedis (ten-foot poles) vel etiam caespitem portantes: Val. Max. ii 7, 9, L. Calpurnius Piso consul, cum in Sicilia bellum adversus fugitivos gereret, et C. Titius, equitum praefectus, fugitivorum multitudine circumventus arma iis tradidisset, his praefectum ignominiae generibus adfecit. Iussit eum toga laciniis abscissis amictum, discinctaque tunica indutum, nudis pedibus, a mane in noctem usque ad principia per omne tempus militiae adesse; interdixit etiam ei convictum hominum, usumque balnearum: Frontin. Strateg. iv 1, 26, 27, 28. See Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 572.

: ''mourning garb." It was a regular artifice for an accused person (reus) to appear in public unwashed and unkempt (squalidus), clad in mean and soiled apparel (sordidatus); cf. Quintil. vi 1, 33, At sordes et squalorem et propinquorum quoque similem habitum scio profuisse: Cic. Cluent. 18, squalore huius et sordibus laetatur (where see Ramsay). So sordes is used in describing those who have a trial hanging over their heads; e.g. Cic. Att. i 16, satius esse illum (Clodium) in infamia relinqui ac sordibus quam infirmo iudicio committi: Suet. Aug. 32, 2, diuturnorum reorum et ex quorum sordibus nihil aliud quam voluptas inimicis quaereretur nomina abolevit.

: Vitellius had taken over command in Lower Germany about Dec. 1, 68 A.D.; on the evening of Jan. 1, 69, while dining at Cologne he received news that two legions (iv and xxii) in Upper Germany had refused to renew the oath of allegiance to Galba. He made known this news to his army, and on the following day Fabius Valens, the legatus of the First legion, with the cavalry of that legion and of the auxiliaries appeared at Cologne and greeted him as Imperator (Tac. H. i 56, 57).

: the days following the Kalends, the Nones, and the Ides were "black" (atri) or unlucky days for beginning an enterprise; cf. Macrob. Sat. i 16, 21, dies autem postriduanos ad omnia maiores nostri cavendos putarunt, quos etiam atros velut infausta appellatione damnarunt: ib. 15, 22, omnes autem postriduani dies seu post Kalendas sive post Nonas Idusve ex aequo atri sunt: Gell. v 17: Varr. L.L. vi 4, 29: Liv. vi 1, 12. In the Fasti Praenest. the 2nd of Jan. is: marked as a “dies religiosus, ut sunt dies postridie omnes Kalendas, quod iis sacrificium non fit."
: 'the time of the day," explained by the following ac iam vespere.

: cf. Claud. 17, 3, in veste palmata: Oth. 12, 1, in lintea veste: Ner. 25, 1, in veste purpurea. Suetonius, like other post-Aug. authors, uses in c. abl. (cf. ἐν) or the simple abl. (e.g. Iul. 6, 2, muliebri veste) in describing dress, where the best prose writers prefer сит. For “vestis domestica,” common clothes worn in the house, cf. Aug. 73, veste non temere alia quam domestica usus est, ab sorore et uxore et filia neptibusque confecta: Sen. Tranq. i 5, placet non ex arcula prolata vestis .. sed domestica et vilis, nec servata nec sumenda sollicite: Cic. Fin. ii 24, 77, aut etiam, ut vestitum, sic sententiam habeas aliam domesticam, aliam forensem, ut in fronte ostentatio sit, intus veritas occultetur. The garments worn out of doors were called “forensia” or ““vestis forensis”; cf. Aug. 73, Et forensia autem et calceos numquam non intra cubiculum habuit ad subitos repentinosque casus parata: Calig. 17, 2, posteriore epulo forensia viris distribuit. Among the equipment provided by Alexander Severus for provincial governors (praesides provinciarum) were “vestes forenses binae, domesticae binae, balneares singulares" (Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 42).

: cf. Galb. 10, 1: Tac. H. i 57, Proxima legionis primae hiberna erant et promptissimus e legatis Fabius Valens. Is die proximo (Jan. 2) coloniam Agrippinensem cum equitibus legionis auxiliariorumque ingressus imperatorem Vitellium consalutavit. Secutae ingenti certamine eiusdem provinciae (i.e. Lower Germany) legiones.

: the most crowded streets or quarters of Colonia Agrippinensis itself. vicos is explained as "villages" or "towns" by Rolfe, Thomson-Forester, Clarke, and Holland (who however gives "streets" as an alternative rendering).
: the dagger (pugio) or sword was one of the insignia assumed by a new emperor; see on Galb. 11.
: cf. c. 10, 3, where Vitellius dedicates at the same shrine of Mars in Cologne the sword with which Otho had slain himself.

div.p: § 2. praetorium: the general's quarters in the camp; see on "principia,” Oth. 1, 2.

p.note: : these words are difficult: Stahr translates, "als das Speisezimmer durch Ansteckung eines Kamins in Flammen stand"; Rolfe, "the dining-room caught fire from the stove and was ablaze"; but it is doubtful if ex conceptu camini could mean "owing to a catching fire, or an ignition, caused by the stove." The only other passage where the subst. "conceptus" is used of fire seems to be Plin. N.H. xvi 208, Teritur lignum ligno ignemque concipit attritu, excipiente materia aridi fomitis ("tinder''), fungi vel foliorum facillimo conceptu, i.e. the fungi and leaves most readily ignite; on the analogy of this, "conceptus camini'' should mean that the fireplace, or rather the chimney, itself caught fire (and so set fire to the room). The caminus was a fireplace, often arched in shape, fitted with a chimney (‘chimney" comes through “cheminée” from caminus), and was fed with logs. Its use in the winter-quarters of troops is mentioned in Cic. Fam. vii 10, metuo ne frigeas in hibernis; quamobrem camino luculento utendum censeo. Sidonius (Ep. ii 2) mentions its use for heating dining-rooms in winter: in hiemale triclinium venitur, quod arcuatili camino saepe ignis animatus pulla fuligine infecit ("a roaring fire on an arched hearth often fills it with smoke and smuts." Dalton). For ante quam with the participle see on Galb. 11, prius quam.. oppressis. ..

: for this use of cum quidem introducing a memorable utterance on a certain occasion cf. Iul. 50, 2, cum quidem plerisque vilitatem mirantibus facetissime Cicero: “Quo melius,” inquit, “emptum sciatis, tertia deducta” (“It's a better bargain than you think, for a third has been knocked off the price'"): Cic. Sen. 4, 11, cum quidem Salinatori, qui amisso oppido fugerat in arcem, glorianti atque ita dicenti: “Mea opera, Q. Fabi, Tarentum recepisti”; “Certe," inquit ridens, “nam nisi tu amisisses, numquam recepissem.” See Draeger, Hist. Synt. ii 568.

: Frontinus, Strateg. i 12 (a chapter entitled “De dissolvendo metu quem milites ex adversis conceperint ominibus''), gives many historical examples of commanders promptly construing unfavourable omens as favourable; e.g., Epaminondas, cum fax de caelo nocte delapsa eos qui adverterunt terruisset: ‘“Lumen,” inquit, “hoc numina ostendunt.'" Chabrias Atheniensis classe dimicaturus, excusso ante navem ipsius fulmine, exterritis per tale prodigium militibus: ‘“Nunc,” inquit, ““potissimum ineunda pugna est, cum deorum maximus Iuppiter adesse numen suum classi nostrae ostendit."

: this impersonal use (cf. illucescit) is only found here. A. А. Howard (Harvard Studies x 28) plausibly suggests that Bono animo estote! nobis adluxit is a quotation from some tragedy, and he would complete the line as an iambic senarius by the addition of deus.

: cf. Tac. H. i 57, Et superior (= superioris provinciae) exercitus speciosis senatus populique Romani nominibus relictis tertium nonas Ianuarias (i.e. Jan. 3) Vitellio accessit: scires illum priore biduo non penes rem publicam fuisse (i.e. it had not been under the control of or subject to the Republic, though on Jan. 1 the legions, iv and xxii, stationed at Moguntiacum, when required to renew the oath of fealty to Galba, dashed down his images and swore allegiance to the senate and the Roman people, i.e. the Republic; see on Galb. 16, 2): Plut. Galb. 22, Εὐθὺς δὲ καὶ τὸ μετὰ Φλάκκου (i.e. Hordeonius Flaccus, commander in Upper Germany) στράτευμα τοὺς καλοὺς ἐκείνους καὶ δημοκρατικοὺς εἰς σύγκλητον (senatum) ὅρκους ἀφέντες ὤμοσαν Οὐϊτελλίῳ τῷ αὐτοκράτορι (imperatori) ποιήσειν τὸ προστασσόμενον.

: Tac. H. i 62, nomen Germanici Vitellio statim additum. Plutarch (l.c.) says that for some days previously Vitellius had seemed to dread the weight of sovereign power and to decline it, but on the day when Fabius Valens and the cavalry saluted him as imperator he had been entertaining his officers at a great banquet from midday, and replete with food and drink he went out to them and accepted the title of "Germanicus." For his mother's refusal to recognize her son Vitellius under the name “Germanicus" see on c. 3, 2.

: Tac. H. ii 62, praemisit in urbem edictum, quo vocabulum Augusti differret, Caesaris non reciperet, cum de potestate nihil detraheret (i.e. though he relinquished nothing of his actual powers). The senate, on the receipt of the news of the defeat and death of Otho and the acceptance of Vitellius by the city soldiery, had at once decreed to him all the customary honours, the tribunician power, the title of Augustus, etc. (H. ii 55). He was constrained by the people to accept the title of "Augustus" on the day after he made his imposing entry into Rome in Aug. 69 A.D.; H. ii 90, abnuentique nomen Augusti expressere, ut adsumeret, tam frustra quam recusaverat. Vitellius reckoned the first day of his reign (dies imperii) to be April 19, 69 A.D., when he was recognised by the senate; Vespasian reckoned his dies imperii to be the day on which he was first proclaimed by the legions in Egypt (see Vesp. 6, 3).

: cf. Plut. (l.c.) φασὶν (τὸν Οὐϊτέλλιον) .. προελθεῖν καὶ ὑπακοῦσαι Γερμανικὸν ὄνομα θεμένων αὐτῷ, τὸ δὲ Καίσαρος οὐ προσδεξάμενον. Tacitus mentions that Vitellius at first declined the title (see H. ii 62, quoted in preceding note, and i 62 Caesarem se appellari etiam victor prohibuit); but he also states that Vitellius afterwards, when the Flavian forces were advancing on Rome, expressed a wish to be saluted as "Caesar': iii 58, quin et Caesarem se dici voluit, aspernatus antea; sed tunc superstitione nominis (“a superstitious feeling about the name''), et quia in metu consilia prudentium et vulgi rumor iuxta audiuntur. In the Acta Fratr. Arv. he appears as "Vitellius Germanicus Imperator'' (C.I.L. vi 2051, Henzen Act. Fr. Arv. xcii sqq.). On his earlier coins he is styled "A. Vitellius Imperator Germanicus"; on the later the title "Augustus" is added. On some Alexandrian coins his name appears as Ώλος (= Aulus) Οὐιτ. Καισ. Σεβ. (Σεβαστός = Augustus) Γερμ. αὐτ. (αὐτοκράτωρ Imperator). It is probable that these coins were struck before the news that Vitellius had rejected the title of "Caesar" reached the provinces (Eckhel, vi 309). =

: described in Galb. 19 and 20. Tacitus (H. i 64) says that Valens (see next note) was already on his march when he received the news of Galba's death: Nuntium de caede Galbae et imperio Othonis Fabius Valens in civitate Leucorum (in N.E. Gaul, on the Moselle) accepit. Nec militum animus in gaudium aut formidine permotus: bellum volvebat.

: Suetonius mentions only the division of the forces of Vitellius into those sent in advance and those with which he followed in person; the further division of the advance forces is described in Tac. H. i 61. Vitellius decided that there were to be two generals and two lines of march. Fabius Valens was ordered to advance through Gaul (winning it over or, if necessary, ravaging it) and to invade Italy by way of the Cottian Alps, the chain which divides Dauphiné from Piedmont, with the pass over Mont Genèvre where Pompey and later Augustus had made a military road. Aulus Caecina was to take the nearer route coming down through Switzerland into Italy by the Pennine Alps, over the Great St. Bernard pass from Martigny to Aosta. To Valens were entrusted the picked troops of the army of Lower Germany, including the main part of the Fifth legion, detachments from legions i, xv, and xvi, and the auxiliary infantry and cavalry, the total force numbering about 40,000 men. Caecina led 30,000 from the army of Upper Germany, the flower of his force being the 21st legion, called Rapax. Vitellius followed later with about 60,000 men, comprising the strength of the Germanic armies and some 8000 who had been sent from Britain.

: mentioned also in Tac. H. i 62: Laetum augurium, Fabio Valenti exercituique, quem in bellum agebat, ipso profectionis die aquila leni meatu, prout agmen incederet, velut dux viae praevolavit; longumque per spatium is gaudentium militum clamor, ea quies interritae alitis fuit, ut haud dubium magnae et prosperae rei omen acciperetur. A similar favourable omen preluded a great victory of Germanicus over Arminius; cf. Tac. A. ii 17 Interea pulcherrimum augurium, octo (i.e. one for each of the 8 legions) aquilae petere silvas et intrare visae imperatorem advertere. Exclamat irent, sequerentur Romanas aves, propria legionum numina. lustratis: = circu(m)itis. lustrare primarily meant "to purify," and as the purification was often effected by processions round a place or by the priest going round the persons to be purified and sprinkling them with water, lustrare came to be used in the sense of circu(m)ire and also of peragrare; e.g. Aen. x 224, adgnoscunt (Nymphae) longe regem, lustrantque (= circumnatant) choreis: ib. vii 391, te (Bacchum) lustrare choro (= circum te saltare): Cic. Fin. v 87, Pythagoras Aegyptum lustravit.

: cf. Curt. iv 7, 15, corvi modico volatu prima signa antecedentes et modo humi residebant, cum lentius agmen incederet, modo se pennis levabant ducentium iterque monstrantium ritu: Vell. Pat. i 4, 1, classis cursum esse directum columbae antecedentis volatu ferunt.

: for movere used absolutely, in the sense of moveri or se movere, cf. Calig. 13, ut a Miseno movit: Iul. 60, cum minime quis moturum putaret: Liv. xxxvii 28, 4, postquam movisse a Samo Romanos audivit: Cic. Att. ix 1, 1, postquam ille Canusio moverat (where see Tyrrell and Purser, who rightly deny that there is an ellipse of castra).

: cf. Aug. 46 and 80; Tib. 43, 2; Calig. 54, 1; Claud. 21, 4; Ner. 24, 23; not found in any earlier writer. Suetonius also uses multifariam in many places" (e.g. Galb. 19, 1); bifariam "in two places" (Aug. 100, 3); trifariam, quadrifariam ‘“in three (four) parts" (Vitell. 13, 1). Other similar adverbs collected by Neue, Formenlehre ii 677, are alifariam, aliquotfariam, ambifariam, omnifariam, septifariam. All such forms are Acc. Sg. Fem. of adjs. in -fārius; cf. Gr. -φάσιος from -φατιος, e.g. τριφάσιος (Lindsay, Lat. Lang. p. 552).

: so when Julius Caesar was setting out for the senate on the fatal Ides of March, an image of him in the vestibule of his house fell down of its own accord and was shattered (Dio xliv 18). Before Nero's death exornati Lares in ipso sacrificii apparatu conciderunt (Ner. 46, 2). ..

: see on Galb. 18, 3, sacrificanti coronam de capite excidisse. Vitellius offered sacrifice when the expedition was setting out. Suetonius uses either laurea corona (Iul. 45, 2; 79, 1; Tib. 69) or laurea by itself (as in Dom. 6, 1; etc.).

: sc. aquam. For this ellipse cf. Cic. Inv. ii 149, dum culeus, in quem coniectus in profluentem deferretur, compararetur: Auct. ad Herenn. i 23, Et lex: qui parentem necasse iudicatus erit, ut is obvolutus et obligatus corio devehatur in profluentem: Flor. i 1, abiectus in profluentem: id. iv 12, arma in profluentes data. The full phrase aqua profluens occurs in Cic. Q. Fratr. iii 1. The ellipse of aqua with frigida, calida, etc., is common.

: Vienna, mod. Vienne, was on the Rhone, in the province of Gallia Narbonensis. It had been the capital of the Allobroges, and seems to have been made a Roman colony under Caligula. The fierce rivalry and enmity which existed between it and Lugdunum (Lyons), on the opposite bank of the Rhone, are described in Tac. H. i 65.
: see on Vesp. 7, 2.

: used absolutely (as in Plin. N.H., and Columella) for gallus gallinaceus (Plaut., Cic., etc.) "a poultry-cock." It is fortunate that Suetonius explains in c. 18 what was portended by the strange occurrence mentioned here, as otherwise we should have been at a loss to divine it. Cf. the story of the hen (gallina) in Galb. 1.

: though the cock perching on his shoulder and head was an omen of doom to Vitellius, an eagle lighting on the shoulder or head was regarded as a sign of coming power; cf. Claud. 7, evenit ut primitus ingredienti cum fascibus (i.e. as consul) Forum praetervolans aquila dexteriore umero consideret: Lact. Inst. i 11, 65, consedisse (Iovi) aquilam in capite atque ei regnum portendisse. Valerius Maximus (v 6, 4) tells a curious tale of a bird lighting on the head of Q. Aelius Paetus when he was administering justice as praetor: Cui ius dicenti cum in capite picus consedisset haruspexque affirmasset, conservato eo fore domus ipsius statum felicissimum, reipublicae miserrimum; occiso, in contrarium utrumque cessurum: e vestigio picum morsu suo in conspectu senatus necavit.
: cf. Liv. ix 15, Papirio quoque brevi ad spem eventus respondit: Cic. Div. ii 24, 52, quae (responsa haruspicum) aut nullos habuerint exitus aut contrarios.

: Aulus Caecina and Fabius Valens, who defeated the forces of Otho at Betriacum. For the career of Caecina see on Tit. 6, 2. Valens was appointed by Nero to command the 1st legion in Germany, and after Galba's accession he put to death Fonteius Capito (see Galb. 11), governor of Lower Germany, alleging that he was plotting revolution. Thinking this service insufficiently rewarded by Galba, he persuaded Vitellius to seize the empire. When Vitellius reached Rome, Valens and Caecina were made consuls (Sept., 69 A.D.). They were sent from Rome against the advancing forces of Vespasian. Valens was delayed in starting, and when he heard of the rout of the rest of the Vitellian army by Antonius Primus, he tried to cross over by sea to Gaul, to rouse that province for Vitellius, but was captured and shortly afterwards executed. Tacitus denounces in the strongest terms the profligacy, venality, and cruelty of Valens (H. i 66, ii 56, iii 62).
: see Oth. 9, 2 and notes.
: see Oth. 11.

: Dio lxv 1 (Zon. xi 16), ὄντι δ' ἐν τῇ Γαλατίᾳ ὁ θάνατος ἠγγέλθη τοῦ Ὄθωνος. Vitellius was still on the road to Lugdunum when he heard the tidings; cf. Tac. H. ii 57, Interim Vitellius victoriae suae nescius ut ad integrum bellum reliquas Germanici exercitus vires trahebat. Pauci veterum militum in hibernis relicti, festinatis per Gallias dilectibus, ut remanentium legionum nomina supplerentur. Cura ripae (i.e. the left bank of the Rhine) Hordeonio Flacco permissa: ipse e Britannico exercitu delecta octo milia sibi adiunxit. Et paucorum dierum iter progressus prosperas apud Bedriacum res ac morte Othonis concidisse bellum accepit.
: see on Galb. 1.

: for their history and organisation see on Tit. 4, 2. Though disbanded by Vitellius they took service again to support Vespasian; cf. Tac. H. ii 67, Proximus Vitellio e praetoriis cohortibus metus erat. Separati primum, deinde addito honestae missionis lenimento, arma ad tribunos suos deferebant, donec motum a Vespasiano bellum crebresceret: tum resumpta militia robur Flavianarum partium fuere. Vitellius enrolled 16 new praetorian cohorts when Vespasian's forces were advancing (Tас. Н. ii 93).

: by reason of their desertion of Galba and their appointment of Otho as emperor without the authority of the senate and people. For pessimi exempli cf. Aug. 32, 1, pleraque pessimi exempli exstiterant: Plin. Ep. x 97, Sine auctore propositi libelli (i.e. anonymous accusations) in nullo crimine locum habere debent. Nam et pessimi exempli nec nostri saeculi est (i.e. "not in accordance with the spirit of our times''). The abl. is also used by Suetonius, Dom. 14, 4, utque domesticis persuaderet ne bono quidem exemplo audendam esse patroni neceт.

: see on Vesp. 8, 2. This power belonged to the emperor as head of the army (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 854). Suetonius says nothing of the praetorians having been granted the honesta missio which is mentioned by Tacitus (ii 67, quoted above); this would carry with it the bounty of 20,000 sesterces granted to time-expired praetorians (Dio lv 23).

: Tac. (l.c.), arma ad tribunos suos deferebant. Their standard-bearers (signiferi) also handed over their standards, and so Antonius Primus, the general of Vespasian, when he was exhorting his forces to a fresh attack on the Vitellians, said to the praetorians (who had taken service again with Vespasian): “illic (i.e. in the hands of the Vitellians) signa armaque vestra sunt'' (Tac. H. iii 24).

: "petitions"; see on Dom. 14, 4, Epaphroditum a libellis. Plutarch (Galb. 27) mentions the 120 petitions (βιβλία) presented to Otho by those who claimed to have taken part in the murders of Galba, Piso, Laco, and Vinius. With reference to the great number of these claimants Plut. neatly quotes the words of the poet Archilochus “ ἑπτὰ γὰρ νεκρῶν πεσόντων, οὓς ἐμάρψαμεν ποσίν, | χίλιοι φονῆες ἐσμέν.”

: very similar words are used by Tacitus, H. i 44: Plures quam centum viginti libellos praemium exposcentium ob aliquam notabilem illa die operam Vitellius postea invenit, omnesque conquiri et interfici iussit. For supplicium in the sense of "capital punishment'' see on c. 14, 1.
: cf. Galb. 14, 1, quanquam multa documenta egregii principis daret.
: sc. sua; cf. Tib. 59, 1, magis naturae obtemperans ("more in obedience to his natural instincts'').

div.p: § 2. ritu triumphantium vectus est: Tacitus (ii 59) says that it was Junius Blaesus, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, who first enabled Vitellius to assume regal splendour: Ipse (Vitellius) Arare flumine devehitur nullo principali paratu, sed vetere egestate conspicuus, donec Iunius Blaesus, Lugdunensis Galliae rector, genere illustri, largus animo et par opibus, circumdaret principi ministeria, comitaretur liberaliter.

p.note: : the Arar (Saone) and the Rhodanus (Rhone).

: cf. Calig. 43, iter ingressus est confecitque interdum adeo segniter delicateque (‘luxuriously") ut octophoro ("a litter with eight bearers'') veheretur: Eumen. Paneg. Constantin. Aug. 13, delicata fuit illa vectatio Principis otiosi: Cic. Att. ii 14, 1, delicatum convivium. Casaubon compares the navis thalamegus (= cubiculata), the royal barge fitted with staterooms, in which Cleopatra and Caesar sailed on the Nile (Iul. 52).

: Bentley's vario is approved by Ihm, but the text is defended by Claud. 46, ex omnium magistratuum genere, and by the many instances of similar transference (hypallage) of the epithet belonging to genus which are collected in Thes. Ling. Lat. vi 1906.
: cf. Curt. iv 4, 5, navigia conscendunt redimita coronis floribusque: Ov. Am. iii 11, 29, puppis redimita corona: Sil. Ital. Pun. xi 484, lauro redimita subibat | optatos puppis portus.
: see on Tit. 7, 1.
: see on Dom. 4. 5.

: cf. Tac. H. ii 62, epularum foeda et inexplebilis libido: ex urbe atque Italia inritamenta gulae gestabantur, strepentibus ab utroque mari itineribus; exhausti conviviorum apparatibus principes civitatum; vastabantur ipsae civitates; degenerabat a labore ac virtute miles adsuetudine voluptatum et contemptu ducis. See on Dom. 4, 1.

: Tac. c. 68, apud Vitellium omnia indisposita, temulenta, pervigiliis ac bacchanalibus quam disciplinae et castris propiora: c. 69, et vires (militum) luxu corrumpebantur contra veterem disciplinam et instituta maiorum. The outrages committed by the followers of Vitellius are denounced by Tac. in c. 56: Ceterum Italia gravius atque atrocius quam bello adflictabatur. Dispersi per municipia et colonias Vitelliani spoliare, rapere, vi et stupris polluere: in omne fas nefasque avidi aut venales non sacro, non profano abstinebant. Ipsique milites regionum gnari refertos agros, dites dominos in praedam, aut, si repugnatum foret, ad excidium destinabant, obnoxiis ducibus et prohibere non ausis. Cf. ib. 71, 87.

: in Ner. 26, 1, Suet. describes the petulantia of Nero who went about the streets like a footpad (grassator) at night: Petulantiam... exercuit,.. redeuntes a cena verberare ac repugnantes vulnerare cloacisque demergere assuerat, tabernas etiam effringere et expilare. Juvenal (iii 278 sqq.) gives a similar description of the wantonness of a drunken bully (ebrius ac petulans).
: cf. Aug. 67, 1, rem in iocum vertit: Liv. v 14, in religionem vertentes: Tac. H. i 86, in prodigium et omen vertebatur: Aristoph. Vesp. 1260, ἐς γέλων τὸ πρᾶγμ᾽ ἔτρεψας.
: see on Vesp. 3.
: see on Oth. 5, 2. Holland renders: "they paid as many as withstood them with whipping-cheer, blows, knocks, bloody wounds oftentimes, yea and otherwhiles with present death.”

div.p: § 3. campos adit: Tacitus (H. ii 70) gives a vivid account of the visit of Vitellius to Bedriacum: Inde Vitellius Cremonam flexit et spectato munere (gladiatorial show'') Caecinae insistere Bedriacensibus campis ac vestigia recentis victoriae lustrare oculis concupivit. Foedum atque atrox spectaculum intra quadragensimum pugnae diem: lacera corpora, trunci artus, putres virorum equorumque formae, infecta tabo humus, protritis arboribus ac frugibus dira vastitas, etc. Cf. Dio lxv 1, ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος δὲ εἶδεν ἐν Λουγδούνῳ μονομάχων (gladiatorum) ἀγῶνας καὶ ἐν Κρεμώνῃ· ὥσπερ οὐκ ἀρκοῦντος τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἐν ταῖς μάχαις ἀπολωλότων, καὶ τότε καὶ ἔτι ἀτάφων ἐρριμμένων, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐθεάσατο, διεξῆλθε γὰρ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ χωρίου ἐν ᾧ ἔκειντο ἐμπιμπλάμενος τῆς θέας, ὥσπερ τότε νικῶν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκέλευσέ σφας οὐδ᾽ ὡς ταφῆναι. For adit perf. cf. petit, Oth. 7, 1.

p.note: : for abhorrere c. acc. see on Galb. 4, 2. Vitellius displayed a callous insensibility to the awful spectacle; cf. Tac. (l.c.), erant quos varia sors rerum lacrimaeque et misericordia subiret; at non Vitellius flexit oculos nec tot milia (40,000, Dio lxiv 10) insepultorum civium exhorruit, laetus ultro et tam propinquae sortis ignarus instaurabat sacrum dis loci.

: Tacitus does not give this particular utterance of Vitellius at Bedriacum, but in describing the death of Blaesus (see c. 14, 2 infr.) he cites one of similar brutality: H. iii 39, Quin et audita est saevissima Vitellii vox, qua se (ipsa enim verba referam) pavisse oculos spectata inimici morte iactavit. ..

: this form of expression by which a comparative expresses a higher degree of a quality than a superlative is not uncommon in Latin; e.g. Cic. Off. iii 121, Tibi persuade esse te quidem mihi carissimum, sed multo fore cariorem, si talibus praeceptis laetabere: id. Fam. xiv 3, 2, Ego hoc miserior sum quam tu, quae es miserrima: id. Marcell. 33, Maximas tibi omnes gratias agimus, maiores etiam habemus: Liv. iii 72, ne pessimum facinus peiore exemplo admitterent: Apul. Met. x 12, servus nequissimus atque mulier nequior. Kühner-Stegmann (ii 481) give the title "elative" to the use of the superlative to denote merely a very high degree.
: Ernesti suggested at, G. Becker set (sed).
: see on Tit. 5, 3.

: the soldiers buried the remains of Otho in a simple tomb, with no splendid monument, and no boastful inscription; cf. Tac. H. ii 49, Othoni sepulchrum extructum est modicum et mansurum. Plutarch visited the tomb and thus describes it (Oth. 18): κρύψαντες δὲ τῇ γῇ τὰ λείψανα τοῦ ῎Οθωνος οὔτε μεγέθει σήματος οὔτ᾽ ἐπιγραφῆς ὄγκῳ ("pomp of epitaph ") τὸν τάφον ἐποίησαν ἐπίφθονον. Εἶδον δὲ ἐν Βριξίλλῳ γενόμενος καὶ μνῆμα μέτριον καὶ τὴν ἐπιγραφὴν οὕτως ἔχουσαν, εἰ μεταφρασθείη· “ Δαίμοσι Μάρκου Ὄθωνος.” (Δαίμοσι = Dis Manibus is a probable correction by Lobeck of Δήλωσει “for the pointing out of Marcus Otho." Hardy ad loc. says "It is difficult to see of what Latin formula Δηλώσει Μάρκου Όθωνος could be the translation. It could hardly be “Memoriae M. Othonis,” as δηλώσει would not be the natural rendering of this, and, besides, this form of dedication was not in use before the end of the 2nd century. See Wilm. 244.'")
: see on Vesp. 23, 4; the word, of course, is used derisively by Vitellius. pugionem

: swords and daggers were frequently dedicated to the gods in their temples: Caligula dedicated to Mars Ultor three swords of his would-be assassins (Calig. 24, 3); Nero dedicated to Jupiter Vindex the dagger of Scaevinus, who was involved in the conspiracy of Piso against Nero (Tac. A. xv 74); Caracalla dedicated the sword with which he slew his own brother (Dio lxxiii 4); the Arverni dedicated a dagger which they claimed to have captured from Julius Caesar in Gaul (Plut. Caes. 26).

: Cologne (Köln), where Vitellius had been first saluted as emperor (c. 8, 1). The original name of the town was "Oppidum Ubiorum" (Tac. A. i 36). The Ubii, a German tribe on the E. of the Rhine, were induced (c. 38 в.с.) by M. Vipsanius Agrippa to cross and settle on the left bank to avoid the attacks of the Chatti. Agrippina, grand-daughter of this Agrippa, daughter of Germanicus, and wife of Claudius, was born in this town and she persuaded Claudius to plant a colony of veterans there (51. A.D.); from that time the place was called after her "Colonia. Agrippinensis" (Tac. A. xii 27; see also Furneaux on Tac. Germ. 28).
: from the same shrine of Mars at Cologne had been taken the sword of Julius Caesar which was presented to Vitellius when he was acclaimed emperor; see c. 8, 1.

: from Cremona Vitellius went to Bononia (Tac. H. ii 71) which lies immediately at the foot of the Apennines; there was a pass across the Apennines traversed by the modern highroad from Bologna (Bononia) to Florence (Florentia), and Vitellius may have crossed by this pass and then proceeded by the Via Cassia to Rome; see Hofstee ad loc.

: see on Galb. 4, 3. This pervigilium of Vitellius was nominally a religious thanksgiving for his victory over Otho, but presumably it took the form of those all-night orgies (pervigilia ac bacchanalia) of which Tacitus speaks so contemptuously in H. ii 69 (quoted above on ‘nulla disciplina''). Caligula, according to Suet. Calig. 54, ordered a pervigilium for the sole purpose of taking advantage of the licence of the occasion to make an auspicious first appearance on the stage: Nec alia de causa videtur eo die, quo periit, pervigilium indixisse quam ut initium in scaenam prodeundi licentia temporis auspicaretur. Dessau (Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit ii 1, 338) thinks it probable that the pervigilium of Vitellius took place at the temple of Jupiter Appenninus, which was at the highest point of the pass by which the Via Flaminia crossed the Apennines.

: classicum primarily meant a signal given by the trumpet (classicum appellatur quod buccinatores per cornu dicunt, Veget. ii 22), and at times denoted the trumpet itself. As a signal the classicum seems to have been given by all the trumpeters together (e.g. as a signal for battle) and it was always given in the presence of the commander-in-chief (imperator) and by his orders. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 753.

: Tacitus is probably right in stating that Vitellius laid aside the paludamentum (see on Galb. 11) and assumed the toga praetexta before entering the city, to avoid entering it as a conqueror: H. ii 89, Ipse Vitellius a ponte Mulvio (2 miles N. of Rome) insigni equo, paludatus accinctusque senatum ac populum ante se agens, quo minus ut captam urbem ingrederetur, amicorum consilio deterritus, sumpta praetexta et composito agmine incessit. Alexander Severus on his accession made a similar concession to established usage by assuming the toga and entering the city on foot (Dio lxxiv 1). The theory of Heraeus (on Tac. l.c.) is that Vitellius wore military garb when entering by the Porta Flaminia (which was extra pomerium and therefore ad urbem), but donned the toga before passing through the Porta Carmentalis (?) into the city itself, and that Suetonius, prone to exaggerate, describes him as paludatus when entering the city. One of the coins in honour of his entry represents him as togatus, another as paludatus.

: the signa were the standards of the maniples (see on Galb. 12, 2); the vexilla here mentioned are probably the standards of the cavalry, as in Tac. H. ii 18, 43, and other passages where we find the two words joined.

: the form sagulatus is only found here; sagatus (Cic., etc.) occurs in Iul. 48. The sagum, or cloak, of the ordinary soldier was known as the sagum (sagulum) gregale (e.g. Liv. vii 34), more rarely as paludamentum (e.g. Liv. i 26); the cleak of the officers was also called sagum (Sall. Hist. ii frag. 21) but more frequently sagulum (e.g. Suet. Aug. 26, 1: Val. Max. iii 2, 21); it differed from that of the private by its brighter colour; the sagulum of the commander-in-chief, which was usually called paludamentum, was, as a rule, scarlet or purple (sometimes white): cf. Sil. Ital. Pun. iv 516, umeroque refulget | sanguinei patrium saguli decus: ib. xvii 526, umeris imponit honorem | fulgentis saguli: Auct. Bell. Afr. 57, cum Scipio sagulo purpureo uti solitus esset: Val. Max. i 6, 11, сит in proelium exeuntibus album aut purpureum (paludamentum) dari soleret.
: “staff” “suite"; see on Vesp. 4, 4.

: this is cited in the Thes. Ling. Lat. among the passages where commilito (“evanida vi praepositionis'") is nearly synonymous with miles gregarius; cf. Curt. vi 11, 2: Apul. Met. ix 39: Macer Dig. xlix, 16, 12. Julius Caesar addressed his soldiers by the blandius nomen of commilitones (Iul. 67). After the civil wars Augustus never did so, and he forbade the use of the term by his sons and stepsons who held military commands, regarding it as undignified and subversive of discipline (Aug. 25). But when the Julio-Claudian line ended with Nero, the emperors became much more dependent on the soldiers, and freely addressed them as commilitones; cf. Galb. 20, 1 and Tac. H. i 35 (quoted on Galb. 19, 2). See Hardy on Plin. Ep. x 19 and 20, where Pliny as governor of Bithynia asks Trajan whether he should use publici servi or milites to guard prisoners, and Trajan replies: ‘“Nihil opus est ad continendas custodias plures commilitones converti.”

div.p: §2. divino humanoque iure neglecto: cf. Tac. H. ii 91, adeo omnis humani divinique iuris expers pari libertorum, amicorum socordia, velut inter temulentos agebat: Dio lxv 2, αὐτὸς δὲ τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ προσκείμενος οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων οὔτε τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων οὔτε τῶν θείων ἐφρόντιζεν.

p.note: : July 18, the day on which in 390 B.C. the Romans suffered a disastrous defeat from the Gauls under Brennus at the Allia, a tributary of the Tiber, 11 miles N. of Rome. On the same day in 477 B.C. the 300 Fabii were annihilated at the Cremera (another tributary of the Tiber) by the Veientes. Cf. Tac. H. ii 91, Apud civitatem cuncta interpretantem funesti ominis loco acceptum est, quod maximum pontificatum adeptus Vitellius de caerimoniis publicis xv kalendas Augustas edixisset antiquitus infausto die Cremerensi Alliensique cladibus. The dies Alliensis became for ever a dies religiosus at Rome; cf. Liv. vi 1, De diebus religiosis agitari coeptum, diemque a.d. quintum decimum Kal. Sextiles, duplici clade insignem a posteriore clade Alliensem appellarunt insignemque religione rei ullius publice privatimque agendae fecerunt: Cic. Att. ix 5. ...
: see on Tit. 9, 1.

: Tac. H. iii 55, ipse festinare comitia, quibus consules in multos annos destinabat. For ordinavit see on Vesp. 23, 2. The naming of magistrates for several years in advance had been first done by the dictator Julius Caesar; Iul. 76, 3, Eadem licentia spreto patrio more magistratus in plures annos ordinavit. Though the senate nominally had the right of choice, the emperor under the Lex de imperio had the right of commendatio of his own candidates (candidati Caesaris) for a certain number of places (e.g. 2 out of 20 quaestors, 4 out of 12 praetors; see Furneaux, Tac. Ann. Introd. c. vi); these candidates: were elected as a matter of course. The emperor also claimed a wider right of nominatio to all vacant posts, and as those "nominated" by him were sure of the preference, the elections became a mere farce. Vitellius however at the elections in July 69 went through the pretence of speaking and canvassing for the candidates whom he had named as consules suffecti for the rest of that year (Tac. H. ii 71, 91).

: so he is described in an inscription at Rome (C.I.L. vi 929, Dessau 242): A. Vitellius L. f. imperator cos. perp.; on a fragmentary milestone in Sardinia there is an inscription (C.I.L. x 8016, Dessau 243) which Dessau restores as : [a] Turre xliii | [im]p. A. Vitellius c[os. perp]. A life consulship was decreed to Caligula, but he declined it (Dio lix 6); the senate also decreed continui consulatus to Nero (Tac. 4. xiii 41); Domitian was made consul for a period of ten years (Dio lxvii 4), and Tiberius for five years (Dio lviii 4).

: Tac. H. ii 95, Laetum foedissimo cuique apud bonos invidiae fuit, quod extructis in campo Martio aris inferias Neroni fecisset. Caesae publice victimae cremataeque; facem Augustales subdidere, quod sacerdotium Caesar Tiberius Iuliae genti sacravit: Dio 1xv 7, ὅτι μέντοι τὸν Νέρωνα μιμεῖσθαι ἤθελε καὶ ἐνήγισε (= inferias dedit) τε αὐτῷ, καὶ ὅτι τοσαῦτα ἐς τὰ δεῖπνα ἀνήλισκεν, οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι καὶ κατὰ ταῦτ᾽ ἔχαιρον, οἱ δὲ δὴ νοῦν· ἔχοντες ἤχθοντο: Eutrop. vii 18, 4, Hic cum Neroni similis esse vellet atque id adeo prae se ferret, ut etiam exequias Neronis, quae humiliter sepultae fuerant, honoraret. From the Campus Martius one could look up to the "Hill of Gardens" (Collis Hortulorum, Monte Pincio) and see the tomb of the Domitii where the ashes of Nero were placed; cf. Suet. Ner. 50, Reliquias gentili Domitiorum monimento condiderunt, quod prospicitur e campo Martio impositum colli Hortulorum. For the slavish devotion of Vitellius to Nero see on c. 4 supr.
: see on Dom. 4, 4. On citharoedi at Roman banquets see Friedlaender, Sitteng. ii¹º 175; Marquardt, Privatl.2 151. For Nero's performances as a citharoedus cf. c. 4, n.

: dominicus (sc. liber) or dominicum was apparently the name of a book containing Nero's compositions (or favourite pieces) which may have been published by himself. Hofstee proposed to read dominicis (sc. canticis). The adj. dominicus (from dominus "lord and master'') is used at times in reference to the emperors, e.g. Cod. Iust. vii 38, res ("property'") dominica, coloni dominici. For the title dominus applied to the emperor see on Dom. 13, 1. The variant Domitio (XN) is read in the early editions. Nero's original name was L. Domitius Ahenobarbus, but after his adoption by Claudius he was called Nero Claudius Caesar Drusus Germanicus, and the use of his earlier name in addressing him was regarded by him as an insult (Ner. 7 and 41: Tac. A. xii 41); Oudendorp rightly says that an admirer like Vitellius would not so speak of him.
: caneret, a poetical use found also in post-class. prose.

: for cantica see on Galb. 13. References to Nero's = performances are found in Suet. Ner. 21, Niobam se cantaturum .. pronuntiavit Tragoedias quoque cantavit personatus (“wearing a mask") heroum deorumque, item heroidum ac dearum, personis ("masks") effectis ad similitudinem oris sui et feminae, prout quamque diligeret. Inter cetera cantavit Canacen parturientem, Oresten matricidam, Oedipodem excaecatum, Herculem insanum: Dio lxi 20, ἐκιθαρῴδησέ τε῎Αττιν τινὰ ἢ Βάκχας: id. lxii 18, τὴν σκευὴν τὴν κιθαρῳδικὴν λαβὼν ἦσεν ἅλωσιν ᾿Ἰλίου (cf. Suet. Ner. 38, 2, halosin Ilii in illo suo scaenico habitu decantavit; these were probably lines from his own poem Τρωϊκά): Philostrat. vit. Apoll. iv 39: Tac. A. xv 33, xvi 4: Juv. viii 228 sq.

: to jump up (exultare) or rise to one's feet (assurgere) was a regular method of showing approval; e.g. Aug. 53, 1, сит universi exultantes comprobassent: Ner. 24, 1, inter exultationes succlamationesque populi: Plin. Ep. vii 24, exultabant, plaudebant, mirabantur: ix 23, omnes repente consurgerent laudarentque: vi 17, non labra diduxerunt, non moverunt manum, non denique adsurrexerunt, saltem lassitudine sedendi.

: these two classes are mentioned by Tacitus as among the crowd which flocked from the city to welcome Vitellius on his approach: H. ii 87, adgregabantur e plebe flagitiosa per obsequia Vitellio cogniti scurrae histriones aurigae, quibus ille amicitiarum dehonestamentis mire gaudebat: ib. 71, quantoque magis propinquabat, tanto corruptius iter inmixtis histrionibus et spadonum gregibus et cetero Neronianae aulae ingenio. For the interest of Vitellius in aurigae see c. 7, 1 and c. 4.

: within three months after the accession of Vitellius this infamous freedman had acquired a power at Rome which rivalled the sway exercised in Nero's reign by the freedmen such as Polyclitus and Patrobius: Тас. Н. ii 95, Nondum quartus a victoria mensis, et libertus Vitellii Asiaticus Polyclitos Patrobios et vetera odiorum nomina (“the hated names of earlier times") aequabat. Nemo in illa aula probitate aut industria certavit; unum ad potentiam iter, prodigis epulis et sumptu gula ganeaque satiare inexplebiles Vitellii libidines. Asiaticus paid a heavy penalty for this "mala potentia"; after the death of Vitellius, when Mucianus and the victorious Flavians entered the city, he was crucified as a slave, though Vitellius had made him an eques: H. iv 11, Asiaticus enim (is libertus) malam potentiam servili supplicio expiavit. In Sidon. Apollin. Εp. v 7 he is mentioned in a list of Rome's most notorious freedmen: Hi sunt, quorum comparationi digitum tollerent (i.e. "would acknowledge themselves inferior'") Narcissus, Asiaticus, Massa, Marcellus, Carus, Parthenius, Licinus, et Pallas. Plutarch (Galb. 20) inaccurately says that he was a freedman of Galba.
: Puteoli, mod. Pozzuoli, on the coast of Campania near Baiae and Naples.

: a mixture of vinegar and water (ὀξύκρατον), which was drunk by the lower classes, by slaves (e.g. Plaut. Mil. 836, alii [servorum] ebrii sunt, alii poscam potitant), and by soldiers (e.g. Spart. Hadr. 10, cibis etiam castrensibus libenter utens, hoc est larido, caseo, et posca).

: -que is here used nearly as equivalent to autem or sed; cf. Iul. 19, 1, is quoniam inferior gratia esset, pecuniaque polleret. This use is generally found after a negative, e.g. Cic. Tusc. i 29, 71, Socrates nec patronum quaesivit nec iudicibus supplex fuit, adhibuitque liberam contumaciam: Ov. Met. ii 811, quae neque dant flammas lenique vapore cremantur; less often after an affirmative, e.g. Sall. Cat. 3, 3, studio ad rempublicam latus sum ibique multa mihi advorsa fuere.
: this reading is found in the ed. Basil., 1533; the MSS. give coluit. Oudendorp proposed ex(s)olvit.
: = usus est ut delicato suo (see on Tit. 7, 2).

: this verb is always a deponent in Suetonius (as in Cic.) and is used either with the acc. (Aug. 72, 3; Tib. 50, 2; Ner. 34, 1; cf. Hor. C. iv 11, 27, Pegasus terrenum equitem gravatus) or with the infin. (Aug. 34, 2; so Cic., Caes., Liv.); this is the only place where it is used with ob.

: “journeying about to market-towns or fairs (fora)''; cf. Cic. Cluent. 40, pharmacopola circumforan(e)us “an itinerant quack": Apul. Met. ix 4, circumforaneum mendicabulum “a vagrant beggar." The termination -anus (not -aneus) is strongly attested here; for the variations in the MSS. of other authors see Thes. Ling. Lat.

: lanista (connected with lanius "butcher'") was the title of the trainer in the school (ludus) where gladiators were kept; cf. Juv. xi 8, scripturus leges et regia verba lanistae (see Mayor's note): Suet. Iul. 26, 3, Tirones neque in ludo neque per lanistas sed in domibus per equites Romanos erudiebat. The body of gladiators under a lanista was called a familia; Augustus during a scarcity of food at Rome expelled the lanistarum familiae (Aug. 42, 3). The lanistae not merely trained gladiators, they also bought, sold, and let them out for hire. Itinerant lanistae engaged in trafficking of this kind, and gave gladiatorial spectacles in country towns or supplied gladiators; cf. Tac. A. iv 62, where there is a description of a terrible disaster at Fidenae, in which 50,000 were killed or maimed, owing to the collapse of a badly constructed amphitheatre where a speculative freedman was giving a display of gladiators.
: sc. gladiatorii; cf. Tit. 8, 2.
: Africa; see cс. 5.

: April 19, 69 A.D.; see on Oth. 11, 2 and Vesp. 6, 3, principatus dies. Tacitus (H. ii 57) says that the honour was conferred on Asiaticus when Vitellius, on his march from Germany, heard of his victory at Bedriacum and the death of Otho.
: the sign of equestrian rank; see on Galb. 10, 3; 14, 2.
: for this use of super see on Tit. 8, 1.

: Tac. H. ii 57, Postulante exercitu, ut libertum suum Asiaticum equestri dignitate donaret, inhonestam adulationem compescuit. Dein mobilitate ingenii, quod palam abnuerat, inter secreta convivii largitur, honoravitque Asiaticum anulis, foedum mancipium ('slave'") et malis artibus ambitiosum.
: see on Dom. 19.

: cf. Dio lxv 2, τῇ τε τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ προσκείμενος : ib. c. 3, καὶ ἐγένετο ὁ χρόνος ὁ τῆς ἀρχῆς αὐτοῦ σύμπας οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ μέθαι τε καὶ κῶμοι: Eutrop. vii 18, Vitellius cum multo dedecore imperavit, et gravi saevitia notabilis, praecipue ingluvie et voracitate, quippe cum de die quarto vel quinto (i.e. 4 or 5 times a day) feratur epulatus: Oros. vii 8, 7, incredibili voracitatis appetitu: Sidon. Carm. iv 1.08, mihi (i.e. Rome) foeda Vitelli | intulit ingluvies ventrem, qui tempore parvo|regnans sero perit: Tac. H. ii 62, 95 (quoted on c. 10, 2 and c. 12): Lamprid. Heliogab. 24, cenas et Vitellii et Apicii vicit (Heliogabalus). saevitiae: Suetonius deals with this in the following chapter.

: for the formation of these adverbs see on plurifariam, c. 9. Dio (lxv 4) enumerates the feasts of Vitellius each day: ἀκράτισμα (iantaculum), ἄριστον (prandium), δεῖπνον (cena), and μεταδόρπια (comissationes).
: see on c. 7, 3. Though usually the iantaculum was a very frugal meal, Vitellius made it a luxurious repast.
: see on Dom. 21, prandebat ad satietatem.

: after the prandium, or lunch, a siesta (meridiatio) was taken; then came gymnastics or other exercises, followed by the bath, and dinner (cena) was usually taken about the 9th hour (3.45 p.m. in summer, 2.15 in winter). For a detailed account of the cena see Marquardt, Privatl.2 297 sqq. comissationes: see on Dom. 21. To eat anything during a comissatio, except as a relish to the wine, was most unusual.

: though Vitellius was able to stand this gluttony, his fellow-diners suffered badly from over-eating; cf. Dio lxv 2, ἀφ' οὗπερ (sc. τὸ ἐξεμεῖν) καὶ ἀνταρκεῖν ἠδύνατο· ἐπεὶ οἵγε συνδειπνοῦντες αὐτῷ πάντες κακῶς ἀπήλλασσον. Dio adds a good story about Vibius Crispus (Dom. 3, 1) who was ill from the effects for some days and not able to attend the banquets, and who wittily remarked "Had I not been ill, I would have been killed entirely” (εἰ μὴ ἐνενοσήκειν, πάντως ἂν ἀπολώλειν).

: cf. Dio, l.c., τὸ πλεῖστον καὶ τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῆς νυκτὸς ἐδαπάνα, ἀπλήστως τε ἐμφορούμενος (‘"filling himself”) καὶ συνεχῶς πάντα ἐξεμῶν, ὡς μόνῃ τῇ παρόδῳ τῶν σιτίων τρέφεσθαι. Vomiting, as a remedy for over-eating, was not confined to mere gluttons like Vitellius; it was commonly resorted to by the wealthier classes at Rome, and the utility of it is recognised, and its use defined, by medical writers, e.g. Celsus (i 3). The emperor Claudius was relieved in this way; Claud. 33, Nec temere umquam triclinio abscessit nisi distentus ac madens, et ut statim supino ac per somnum hianti pinna in os induceretur ad exonerandum stomachum. Martial refers to the practice (iii 82, 9; vii 67, 10; etc.); Seneca (ad Helv. 10, 3) denounces it: vomunt ut edant, edunt ut vomant, et epulas quas toto orbe conquirunt, nec concoquere ("digest'") dignantur. See Marquardt, op. cit. 330.

: cf. Ner. 27, 3, indicebat familiaribus cenas (“he invited himself to dinner at his friends' houses"). Dio (lxv 4) says that the providing of feasts for Vitellius was a heavy burden on his hosts, but that the wealthy vied in their eagerness to entertain him. Elagabalus had each course of a banquet served at the house of a different friend: Lamprid. Heliogab. 30, Celebravit item tale convivium, ut apud amicos singulos singuli missus appararentur, et cum alter maneret in Capitolio, alter in Palatio, alter super Aggerem, alter in Caelio, alter trans Tiberim, et ut quisque mansisset, tamen per ordinem in eorum domibus singula fercula ederentur, ireturque ad omnium domos: sic unum convivium vix acto die finitum est.
: Ursinus would read minoris, but cf. Ner. 30, 3, numquam minus mille carrucis fecisse iter traditur. Such constructions are common in the Latin of all periods (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 471).

: about £3,400. In Ner. 27, 3 Suetonius tells us that one of Nero's friends, to whose house Nero had invited himself for dinner, expended 4,000,000 sesterces on a cena mitellita, and another expended considerably more on a cena rosaria. Dio says that Vitellius in his brief reign spent 900 million sesterces on dinners, and that on one dinner he expended 4 million sesterces; cf. Tac. H. ii 95, noviens milliens sestertium paucissimis mensibus intervertisse ("squandered'') creditur: iii 36. Gibbon (Decline and Fall of the Rom. Emp., c. 3) stigmatizes "the beastly Vitellius, who consumed in mere eating at least six millions of our money in about seven months, and whose vices it is not easy to express with dignity or even decency.”

div.p: § 2. famosissima: cf. Eutrop. vii 18, notissima certe cena memoriae mandata est, quam ei Vitellius frater exhibuit, in qua super ceteros sumptus duo milia piscium, septem avium adposita traduntur. Suetonius nearly invariably uses famosus in a bad sense ("infamous" "notorious”), but in Calig. 19, 2, we find curriculo biiugi famosorum (= celebrium) equorum.

p.note: : for this pleonastic addition cf. Dom. 12, 2, praeter ceteros acerbissime: Galb. 9, 1, multo praeter ceteras altiorem crucem.

: it was customary to give a dinner to a friend or relative who had arrived safely from a journey (Gr. δεῖπνον ὑποδεκτικόν); cf. Plaut. Bacch. 534, Salvos quom peregre advenis | cena detur: id. Stich. 512, Et magis par fuerat me vobis dare cenam advenientibus. The phrase “adventicia (cena)" is used metaph. in Petron. Satyr. 91, quoties theatrum, ut recitarem aliquid, intravi, hac me adventicia (sc. lapidibus) excipere frequentia solet. Martial (xii praef.) uses “adventoria (cena)" of a book of epigrams which he has provided to entertain a friend on his arrival. The ante-penult. is long in adjectives in -icius formed from participles; see Duff on Juv. iii 265.
: Lucius Vitellius; see c. 3, 1; 5, 1.

: cf. Plaut. Most. 730, Vino et victu, piscatu probo electili | vitam colitis. The fish most highly esteemed at Rome were the acipenser (sturgeon), aurata (gilt-bream), lupus (pike), scarus (wrasse ?), mullus (mullet), murena (lamprey), and rhombus (turbot). See Marquardt, op. cit. 432 sqq.

: these might include the lagopus (white grouse), scolopax (snipe), attagen (hazel-hen), turdus (fieldfare), perdix (partridge), miliaria (ortolan), ficedula (beccafico), coturnix (quail), pavo (peacock), Africa or Numidica avis (guinea-fowl), phasianus or tetrao (pheasant), grus (crane), ciconia (stork), phoenicopterus (flamingo). patina: a deep earthenware dish (like the Gr. τρύβλιον) used for cooking (especially fish, also ragoûts, etc., cf. Plaut. Asin. 180 where patinarius "stewed" is opposed to assus "roast'"), and also for serving food (cf. Plaut. Pseud. 840, Hor. Sat. ii 8, 43, Affertur squillas inter murena natantes | in patina porrecta). Costly patinae for use at table were sometimes made of silver. Aesopus, the tragic actor, had a patina (of pottery) worth 100,000 sesterces (Plin. N.H. xxxv 163). Pliny (l.c.) says that the patina of Vitellius cost 1,000,000 sesterces (£8,500) and that a special oven had to be built for the making of it: At, Hercules, Vitellius in principatu suo decies sestertium condidit patinam, cui faciendae fornax in campis exaedificata erat, quoniam eo pervenit luxuriae ut etiam fictilia pluris constent quam murrina (‘‘myrrhine vases''). Propter hanc Mucianus (Vespasian's general, see Vesp. 6, 4) altero consulatu suo in conquestione exprobravit patinarum paludes ("dishes as broad as the Pomptine marsh'') Vitellii memoriae, non illa foediore, cuius veneno Asprenati reo Cassius Severus (see Vitell. 2, 1) accusator obiciebat interisse convivas cxxx. (lxv 3) differs in saying that the patina of Vitellius was made of silver, being too large for pottery, and adds that it was afterwards melted down by Hadrian: ἐπειδὴ ἀδύνατον ἦν κεραμεᾶν τηλικαύτην γενέσθαι, ἀργύρου τε ἐποιήθη, καὶ ἔμεινε πολὺν χρόνον, ὥσπερ τι ἀνάθημα (res deis consecrata), μέχρις οὗ ῾Αδριανὸς αὐτὴν ἰδὼν συνεχώνευσεν. Dio clipeum Minervae πολιούχου: the reference, most probably, is to the colossal bronze statue of Athena Promachos by Pheidias on the Acropolis at Athens. It was 50-60 ft. high, and represented the goddess holding up her spear and shield in the attitude of battle; the shield is said to have been engraved at a later period by Mys. Some think that the statue referred to is the chryselephantine (gold and ivory) statue of Athena in the Parthenon, the greatest of Pheidias' works at Athens. It was 40 ft. high and represented the goddess with a spear in her left hand and an image (4 cubits high) of Victory in her right. On the inner side of her shield, which rested on the ground beside her, was embossed the battle of gods and giants, and on the outer side the battle of the Amazons and Athenians. πολιούχου was restored by Stephanus for τονδυχου of the MSS. The title πολιοῦχος “protectress of the city" was often applied to Athena, e.g. Aristoph. Eq. 581, Nub. 602, Αυ. 827; so Παλλάς πολιάοχος, Pind. 0. 5, 24, etc. Boissevain thinks that Vitellius was playing on the two words πολιοῦχος and πολυοῦχος ("holding much'').

: it is uncertain what particular fish the scarus was; it has been identified with the wrasse ("parrot-wrasse, Butler and Owen on Apul. Apol. 39). Pliny (N.H. ix 62) describes it as the most highly prized of fish, brought originally from the Carpathian sea (between Rhodes and Crete) by Optatus, praefectus classis under Tiberius, and planted in the sea between Ostia and Campania, where it was preserved for the first five years. Ennius in his Hedyphagetica (cited in Apul. Apol. 39) calls it "cerebrum Iovis" (a proverbial expression with the Persians for a rare delicacy): Quid scarŭ(m) praeterii cerebrum Iovi' paene supremi? See also Athenaeus vii 113; Hor. Epod. 2, 50; id. Sat. ii 2, 22; Petron. Satyr. 119; Mart. xiii 84.

: the fem. form is used also in Plin. N.H. instead of the more usual phasianus. According to tradition the pheasant was introduced from the Phasis in Colchis by the Argonauts; cf. Mart. xiii 72, Argoa primum sum transportata carina: | ante mihi notum nil nisi Phasis erat: Petron. Satyr. 79, iam Phasidos unda | orbata est avibus. Seneca (ad Helv. 10) denounces those who imported them to Rome: Dii istos deaeque perdant, quorum luxuria tam invidiosi imperii fines transcendit. Phasin capi volunt, quod ambitiosam popinam instruat. Ultra

: the peacock was said to have been brought from Asia to Samos and thence to Greece and Italy. The orator Hortensius, Cicero's rival, first had it served at a banquet in Rome to celebrate his entry to the college of augurs (Plin. N.H. x 45). It became a regular dish at all sumptuous entertainments; cf. Varr. R.R. iii 6; Hor. Sat. ii 2, 23; Juv. i 143; etc. among the contents of ἐγκεφάλους (cerebella) καὶ "redcerebella: mentioned also by Dio (lxv 3) the mighty patina of Vitellius: γλώττας τε καὶ ἥπατα (iocinera) καὶ ἰχθύων καὶ ὀρνίθων τινῶν ἐμβαλών. The dimin. cerebellum was properly only used of the brains of animals other than man. The brains of various birds were esteemed a dainty; cf. Lamprid. Heliogab. 20, exhibuit magides (“dishes'') extis mullorum refertas et cerebellis phoenicopterum ... et cerebellis turdorum: ib. 30, sescentorum struthionum ("ostriches") capita una cena multis mensis exhibuit ad edenda cerebella.

: the flamingo (Gr. φοινικόπτερος winged'') was a native of the banks of the Nile (Heliod. Aethiop. vi 268); the delicate flavour of its tongue was discovered by the notorious gourmet Apicius (fl. 25 A.D.): Plin. N.H. x 133, Phoenicopteri linguam praecipui saporis esse Apicius docuit nepotum omnium altissimus gurges; cf. Mart. xiii 71: Sen. Ep. 110, non magnam rem facis, quod non desideras linguas phoenicopterorum et alia portenta luxuriae iam tota animalia fastidientis et certa membra ex singulis eligentis. In the temple which Caligula erected to himself as a god flamingoes were among the victims offered (Calig. 22). Siculo

: lampreys were brought from the Straits of Messina (fretum Siculum) to the fish ponds (piscinae) at Rome: Macrob. Sat. iii 15, 7, arcessebantur murenae ad piscinas nostrae urbis ab usque freto illic enim optimae a prodigis esse creduntur; cf. Juv. v 99, Virroni murena datur, quae maxima venit | gurgite de Siculo. A family of the gens Licinia was given the name "Murena" from the fish: Colum. viii 16, 5, Iam enim celebres erant deliciae popinales cum ad mare deferrentur vivaria, quorum studiosissimi, velut ante devictarum gentium Numantinus et Isauricus, ita Sergius Aurata (the fish "aurata" was the gilt-bream) et Licinius Murena captorum piscium laetabantur vocabulis.

: Gr. γαλακτίδες, the smaller entrails, "tender small guts" (Holland). Priscian says that the sing. is haec lactis. Lampridius (Heliogab. 23) mentions among the extravagant eccentricities of Elagabalus ““murenarum lactibus et luporum (“pikes'') in locis mediterraneis rusticos pavit." The lactes of both men and beasts are often mentioned, especially by the comic writers and satirists, e.g. Titin. (90, Ribb.): Pompon. (61, • Ribb.): Plaut. Curcul. 319, Pseud. 320: Persius 2, 30, Qua tu mercede deorum | emeris auriculas? pulmone et lactibus unctis? ("a dishful of lungs and greasy chitterlings," Conington).

: the ransacking of sea and land to provide dainties for Vitellius is described in Dio lxv 3: πάντα τε γὰρ τὰ τιμιώτατα καὶ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ ὠκεανοῦ, ἵνα μηδὲν εἴπω πλέον, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς καὶ ἐκ τῆς θαλάσσης συνήγετο, καὶ πολυτελῶς οὕτως ἐσκευάζετο ὥστε Οὐιτελλιανὰ καὶ νῦν ἐξ ἐκείνου καὶ πέμματα καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ βρώματα ὀνομάζεσθαι. Parthia and the fretum Hispanicum are used here for the extreme E. and W., usually denoted by India and Spain (e.g. Sen. N.Q. i pr. 13, ab ultimis litoribus Hispaniae usque ad Indos). The genuineness of the reading Parthia has been suspected, and various conjectures have been made, such as Carpathio (R has pathia), Carteia, Carpetano. freto Hispanico: the Straits of Gibraltar, also called fretum Gaditanum, fretum Herculeum, fretum Tartessium, fretum Iberum, etc.

: in the Roman fleet the title navarchus (ναύαρχος) seems to have been applied strictly to the captain of a larger ship (quadrireme, quinquireme, etc.), trierarchus denoting the captain of a smaller; but at times we find navarchus used for a commander of a squadron. Cf. Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 513; Mommsen on C.I.L. x 3340; Furneaux-Pelham on Tac. A. xv 51. For an example of the use of the Roman fleet to import luxuries see on “scarorum” above.

div.p: § 3. non.. modo sed quoque: when quoque is thus used in the second clause in place of the regular etiam, it marks a mere addition and not an intensification or climax. See Kühner-Stegmann, ii 59, where numerous instances from Cic. and Liv. are given.

p.note: : see on c. 7, 1.

: the sing. is only found in poetry and post-Aug. prose. Both viscus and viscera are used at times for “flesh"; cf. Serv. on Aen. vi 253 (et solida imponunt taurorum viscera flammis): Non exta dicit, sed carnes; nam viscera sunt quidquid inter ossa et cutem est; unde etiam visceratio dicitur convivium de carnibus factum. See Munro on Lucr. i 837.

: "bits of the sacrificial cakes (liba)." Servius, commenting on adorea liba in Aen. vii 109, says: Ador proprie est genus farris, Liba autem sunt placentae de farre, melle, et oleo, sacris aptae. These cakes were either simply placed on the altar during the religious ceremony or burnt in the fire. The reading is very uncertain; the principal MSS. have merely farris, the others farra and farris frusta (-tra). Preud 'homme reads farris frusta; Ihm, keeping farris, marks paene as corrupt. Various corrections have been proposed: farris grana (Oudendorp); farcimina (Bentley); farris panes (G. Becker, regarding the following paene as a corruption of panes); liba farris (Roth). Of these conjectures Becker's is the most attractive, though panem (cf. Catull. 59, quoted below) seems preferable to panes and more likely to be corrupted into paепе.

: cf. Ter. Eunuch, 491, e flamma petere cibum (of stealing food placed on the funeral pyre as an offering to the di inferi): Catull. 59, uxor Meneni, saepe quam in sepulcretis | vidistis ipso rapere de rogo cenam, | cum devolutum ex igne prosequens panem | ab semiraso tunderetur ustore. The Gr. βωμολόχος was derived from βωμός "altar" and 2 A λοχάω “to lie in wait," and originally meant one who hung about the altars to steal some of the meat offered. The emperor Claudius, who rivalled Vitellius in gluttony (‘‘cibi vinique quocumque et tempore et loco appetentissimus,” Claud. 33), on one occasion was sitting in court when his nostrils caught the savour of a meal being made ready for the Salii in the temple of Mars close by; he left the tribunal and went and joined the priests at table.
: cf. Mart. i 41, 9, quod fumantia qui tomacla raucus | circumfert tepidis cocus popinis: Sid. Ep. viii 11.

: cf. Tib. 34, 1, Et ut parsimoniam publicam exemplo quoque iuvaret, sollemnibus ipse cenis pridiana saepe ac semesa obsonia apposuit; Calig. 58, 1, marcente adhuc stomacho pridiani cibi onere. The adj. pridianus (= ἕωλος, hesternus) is post-Aug.; cf. Apul. Apol. 6: id. Met. vii 20, xi 7. For other compounds with semi- used by Suetonius see on seminudus c. 17, 1. cuiuscumque: =

div.p: cuiusvis, cuiuslibet; see on Galb. 4, 3.

p.note: : Bremi rightly regards this as one of the places where Suetonius couples two expressions which denote practically the same thing; cf. Iul. 49, 2, ad cyathum et vinum stetisse: ib. 68, 1, gratuitam et sine frumento stipendioque operam: Aug. 17, 4, venenum et virus: Ner. 15, 2, dilationis ac morae: Galb. 9, 1, desidiam segnitiamque: Calig. 11, animadversionibus poenisque. Suetonius (like Tacitus, see Gerber and Greef Lex. Tac.) very often uses supplicium in the sense of supplicium capitale or capitis, e.g. a few lines later we find quendam supplicio traditum; cf. c. 10, 1. supplicium can, of course, be used of other punishments especially torture; cf. Cic. Imp. Pomp. 5, 11, aliquem vinculis ac verberibus atque omni supplicio excruciatum necare. A passage which resembles ours is Tib. 62, 1, neque tormentis neque supplicio cuiusquam pepercit, but there supplicium denotes the execution which followed the torture. ..
: cf. Tib. 25, 3, celerem successionem vel certe societatem principatus opperiri; Oth. 8, 1, and Tit. 9, 3, consors imperii.
: this post-class. compound is found also in Sen. Ep. 118, 8, quod invitat ad se et adlicefacit. It is a quite unnecessary addition to the class. adlicere (Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. i 135).

: in the same way as the poison of Locusta was administered to Britannicus: Tac. A. xiii 16, frigida in aqua adfunditur venenum, quod ita cunctos eius artus pervasit, ut vox pariter et spiritus raperentur; cf. Justin xii 14, 9 (the poisoning of Alexander the Great), Philippus et Iollas praegustare ac temperare potum regis soliti, in aqua frigida venenum habuerunt, quam praegustatae iam potioni supermiserunt.

div.p: §2. faeneratorum: Vitellius must often have had to resort to these usurers to try to meet his multitude of creditors (see c. 7, 2). For Vespasian's restriction on faeneratores see Vesp. 11.

p.note: : these stipulatores were those who had given loans to Vitellius by the process of stipulatio or legally enforceable verbal contract (often registered for reference in writing), which took the form of the question and answer Spondesne? Spondeo. The questioner was called stipulator or reus stipulandi ("person concerned with stipulating'"), the answerer usually promissor or reus promittendi. In cases of default the money was recoverable by the summary procedure of a condictio certae creditae pecuniae (the condictio being 30 days' notice). The repayment of the capital, and the payment of interest required two distinct stipulationes (Roby, Rom. Private Law ii 11 sqq., 71 sqq.). publicanorum: like other vectigalia, the portoria here mentioned were levied by the publicani, a title which strictly denoted those who farmed the taxes from the State (qui publica vectigalia conducta habent), but was also used (like portitores) of the actual tax-collectors, slaves or freedmen (qui operas dabant publicanis).

: a "toll" or transit charge levied on merchandise carried through a country or over a bridge, also on vehicles and on persons; cf. Sen. Const. Sap. 14, Quid ergo? Sapiens non accedet ad fores, quas durus ianitor obsidet? Ille vero, si res necessaria vocabit, experietur, et illum, quisquis erit, tanquam canem acrem, obiecto cibo leniet, nec indignabitur aliquid impendere, ut limen transeat, cogitans et in pontibus quibusdam pro transitu dari: Labeo Dig. xix 2, 60, cum (vehiculum) pontem transiret, redemptor eius pontis portorium ab eo exigebat, etc.: Ulp. Dig. xxiv 1, 21, si quis pro uxore sua vectigal, quod in itinere praestari solet, solvisset. Suetonius also uses portoria in its other sense of duties paid on foreign imports into a country: Iul. 43, 1, (Caesar) peregrinarum mercium portoria instituit. See further on Vesp. 1, 2, publicum quadragesimae in Asia egit.

: Caes. B.G. i 16 and Cic. dom. 14 are the only exx. in class. prose of flagitare with two accusatives, except where the acc. of the thing is a neut. pron. (Kühner-Stegmann, i 300). See on “orabat,” Vesp. 16, 3.

: it is generally assumed that this was Junius Blaesus, the governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, who had been so lavishly generous to Vitellius on his march to Rome (see on c. 10, 2). The poisoning of Blaesus by Vitellius is described in Tac. H. iii 39, Trepidanti (Vitellio) inter scelus metumque, ne dilata Blaesi mors maturam perniciem, palam iussa atrocem invidiam ferret placuit veneno grassari. Addidit facinori fidem nobili (= notabili) gaudio, Blaesum videndo. Quin et audita est saevissima Vitellii vox, qua se (ipsa enim verba referam) pavisse oculos spectata inimici morte iactavit. The only point, however, in common between the stories of Tacitus and Suetonius is the remark of Vitellius, and more probably the stories relate to two different acts of tyranny.
: see on Dom. 23, 1.

: cf. Cic. Verr. v 65, cum eius cruciatu atque supplicio pascere oculos animumque exsaturare vellent: id. Phil. xi 3, 8, in eius corpore lacerando atque vexando, cum animum satiare non posset, oculos paverit suos. Contrast "parcere oculis," Dom. 11, 3. 2A2

div.p: §3. heres meus es: for the custom of naming the emperor as heir see on Dom. 9, 2.

p.note: : see on c. 7, 1.
: Domitian behaved in an equally tyrannical manner in the amphitheatre (Dom. 10, 1). =

: spe novarum rerum (mutationis imperii). The plur. novae spes is used in the same way in Tac. A. xiv 58, xvi 23; cf. A. v 4, audiri iam et legi novas ("revolutionary'') contiones, nova patrum consulta.
: this is the reading of X; obstinatus (M); obstinatosque (G). •

div.p: § 4. vernaculis: "scurrilous jesters"; cf. Mart. x 3, 1, vernaculorum dicta, where they are coupled with circulatores “glib cheap-jacks," as also in Sen. Ben. vi 11. The vernae, or home-born slaves, were allowed unusual licence by their masters and encouraged in pert insolence; cf. Hor. Sat. ii 6, 66: Sen. Prov. 1, 6, cogita nos delectari vernularum licentia, horum ali audaciam: Tac. H. ii 88, vernacula utebantur urbanitate. The vernaculi perhaps inspired the parody of Vitellius' proclamation which is mentioned here. A similar mock proclamation ridiculing an enactment of Julius Caesar is quoted below (see note on "bonum factum"), and in Iul. 20, 2, Suetonius describes how, when Julius Caesar utterly ignored Bibulus his colleague in the consulship, the wits (urbani) would sign and seal documents as "Done in the consulship of Julius and Caesar'' (Iulio et Caesare consulibus actum), and also circulated the verses: Non Bibulo quiddam nuper sed Caesare factum est; | nam Bibulo fieri consule nil memini. The reading in our passage has been much disputed. If a change were necessary, the simplest proposal is that of Sabellicus to omit et and read vernaculis mathematicis "saucy astrologers." Scaliger suggested veraculis or vericulis; Turnebus divinaculis; Madvig genethliacis, i.e. those who calculated nativities. The text, however, is probably sound. Suetonius was thinking of the contrast between Vitellius and Nero, who bore with remarkable patience the gibes or lampoons (dicta aut carmina) which were posted or circulated (proscripta aut vulgata) about him; see Ner. 39, where Suetonius gives specimens of these and adds: sed neque auctores requisiit et quosdam per indicem delatos ad senatum adfici graviore poena prohibuit.

p.note: : astrologi were called mathematici from the elaborate mathematical calculations which they employed in casting a horoscope (“genitura,” Tit. 9, 2). Tacitus (H. i 22) describes the mathematici as “genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax, quod in civitate nostra et vetabitur semper et retinebitur." As early as 139 B.C. astrologers were expelled from Rome and Italy by a praetor's edict (Val. Max. i 3, 3). In 33 B.c. Agrippa drove them from the city (Dio xlix 43). They were banished from Italy, either by senatorial decree or imperial edict, under Tiberius in 16 A.D. (Suet. Tib. 36, Tac. A. ii 32); under Claudius in 52 A.D. (Tac. A. xii 52); and now again under Vitellius in 69 A.D. Within a few months they were back, and Vespasian expelled them in 70 A.D., though he himself made use of the masters of the craft, and even allowed the people of Ephesus to celebrate a festival in honour of an astrologer (Dio lxvi 9).

: cf. Dom. 12, 2, ad fiscum deferebantur: ib. 15, 3, hunc delatum. Post-Aug. writers use “deferre aliquem'' (= accusare); Cicero has "deferre nomen alicuius,” e.g. Rosc. Am. 10, 28, ut nomen huius de parricidio deferrent. Suetonius also uses "deferre nomen,” Iul. 30, 3, delaturum se nomen eius. See note on "delatores,” Tit. 8. 5.
: see on Galb. 14, 3. •
: where quod is used by Suetonius with expressions of praising, blaming, accusing, grieving, etc., it is always followed by the subjunctive except here and in Tit. 10, 1, Ner. 6, 2.

: Tacitus mentions this expulsion of the astrologers (H. ii 62, pulsi Italia mathematici), but it is not clear from his account whether the edict ordering it was sent on in advance to Rome from Gaul by Vitellius, like the edict concerning his titles (c. 8, 2). Dio, lxv 1, says that Vitellius was already in the city when he published it: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐν τῇ ῾Ρώμῃ ἐγένετο .. πρόγραμμα ἔθετο (edictum proposuit), δι' οὗ τοὺς ἀστρολόγους ἐξήλασε, προειπών σφισιν ἐντὸς τῆσδε τῆς ἡμέρας (ῥητήν τινα τάξας) ἐξ ἁπάσης τῆς Ἰταλίας χωρῆσαι. ..
: for this constr. see on "iussit ponerent," Vesp. 23, 3.

: another name for the mathematici or astrologers; cf. Gell. i 9, 6, vulgus autem, quos gentilicio vocabulo Chaldaeos dicere oportet, mathematicos dicit: Cic. Div. i 1, Principio Assyrii, propter planitiem magnitudinemque regionum quas incolebant, cum caelum ex omni parte patens atque apertum intuerentur, traiectiones motusque stellarum observaverunt; quibus notatis, quid cuique significaretur, memoriae prodiderunt. Qua in ratione Chaldaei, non ex artis, sed ex gentis, vocabulo nominati, diuturna observatione siderum, scientiam putantur effecisse, ut praedici posset, quid cuique eventurum, et quo quisque fato natus esset. Berosus, a Babylonian priest (c. 340-270 в.с.), was the first Chaldaean who practised astrology in Greece (Vitruv. ix 7), whence it spread to Italy. The calculations of the Chaldaean astrologers are referred to as “Babylonii numeri’” in Hor. C. i 11, 3. See also Mayor on Juv. x 94, xiv 248, Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 91 sqq.
: edicere, the reading of Ursinus, may be correct. ..

: a formula prefixed “ominis causa" (cf. the Gr. τύχῃ ἀγαθῇ) to the praetor's edict; commonly represented by the abbreviation B.F., e.g. Edict. praet. de camp. Esquil. (C.I.L. vi 31614), B.F., nei quis intra terminos ustrinam fecisse velit. Cf. Suet. Iul. 80 (describing a placard posted up in derision of Caesar's admission of Gauls to the senate): Peregrinis in senatum adlectis libellus propositus est: “Bonum factum: ne quis senatori novo curiam (the senate-house) monstrare velit'': Tertull. Pudic. 1, O edictum turpe, cui adscribi non poterit “Bonum factum": Plaut. Poen. 16, bonum factum esse, edicta ut servetis mea: Aur. Vict. Vir. ill. 49, 16. Similar formulae "bene precandi et auspicandi aliquid” are "Quod felix, seu bonum, faustumque sit reipublicae,” and “Quod bene vertat (vortat).”
: for this title of Vitellius see c. 8, 2.

: in the version of the story in Dio lxv 1 the Kalends of Oct. are not mentioned, but we are told that the astrologers in reply published a proclamation that Vitellius should depart this life before the end of the very day on which he actually died (Dec. 18): καὶ αὐτῷ ἐκεῖνοι νυκτὸς ἀντιπροθέντες γράμματα, ἀντιπαρήγγειλαν ἀπαλλαγῆναι ἐκ τοῦ βίου ἐντὸς τῆς ἡμέρας, ἐν ᾗ ἐτελεύτησε. καὶ οἱ μὲν οὕτως ἀκριβῶς τὸ γενησόμενον προέγνωσαν. This version reflects much greater credit on the prophetic powers of the astrologers.

: usquam here means "anywhere in the land of the living"; “nusquam esse" was used (especially in poetry) for "to be no more," e.g. Hor. S. ii 5, 102, Ergo nunc Dama sodalis | nusquam est? : Prop. iii 13, 58, Nusquam est delapsis Amphiaraus equis.

div.p: § 5. suspectus in: for this constr. cf. Suet. Gramm. 16, suspectus in filia patroni (sc. stupri): Tac. H. i 13, suspectus in Popраса.

p.note: : Tacitus uses tamquam with suspectus, e.g. H. iii 35, suspecta Germania, tamquam in auxiliumi Vitellii accingeretur. See also on Tit. 5, 3, suspicio, quasi temptasset. 4

: Sextilia (c. 3, 1). Tacitus does not mention any such scandal, when he describes her death: H. iii 67, Erat illi (Vitellio) et fessa aetate parens; quae tamen paucis ante diebus opportuna morte excidium domus praevenit, nihil principatu filii adsecuta nisi luctum et bonam famam.

: for the Chatti, a German tribe, see on Dom. 6, 1. The MSS. here have the usual variations in the spelling of the name: Chattha (M has this with an erasure point under the first h), Catha, Cata (cf. Pauly-Wissowa s.v.). Preud 'homme reads Cattha. In Prosop. Imp. Rom. (i 323) Klebs treats Cattha as the name of the prophetess, which is probably an oversight.
