The veneration paid to prophetesses by the Germans is described in Tac. Germ. 8: Inesse (sc. feminis) quin etiam sanctum aliquid et providum putant, nec aut consilia earum aspernantur aut responsa neglegunt. Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Velaedam diu apud plerosque numinis loco habitam; sed et olim \Albrunam et complures alias venerati sunt, non adulatione nec tamquam facerent deas. Velaeda (of the tribe of the Bructeri) by her prophecies had fomented the revolt of Civilis (Tac. H. iv 61, etc.); she was brought as a prisoner to Rome, probably under Vespasian, and she was succeeded by another prophetess, Ganna, in the reign of Domitian (Dio lxvii 5). Strabo (vii 2, 293) gives an account of the προμάντεις ἱέρειαι of the Cimbri in Northern Germany.
: see on Tit. 7, 2.

: = tum demum (Germ. so nur = dann nur, so erst = dann erst), used by post-Aug. writers, especially in a conditional proposition; cf. Claud. 25, 3, Seleuco regi amicitiam et societatem ita demum pollicens, immunes praestitisset: Plin. Ep. iii 9, 11, tam numerosum agmen reorum ita demum videbamus posse superari, si per singulos carperetur (Hand Tursell. ii 255). See also on "demum,” Oth. 6, 3. si

div.p: Vitellius had been first

p.note: : i.e. August, 69 A.D. saluted as emperor on Jan. 3; see c. 8, 1. The legions in Egypt took the oath of fealty to Vespasian on July 1; those in Judaea, either on July 3 (Тас. Н. ii 79) or July 11 (Suet. Vesp. 6, 3); those in Syria, before July 15 (Tac. ii 81); the armies in Moesia, Dalmatia, and Pannonia then joined his side, perhaps in August, as Suetonius says here (Tacitus, ii 85 sq., does not fix the exact time). The narrative of Suetonius is at least misleading, for his words give the impression that the armies in Moesia and Pannonia were the first to revolt from Vitellius, and that the armies in Judaea and Syria also revolted in the eighth month; whereas they revolted, according to his own showing (Vesp. 6, 3), in the seventh (July). Hofstee suggests that septimo should be read here for octavo (i.e. VIIIMP ..for VIIIIMP ..). In Vesp. 6, 2 Suetonius describes how the detachment of the Moesian army which arrived too late to aid Otho at Betriacum, when they heard of his death, advanced as far as Aquileia and after a turbulent outburst tried to elect Vespasian as emperor. The movement was checked for the time, and the troops returned to their allegiance to Vitellius; but when their action became known, the prefect of Egypt was the first to compel his legions to take the oath to Vespasian on July 1.

: for the legions constituting the armies in Moesia (later Servia and Bulgaria) and Pannonia (extending along the Danube from Vienna to Belgrade) see on Vesp. 6, 2 and Oth. 9, 3. The plur. "Moesiae" refers to the two provinces called Moesia Superior (Western half) and Inferior (Eastern half) separated by the Ciabrus, a trib. of the Danube. Marquardt (Staatsv. i² 303) shows that the division took place under Domitian; and so Suetonius is guilty of an anachronism. The defection of the Moesian and Pannonian armies from Vitellius is described in Tac. H. ii 85 sq., Dio lxv 9.

: see on Vesp. 6. The form "Syriaticus" is attested by the MSS. here; Sabellicus, Beroaldus, and many subsequent editors altered it to “Syriacus.” The adj. “Syriaticus” (cf. Asiaticus, Hadriaticus, Cibyraticus, etc.) occurs also in Florus ii 9, 1; 11, 1; 12, 1. Elsewhere Suetonius uses ‘“Syriacus” (Vesp. 6, 4; Tib. 48, 2; Calig. 10, 1).
: for this expression see on Galb. 11, 1.
: Tac. H. iii 58, vocari tribus iussit, dantes nomina sacramento adigit; superfluente multitudine curam dilectus in consules partitur; servorum numerum et pondus argenti senatoribus indicit.
: see on c. 6.

: under the normal conditions of service the honesta missio could only be gained after a number of years. In the time of Augustus the legionary had to serve 16 years (later, 20 years), the praetorians 16, the urban cohorts 20, and the auxiliaries 25 (Marquardt, op. cit. ii² 542).

: the "bounties" granted to those who obtained the honesta missio took the form either of land or of money, the praetorians getting 5000 denarii (= 20,000 sesterces) and the legionaries 3000 denarii under Augustus (Dio lv 23); this latter sum was reduced to 1500 by Caligula (Suet. Calig. 44) and raised to 5000 by Caracalla (Dio lxxvii 24). Cf. Galb. 12, 2. iustae militiae: regular service in the army for a definite number of years (legitima stipendia facere); cf. iusti milites (“regular soldiers''), Galb. 12, 2. ..

div.p: § 2. urgenti terra hosti: Mucianus (see Vesp. 6, 4) was advancing from the East to Italy with the 6th legion and 13,000 vexillarii (Tас. Н. ii 83). Before they arrived, Antonius Primus (see c. 18 infr.) with the forces from Moesia and Pannonia had occupied the eastern districts of Italy, won the battle of Betriacum against the Vitellians, and stormed Cremona. mari: Mucianus had ordered the Pontic fleet to muster at Byzantium, contemplating the possibility of blockading the E. coast of Italy (Tac. l.c.); the fleet at Ravenna (in N.E. Italy, on the Adriatic) under Bassus went over to Vespasian's side (Tac. ii 100), and later the fleet at Misenum (in Campania) revolted from Vitellius (Tac. iii 56, 57, 60).

p.note: : i.e. Lucius Vitellius, who was consul in the same year as his brother Aulus, the future emperor (see c. 3, 1), and succeeded him as proconsul of Africa (c. 5). He was put in command of Rome when his brother took the field against Vespasian's generals (Tac. iii 55). Following the revolt of the fleet at Misenum, there was an outbreak in Campania, and Lucius was sent with six cohorts and 500 cavalry to crush it. Suetonius is incorrect in saying that the emperor gave to his brother the fleet and a band of gladiators. We see from Tacitus (iii 57) that it was Claudius Julianus whom the emperor sent to win back the allegiance of the fleet, and that he sent with him a city cohort and a troop of gladiators. Julianus, however, proved a traitor and joining forces with the mutineers he occupied Tarracina in Campania. Lucius Vitellius effected through treachery the capture of this city which was remissly guarded by seamen and gladiators (Tac. iii 76, Dio lxv 16). Tacitus says that if Lucius had returned at once with his victorious army to Rome, a conflict of great magnitude and involving the destruction of the city must have ensued, for Tarracina was captured at about the same time as the burning of the Capitol in the last struggle between the Vitellian and Flavian forces (see below).

: the same generals, Aulus Caecina and Fabius Valens (see c. 9, 1), who had defeated Otho's army at Betriacum (Oth. 9, 2), were again appointed to command for Vitellius. Caecina was sent on in advance; Valens was delayed by illness and took no part in the decisive second battle of Betriacum (Tac. ii 99; Joseph. Bell. Iud. iv 11, 2; Dio lxv 10). The force with Caecina was made up of the 5th and 22nd legions, with detachments of the 1st (Germanica), 14th, 15th, and 16th; the rear was brought up by the 21st (Rapax) and the 1st (Italica) with detachments of three British legions (2nd, 9th, 20th) and a chosen body of auxiliaries. A body of cavalry was sent on in front to occupy Cremona (Tac. ii 100).

: decisively at the second battle of Betriacum in Oct. 69 when his army was vanquished by that of Vespasian under Antonius Primus. See the description of the fighting in Tac. iii 21 sqq. The victors then burned the city of Cremona, a stronghold of the Vitellians.

: the two most notorious traitors to the cause of Vitellius before the battle of Betriacum were Lucilius Bassus, prefect of the fleet at Ravenna (Tac. iii 12, ii 100), and Aulus Caecina, commander-in-chief of the army of Vitellius, who tried to induce his soldiers to throw in their lot with the mutinous fleet and to desert to Vespasian. Some of the officers supported him, but the troops were wildly indignant; they put him in fetters and chose as their leaders Fabius Fabullus, legatus of the 5th legion, and Cassius Longus, prefect of the camp (Tac. iii 13, ii 99). The treachery of Caecina was fatal to Vitellius, as Antonius Primus attacked when the Vitellian forces were thus disordered and without a competent leader. Among those who proved false to Vitellius after the battle were Claudius Apollinaris, prefect of the fleet at Misenum, and Claudius Julianus who was sent by Vitellius to Misenum to check the mutiny (Tac. iii 57); also Alfenus Varus and Julius Priscus, prefects of the praetorians (Tac. iii 61).

: according to Tacitus (iii 63), after the Vitellian army had surrendered at Narnia in Umbria, the generals of Vespasian (Antonius Primus and Arrius Varus) sent messengers to Vitellius at Rome offering him a safe retirement for himself and his children in Campania, together with a sum of money; Mucianus also sent letters to the same effect: Non omisere per eos dies Primus ac Varus crebris nuntiis salutem et pecuniam et secreta Campaniae offerre Vitellio, si positis armis seque ac liberos suos Vespasiano permisisset. In eundem modum et Mucianus composuit epistulas; quibus plerumque fidere Vitellius, ac de numero servorum, electione litorum loqui. Tanta torpedo invaserat animum ut, si principem eum fuisse ceteri non meminissent, ipse oblivisceretur: iii 66, nunc pecuniam et familiam (= servos) et beatos Campaniae sinus promitti.

: sc. centena milia, i.e. 100,000,000 sesterces, about £850,000. Cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, 5, Vitellius ab Sabino urbi praefecto, Vespasiani fratre, sestertium milies pepigerat arbitris militibus imperio decedere. Tacitus nowhere specifies the amount.

: elder brother of Vespasian; for his career see on Vesp. 1, 3. He was praefectus urbi at this period, and after the surrender of the Vitellian army the leading men at Rome invited him to seize the city. Sabinus showed no eagerness to do so and held parleys with Vitellius which are described in Tac. iii 65: Saepe domi congressi, postremo in aede Apollinis, ut fama erat, pepigere. Verba vocesque duos testes habebant, Cluvium Rufum (the historian) et Silium Italicum (the poet). procul visentibus notabantur, Vitellii proiectus et degener, Sabinus non insultans et miseranti propior. When Sabinus was driven to take refuge in the Capitol (see below), he sent a remonstrance to Vitellius for breaking his agreement (Tac. c. 70). Voltus

: "standing forth on the steps of the Palace"; cf. Ner. 8, pro Palati gradibus imperator consalutatus: Tac. H. i 29, Piso pro gradibus domus vocatos in hunc modum adlocutus est: iii 74, stantem pro gradibus Palati Vitellium. For this meaning of pro cf. pro muris (= stans in muris), Tac. A. ii 81; pro vallo (“from the rampart'"), id. Agr. 35, H. i 36; pro ripa, A. xii 29; pro litore, A. xiv 30. See also on pro tribunali, Vesp. 7, 2.
: Tac. H. iii 68, Vitellius, inter suos milites, prospectantibus etiam feminis, pauca et praesenti maestitiae congruentia locutus, cedere se pacis et rei publicae causa, etc.
: Tac. (l.c.), reclamantibus qui in contione adstiterant.

: the same phrase occurs in Cic. S. Rosc. 19, Apul. Met. iii 25; also primulo diluculo (Plaut. Amph. 737), and diluculo (Afran. 70, Cic. Att. xvi 13): “Diluculum” is defined in Censor. De die nat. 24, 2 as "cum sole nondum orto iam lucet."

: "in mourning"; see on "sordes” c. 8, 1. Tacitus (iii 67 sq.) describes how on Dec. 18 Vitellius clad in mourning robes (pullo amictu) and surrounded by his sorrowing household went down from the Palace to the Forum. His little son was carried on a litter as though in a funeral procession. From the Rostra he told the people in a few words that he was abdicating for the sake of peace and the State, and commended to their compassion his wife, children, and brother. Then, when tears choked his utterance, he turned to the consul and tried to surrender to him the dagger which he wore as Imperator. For the different sequence of events in the narrative of Suetonius see below.
: there is nothing in Tac. about Vitellius reading his speech from a written document.

div.p: §3. interpellante milite ac populo: when Vitellius was going down from the Palace to the Forum the people uttered greetings flattering but inappropriate, while the soldiers preserved an ominous silence (Tac. iii 67, voces populi blandae et intempestivae, miles minaci silentio). After his speech, when Vitellius declared that he would go to the temple of Concord and deposit his dagger there, and then go to his brother's house, there was a fierce outcry: maior hinc clamor obsistentium penatibus privatis, in Palatium vocantium. Interclusum aliud iter, idque solum, quo in Sacram viam (the way back to the Palace) pergeret, patebat. Tum consilii inops in Palatium rediit.

p.note: : So Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, quasi renovato furore; it is clear, however, from the account in Tac. that there was no display of spirit by Vitellius at this juncture; he was “inops consilii,” and the events which occurred next were due to the determination of his followers. His vacillation is compared by Dio (lxv 16) to the tossing of a boat in a storm: τῶν δὲ δὴ τοῦ Οὐεσπεσιανοῦ στρατηγῶν ἐπιόντων τῇ Ῥώμῃ, ἐξεπλάγη τε καὶ ἐξέστη. ἓν μὲν γὰρ᾽ οὐδὲν οὔτε ἔπραττεν οὔτε ἐφρόνει, ἐμπλήκτως δὲ ἄνω καὶ κάτω ἐφέρετο ὥσπερ ἐν κλύδωνι.

: an attack was made on the retinue of Sabinus, near the Basin of Fundanius on the Quirinal, and the Vitellians had the better of the encounter; Sabinus then sought safety by occupying the Capitol (Tac. iii 69).

: the Flaviani were the supporters of Vespasian (Flavius Vespasianus); cf. partes Flavianae, Tac. ii 67, iii 1. Mingled with the soldiers who occupied the citadel were the consuls Quintius Atticus and Caecilius Simplex, some senators and knights, and some women, of whom Verulana Gratilla was the most prominent. During the first night, owing to the carelessness of the investing force, Sabinus managed to bring in his own children and his nephew Domitian, the future emperor. succenso templo Iovis: for the storming of the Capitol by the Vitellians and the burning of the temple of Capitoline Jove see Tac. iii 71 sqq. According to Tacitus it is doubtful whether the attackers or defenders were responsible for the conflagration; he denounces it as the most shameful and regrettable event in the history of Rome: Id facinus post conditam urbem luctuosissimum foedissimumque rei publicae populi Romani accidit, nullo externo hoste, propitiis, si per mores nostros liceret, deis, sedem Iovis Optimi Maximi auspicato a maioribus, pignus imperii conditam, quam non Porsenna dedita urbe neque Galli capta temerare potuissent, furore principum exscindi. Tacitus sketches the history of the temple: the foundations were laid by Tarquinius Priscus, and the building progressed under Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus; it was dedicated under the free Republic in 507 B.C.; it was burned down, by persons unknown, in 83 B.C. when Sulla marched on Rome; Sulla undertook the restoration but did not live to dedicate the new building (hoc solum felicitati eius negatum), this honour was reserved for Q. Lutatius Catulus (consul 69 B.C.), and the name of Catulus remained inscribed on the temple down to the time of Vitellius. The temple and its history are fully described by Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 8 sqq.

: when the Vitellians burst into the Capitol, any of the Flavian officers who continued to resist were cut down. The young Domitian succeeded in escaping (see Dom. 1, 2), as did also the sons of Sabinus and the consul Simplex. Sabinus himself was captured along with the consul Atticus and dragged in chains to the Palace of Vitellius. Though Vitellius would have spared Sabinus, the rabble insisted on his being slain; Atticus was saved by his confession, true or false, that he had fired the Capitol, thus acquitting the Vitellians of the crime (Tac. iii 73–75).

: the Palace of Tiberius, at the back of that of Augustus, was on the north-western part of the Palatine hill towards the Capitoline, as is shown by this passage and by the statement that it afforded to Otho an exit into the Velabrum (per Tiberianam domum in Velabrum, Tac. H. i 27; see note on Oth. 6, 2, proripuit se a postica parte Palatii). It was built by Tiberius on the site of the house of his father (Ti. Claudius Nero) and the adjoining private mansions. At a later period it was the favourite residence of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who may have added the library mentioned by Gellius (xiii 19, 1). See also on "Palatina domus,” Vesp. 25.

: Pitiscus comments: Epulatus est Vitellius, ‘‘ne amitteret moriturus prandium; et redundantioribus, ut in extremis solet, mensae sibi ultimae dapibus refarciebatur, obruebatque se vini poculis, ut sensum amitteret futuri, vel opprobrii, vel periculi." (Hegesipp. Exscid. Hierosol. iv 32). 7, optimus est portus paenitens consilii; with The pers. and impers.

: the use of paenitens in a personal sense, either absolutely or c. gen., is found in Cic. Phil. xii 3, paenitenti mutatio consilii: Sall. Hist. frag. i 49, de in Suet. Claud. 43, paenitens de matrimonio. uses of paenitere are discussed and illustrated by Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 287 sqq.; Neue-Wagener, Formenlehre iii 657.

: cf. Tac. H. iii 70, where Sabinus, forced to take refuge in the Capitol, sends an envoy to Vitellius to remonstrate with him for violating the compact whereby he was to have withdrawn peaceably from Rome, and Vitellius puts the blame upon his uncontrollable soldiers: Trepidus ad haec Vitellius pauca purgandi sui causa respondit, culpam in militem conferens, cuius nimio ardori inparem esse modestiam suam.

: Suetonius appears to be inaccurate in stating that the assembly at which Vitellius offered his dagger to the consul was held after the storming of the Capitol. Tacitus (who was probably an eye-witness of these events; see Spooner, Tac. Hist. Introd. p. 14) describes the assembly and the attempt of Vitellius to surrender his imperial dagger as taking place before the attack on Sabinus; see above on "sordidatus.” Dio (lxv 16) agrees with Tacitus.
: there is nothing corresponding to this in Tac.
: see on Vesp. 8, 1.

div.p: § 4. pugionem: the symbol of imperial power; see on Galb. 11, 1. Cf. Tac. iii 68, adsistenti consuli (Caecilius Simplex erat) exsolutum a latere pugionem, velut ius necis vitaeque civium, reddebat. Aspernante consule, reclamantibus qui in contione adstiterant, ut in aede Concordiae positurus insignia imperii domumque fratris petiturus discessit. Dio (lxv 16) says that Vitellius was jeered at by the bystanders for his action: καὶ τά ἄλλα αὐτὸν ἐκερτόμουν, καὶ μάλιστα ὁπότε τὸ ξίφος ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τοῖς τε ὑπάτοις καὶ τοις ἄλλοις βουλευταῖς ἄρεγέν, ὡς καὶ τὴν αὐτοκράτορα ἀρχὴν δι' αὐτοῦ ἀποτεθειμένος. οὔτε γὰρ ἐκείνων τις λαβεῖν αὐτὸ ἐτόλμα, καὶ οἱ προσεστηκότες ἐχλεύαζον. TE

p.note: : Tacitus says that this consul was Caecilius Simplex, who was one of the Flavians afterwards besieged in the Capitol and who managed to escape when it was stormed by the Vitellians. Hofstee acutely points out that if we accept the sequence of events given by Suetonius we must assume that the consul immediately after his escape ventured to appear at a public assembly, which is almost incredible.

: this temple (τὸ Ὁμονόειον, Dio lv 8) on the Clivus Capitolinus overlooking the Forum was founded by Camillus in 367 B.c., and restored and rededicated in 12 A.D. by Tiberius (Suet. Tib. 20). It was used as a meeting-place for the senate (e.g. Cic. Cat. iii 9, 21, Phil. ii 8, 19), and in the 3rd cent. A.D. is called curia ("senate-house''), cf. Lamprid. Alex. Sev. 6, cum senatus frequens in curiam, hoc est in aedem Concordiae templum inauguratum, convenisset. See Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 336 sqq.; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ '928.

: there is no other reference to this as a cognomen of Vitellius. “Concordia" is found as a woman's name in several inscriptions; e.g. C.I.L. vi 2145, Coeliae Concordiae virgini Vestali maximae. The goddess Concordia appears on coins of the emperors from Nero onwards (Cohen, Méd. imp.2 Néron 66, 67, Vitellius 13-16, etc.). Torrentius compares the assumption of the cognomen "Pietas" by L. Antonius who pretended that he was only opposing Caesar in the interests of his brother M. Antonius, the triumvir (Dio xlviii 5; Sturz ad loc. cites as a modern parallel the assumption of the title "Citoyen Égalité" by the Duke of Orleans at the time of the French Revolution).
: for the constructio ad sensum cf. 10, 1; 15, 1; Galb. 10, 2.

: Tac. iii 80, Mox vocato senatu deliguntur legati ad exercitus, ut praetexto rei publicae concordiam pacemque suaderent. The envoys were sent to Antonius Primus, who was advancing by the Via Flaminia, and to Petilius Cerealis, who was advancing by the Via Salaria. The envoys who met Cerealis were rudely rejected; one of them, the praetor Arulenus Rusticus (the Stoic, afterwards executed by Domitian, Dom. 10), was wounded and his lictor killed. Those who met Antonius were more favourably received, as his troops were under better control. Tacitus mentions that the famous Stoic philosopher, Musonius Rufus, a man of equestrian rank, went with the envoys and expatiated to the troops on the perils of war and the blessings of peace; fortunately for himself, he was persuaded to desist from displaying his ill-timed wisdom (intempestiva sapientia).

: the Vestals were sent to Antonius with a letter from Vitellius asking for a delay of one day that a settlement might be arranged. The sacred virgins were sent back with honour, but the answer returned to Vitellius was that his slaying of Sabinus and burning of the Capitol had broken off all the usual courtesies of war (dirempta belli commercia, Tac. c. 81). Dio, lxv 18, says that it was to Cerealis that the Vestals (ἀειπαρθένοι) were sent. The veneration accorded to the Vestals lent great weight to their intercessions. Julius Caesar in his early youth owed his pardon by Sulla to their pleadings (Suet. Iul. 1, 2, per virgines Vestales veniam impetravit). Cf. also Tac. A. xi 32, Messalina .Vibidiam virginum Vestalium vetustissimam oravit pontificis: maximi (i.e. the emperor Claudius) aures adire, clementiam expetere: id. A. iii 69: Val. Max. v 4, 6: Cic. Font. 17, 48. hostem appropinquare: Tacitus (iii 82) describes the advance of the forces of Vespasian in three divisions, the centre along the Via Flaminia, the right wing along the banks of the Tiber, the left along the Via Salaria to the Colline Gate. The rabble and slaves had been armed by the Vitellians, and they tried to prevent the enemy entering, but were driven back into the city. Fierce fighting took place in the streets, recalling the days of Sulla and Cinna. With the storming of the praetorian camp (held by Germanic soldiers, whom Vitellius substituted for the praetorian cohorts which he disbanded) the Flavian army broke down the opposition and the city passed into their hands. According to some accounts 50,000 perished in this capture of Rome.

: Tacitus (c. 84) says that it was after the capture of the city that Vitellius sought concealment in the house of his wife (not his father) on the Aventine: Vitellius capta urbe per aversam Palatii partem Aventinum in domum uxoris sellula defertur.
: see on Oth. 6, 3, abditus propere muliebri sella. For petit = petiit cf. Oth. 7, 1 n.

: where his brother Lucius had captured Tarracina; see on c. 15, 2. The design of Vitellius to escape to Campania is mentioned also by Tac. (c. 84), ut si diem latebra vitavisset, Tarracinam ad cohortes fratremque perfugeret: Dio lxv 20, γνώμην ἔχων τῆς νυκτὸς ἐς τὴν Ταρρακῖναν πρὸς τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀποδρᾶναι. rumore ..,

: a clause with tamquam (as with quasi, see on Tit. 5, 3) often takes the place of the acc. c. inf. in post-class. Latin; cf. Aug. 6, tenet vicinitatem opinio, tamquam natus ibi sit: Aug. 94, 8, quem (puerum) cum detrahi iussisset, prohibitus monitu dei, tamquam is ad tutelam rei p. educaretur.

: Tacitus (c. 84) attributes this return, not to any rumours of peace, but to the characteristic vacillation of Vitellius: dein mobilitate ingenii et, quae natura pavoris est, cum omnia metuenti praesentia maxime displicerent, in Palatium regreditur.
: Tac. (l.c.): Palatium vastum desertumque, dilapsis etiam infimis servitiorum aut occursum eius declinantibus. Terret solitudo et tacentes loci; tentat clausa, inhorrescit vacuis.
: Bentley conjectured simul ierant (G has simulaverant).

: money was often carried in a belt and zona was used in the sense of "purse"; cf. Hor. Ep. ii 2, 40, ibit eo quo vis qui zonam perdidit: Gracchus ap. Gell. xv 12, cum Romam profectus sum, zonas, quas plenas argenti extuli, eas ex provincia inanes rettuli: Liv. xxxiii 29, negotiandi ferme causa argentum in zonis habentes. Plautus (Trin. 862) uses sector zonarius for a "cut-purse” (βαλαντιοτόμος).
: see on Galb. 20, 2.

: cf. Oros. vii 8, cum se in quandam proximam Palatio cellulam contrusisset. There was a small hut or lodge for the porter or doorkeeper beside the entrance to the Palace: Aur. Vict., Caes. 8, calls it "tugurium ianitoris." The small rooms of servants were called cellae (servorum, familiares, etc.); and they were sometimes designated as occupied by a particular functionary; e.g. cella atriensis (cf. Calig. 57). The cella ianitoris was also called cella ostiarii (Petron. Satyr. 29). Dio, lxv 20, says that Vitellius hid in a dark room where the dogs were kept: ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος φοβηθεὶς χιτωνίσκον τε ῥακώδη καὶ ῥυπαρὸν ἐνέδυ, καὶ ἐς οἴκημα σκοτεινόν, ἐν ᾧ ἐτρέφοντο κύνες, ἐκρύφθη. Tacitus (c. 84) uses a vague phrase: pudenda latebra semet occultans.

: the custom of having watch-dogs chained near the porter's cella is illustrated in the description of Trimalchio's house where there was a figure of an enormous dog in mosaic or colours on the wall, and also a live watch-dog, Scylax ("Barker'") chained at the door: Petron. Satyr. 29, ad sinistram intrantibus non longe ab ostiarii cella canis ingens, catena vinctus, in pariete erat pictus superque quadrata littera ("in capital letters'') scriptum “CAVE CANEM”: ib. 64, Trimalchio Scylacem iussit adduci nec mora ingentis formae adductus est canis catena vinctus, admonitusque ostiarii calce, ut cubaret, ante mensam se posuit: ib. 72, ad ianuam venimus, ubi canis catenarius tanto nos tumultu excepit, ut Ascyltos etiam in piscinam ceciderit.

: "mattress"; cf. Ner. 48, 4, receptus in proximam cellam decubuit super lectum modica culcita: Tib. 54, 2, Druso autem adeo alimenta subducta, ut tomentum (“stuffing'") e culcita temptaverit mandere: Sen. Ep. 87, culcita in terra iacet, ego in culcita: Petron. Satyr. 97, institis quibus sponda culcitam ferebat (i.e. the webbing which held up the mattress on the frame of the bed). "culcita” is used at times to denote a pillow (cervical); the emperor Claudius was so apprehensive of assassination that he would never visit a sick person “nisi explorato prius cubiculo culcitisque et stragulis praetemptatis et excussis'' (Claud. 35, 1).

: the advanced guard (of the Flavians), cf. Auct. Bell. Afr. 12, per speculatores et antecessores equites nuntiatur. Another military term for advanced parties was antecursores (πρόδρομοι), e.g. Caes. B.G. v 47; Livy uses praecursores.

: this ablative (for nullo or nulla) does not occur in class. Lat.; the only apparent instance, Cic. orat. tog. cand. frag. 19, neque alio nemine is corrected by Müller into ne quem alium nominem; it is found in Plautus and in post-Aug. writers (3 times in Justin, twice in Tac., and 9 times in Suet.). See Krebs-Schmalz, Antibarb. ii 128. On the other hand, Suetonius uses nullo = nemine 7 times, e.g. Vitell. 15, 4: Vesp. 11. ..
: cf. Tac. H. ii 29, spolia occultari clamitantes (milites seditiosi) tabernacula ducis ipsamque humum pilis et lanceis rimabantur. Suetonius does not use the verb elsewhere.
: Tacitus is more definite: H. iii 84, ab Iulio Placido, tribuno cohortis, protrahitur.

: Madvig would read ubi esset Vitellius num sciret; Bentley ecubi esset Vitellius. Bremi explains the text as meaning "asking him where he knew that Vitellius was"; the form of expression implying that the captors assumed that he did know. Baumg.-Cr. (iii 837) regards the passage as an instance of a “duplex sententia in unam contracta,” the meaning being the same as if Suetonius had actually written num sciret ubi esset Vitellius, and he thinks that the acc. c. inf. (instead of the subjunct. esset) is similar to the ordinary use in orat. obl. of this constr. in questions with the first or third person. This is also the view of Freund (De Suet. genere dicendi p. 6), but neither he nor Baumg.-Cr. cites any parallel for the omission of num. The text seems scarcely defensible, and perhaps Madvig's correction should be adopted, though I would prefer si sciret to his num sciret; the loss of si between Vitellius and sciret would account for the rest of the corruption. For si (= num) in indirect questions see Kühner-Stegmann, ii 426.

: for this use of ignorari cf. Tac. H. iii 74, Domitianus prima inruptione apud aedituum occultatus, lineo amictu turbae sacricolarum inmixtus ignoratusque: ib. iv 36, servili habitu per tenebras ignoratus evasit: Ter. Phorm. 930, fugitive, etiam nunc credis te ignorarier?

: i.e. in the old state prison; he did not claim the privilege of being kept merely in the libera custodia of some distinguished citizen (see on c. 2, 3, in custodiam fratri datus). The carcer (called Mamertinus in mediaeval Latin) was situated between the temple of Concord and the Curia at the foot of the Capitol. religatis manibus, etc.: Tac. iii 84, Vinctae pone tergum manus; lacerata veste, foedum spectaculum ducebatur (sc. laqueo): Dio lxv 20, τὴν ἐσθῆτα αὐτοῦ περιρρήξαντες, καὶ τὰ χεῖρε εἰς τοὐπίσω δήσαντες, τῷ τε αὐχένι σχοινίον περιθέντες, κατήγαγον ἐκ τοῦ παλατίου τὸν Καίσαρα τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ ἐντρυφήσαντα.

: this rare compound is first found in Livy, e.g. ix 6, consules prope seminudi sub iugum missi. Other compounds with semi- in Suet. are semiambustus, semianimis, semibarbarus, semicrudus, semesus, semigraecus, semiperfectus, semiustus, semiustulandus.
: where he had often addressed the people; Dio (l.c.), ἔς τε τὴν ἀγορὰν ἐσεκόμισαν τὸν Αὔγουστον, ἐν ᾗ πολλάκις ἐδημηγόρησε.

: Dio (l.c.), οἱ μὲν ἐρράπιζον αὐτόν, οἱ δὲ τοῦ γενείου ἔτιλλον, πάντες δὲ ἔσκωπτον καὶ πάντες ὕβριζον. Josephus also mentions the despiteful treatment of Vitellius, Bell. Iud. iv 11, 4, συρεὶς δὲ διὰ τοῦ πλήθους καὶ παντοδαπαῖς αἰκίαις ἐξυβρισθεὶς ἐπὶ μέσης τῆς ῾Ρώμης ἀποσφάττεται. Tacitus (l.c.) says: multis increpantibus, nullo inlacrimante, deformitas exitus misericordiam abstulerat.
: down from the Palace to the Forum, the road along which he had so often proudly ridden in state; Dio (l.c.), διὰ τῆς ἱερᾶς ὁδοῦ ἔσυραν τὸν αὐτοκράτορα τὸν ἐν τῷ βασιλικῷ δίφρῳ πολλάκις σοβήσαντα.

: the head was drawn back to make the criminal expose his face to the gaze of all; cf. Plin. Pan. 34, describing the informers being led through the arena with their faces forcibly upturned to the spectators in the amphitheatre: nihil saeculo dignius quam quod contigit desuper intueri delatorum supina ora retortasque cervices.

: sc. trahi; cf. Aur. Vict. Caes. 8, iniecto laqueo, parricidarum more, ad scalas Gemonias pertractus. Casaubon prefers ceu noxiis solet. The adv. ceu (= velut) is used in poetry (Catull., Lucr., Verg., Hor.) and in later prose (Colum., Sen., and especially Plin. N.H.); cf. Suet. Tib. 52, 2, victorias ceu damnosas rei publicae increparet.

: Tac. (l.c.), Vitellium infestis mucronibus coactum erigere os et offerre contumeliis propulere: Dio 1xv 21, αἰσχυνομένου τε ἐπὶ τούτοις αὐτοῦ καὶ κάτω βλέποντος, οἱ στρατιῶται ξιφιδίοις αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τὸ γένειον ὑπεκέντουν, ἵνα καὶ ἄκων (vel invitus) ἄνω βλέπῃ : [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 8, ne homo impudens in extremis saltem malorum, quae gesserat, rubore faciem demitteret, subiecto in mentum gladio: Eutrop. vii 18, 5, erecto coma capite et subiecto ad mentum gladio. The reading subiecto in these last two passages is found also in most of the later MSS. of Suet., and appears in the ed. Veneta (1471). The act. use of subrigo (surgo) occurs in Verg. Aen. iv 183, tot surrigit aures; in Livy, e.g. vii 10 mucrone subrecto, viii 8 hastas subrecta cuspide in terra fixas; later in Sen., Plin. N.H., Stat., Sil. Ital., etc.

div.p: § 2. stercore et caeno incessentibus: Eutrop. (l.c.), stercore in vultum et pectus ab omnibus obviis appetitus: Aur. Vict. (l.c.), multis caeno fimoque et ceteris turpioribus dictu purgamentis vultum eius incessentibus: Oros. vii 8, 8, passim fimum in os eius coniectantibus.

p.note: : referring to his burning of the Capitol (c. 15, 3). Nero also was reviled as an "incendiarius” for having caused the great fire which devastated Rome in his reign (Tac. A. xv 67).
: “trencherman'” “gormandizer," with special reference to his famous patina described in c. 13, 2. corpore
: cf. Calig. 50, statura fuit eminenti enormi. The adj. enormis is post-Aug. and means (1) huge, enormous, (2) shapeless, constructed on no plan or rule (norma), e.g. enormes vici, Tac. A. xv 38.
: a Plautine adj.; cf. Gell. ii 26, 14, ‘rubidus” autem est rufus atrior et nigrore multo inustus.

: Dio lxv 20, τά τε ἄλλα καὶ τὴν ἀσωτίαν αὐτοῦ ἐπιλέγοντες (exprobrantes), ἐπειδὴ καὶ γαστροπίων (ventre obeso) ἦν. Cf. Dom. 18, deformis obesitate ventris: Ner. 51, ventre proiecto: Tit. 3, 1, ventre paulo proiectiore.
: this word apparently does not occur elsewhere. Suetonius also uses subflavus (Aug. 79, 2; Ner. 51), and subrutilus (Dom. 20).

: the sing. quadriga is poetical and occurs at times in post-class. prose. Gellius (xix 8, 17) notices its use by Varro: “quod unum ergo rarissimum videbatur, invenimus quadrigam numero singulari dictum in libro saturarum M. Varronis qui inscriptus est Ecdemeticus." Suetonius also uses the post-Aug. sing. biga (Tib. 26, 1).
: see on c. 4, Gaio per aurigandi studium familiaris.

: for the ellipse of se cf. Quintil. xii 2, 7, qui vere civilem virum exhibeat: Justin xxvii 2, pro fratre hostem exhibuit: Ov. Met. vi 43, formamque removit anilem | Palladaque exhibuit. Several of the MSS. (GPOST) give ministratorem se. Vitellius may have been acting as one of the sparsores, whose duty seems to have been either to refresh the horses or to pour water on the wheels of the chariot to prevent their taking fire (Daremberg-Saglio, i 1199). For Dio's mention of Vitellius rubbing down or currying the horses of the Blue faction in the Circus see note on "factionis Venetae,” c. 7, 1.

: Tac. iii 85, Vitellium ... postremo ad Gemonias, ubi corpus Flavii Sabini iacuerat, propulere. Una vox non degeneris animi excepta, cum tribuno insultanti se tamen imperatorem eius fuisse respondit. Ac deinde ingestis volneribus concidit. The full phrase Gemoniae scalae occurs in Val. Max. vi 3, ix 13, Oros. vii 8; but the subst. is regularly omitted in Tac. and Suet. Pliny (N.H. viii 145) uses gradus gemitorii. These "Stairs of Groanings" were a flight of steps from the Capitol to the Forum, near the Mamertine prison; on them the bodies of executed criminals were exposed (e.g. that of Sejanus for 3 days, Dio lviii 11). We find no mention of the Gemoniae (scalae) before the time of Tiberius. See Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 324. Dio (lxv 21) says that when the soldiers dragged Vitellius to the Gemoniae (πρὸς τοὺς ἀναβαθμούς), they slew him and cut off his head which they carried round the city, and that the body was buried by his wife Galeria Fundana; but according to Eutrop. vii 18, 5 (followed by Oros. vii 8, 8) ‘“in Tiberim deiectus etiam communi caruit sepultura." 2 в

: cf. the fiendish cruelty of Caligula described in Calig. 30, 1, Non temere in quemquam nisi crebris et minutis ictibus animadverti passus est, perpetuo notoque iam praecepto: ‘“Ita feri ut se mori sentiat." Josephus (Ant. Iud. xix 1, 107) mentions that Chaerea arranged that Caligula himself should be slain by the conspirators with a multitude of wounds: προνοίᾳ τοῦ Χαιρέου . · τὸ μὴ μιᾷ πληγῇ διεργάσασθαι τὸν Γάϊον, ἀλλὰ τιμωρεῖσθαι μειζόνως πλήθει τραυμάτων.

: this compound is found earlier in Cicero, N.D. iii 33, 82, Anaxarchum Democriteum a Cyprio tyranno excarnificatum accepimus. Seneca has it once of bodily tortures (Ep. 24 mille alia instrumenta excarnificandi particulatim hominis) and twice of mental anguish (Ira iii 4, 3: Clem. i 16, 33 so too in Ter. Heaut. 813). Livy (xxiv 15) uses the simple verb carnificare. Suetonius does not mention here what is related by Dio (lxv 21) that the first wound dealt to Vitellius was by a Gallic (?) soldier out of pity for his humiliating sufferings: ἰδὼν δὲ τοῦτο Κελτός τις, οὐκ ἤνεγκεν, ἀλλ' ἐλεήσας αὐτόν “ ἐγώ σοι,” ἔφη “ βοηθήσω, ὡς μόνως δύναμαι.” καὶ ὁ μὲν ἐκεῖνόν τε ἔτρωσε καὶ ἑαυτὸν ἔσφαξεν. οὐ μέντοι καὶ ὁ Οὐιτέλλιος ἀπέθανεν ἐκ τοῦ τραύματος. Tacitus (iii 84) suggests various explanations for this soldier's action: Obvius e Germanicis militibus Vitellium infesto ictu per iram vel quo maturius ludibrio eximeret an tribunum adpetierit, in incerto fuit: aurem tribuni amputavit ac statim confossus est (the tribune referred to is Julius Placidus who had dragged Vitellius from his hiding-place).

: when criminals were strangled in the Mamertine prison, their bodies were dragged by a hook to the Gemoniae scalae and after being exposed there for some time were dragged to the Tiber; cf. Suet. Tib. 54, 2, cum ei carnifex laqueos et uncos ostentaret: ib. 61, 4, nemo punitorum non in Gemonias abiectus uncoque tractus: ib. 75, 1, alii uncum et Gemonias cadaveri minarentur: Juv. x 66, Seianus ducitur unco (where see Mayor): Ov. Ibis 163, carnificisque manu populo plaudente traheris | infixusque tuis ossibus uncus erit. Tacitus (A. vi 19) gives a gruesome picture of those executed by Tiberius for complicity with Sejanus; their bodies were cast down the Gemoniae and lay guarded by soldiers till corruption began; they were then dragged by the flesh-hook to the Tiber. Dio (lx 35) relates a jest of Gallio, Seneca's brother, on the "deification of the emperor Claudius: ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τοὺς ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ (carcere) θανατουμένους ἀγκίστροις (uncis) τισὶ μεγάλοις οἱ δήμιοι (carnifices) es te τὴν ἀγορὰν (forum) ἀνεῖλκον, κἀντεῦθεν ἐς τὸν ποταμὸν (Tiberim) ἔσυρον, ἔφη τὸν Κλαύδιον ἀγκίστρῳ ἐς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνενεχθῆναι.

: Lucius Vitellius had set out from Tarracina in Campania (see on c. 15, 2) to bring help to his brother Aulus, the emperor, but learned on his march of his death; he was met by forces sent by Antonius Primus, and surrendered to them. Dio (lxv 22) says that they agreed to spare his life; but he and his followers were brought captive to Rome and thrown into prison, and shortly afterwards Lucius was executed. Tacitus mentions his death, and describes his character in very unfavourable terms: H. iv 2, dein Lucius Vitellius interficitur, par vitiis fratris, in principatu eius vigilantior, nec perinde prosperis socius quam adversis abstractus ("dragged down by his brother's fall''): iii 77, quippe L. Vitellio quamvis infami inerat industria; nec virtutibus, ut boni, sed quomodo pessimus quisque, vitiis valebat.

: named Germanicus; see on c. 6, de hac (i.e. Galeria Fundana) liberos tulit. Dio (l.c.) says that he was put to death at the same time as his uncle Lucius Vitellius. According to the account in Tacitus (iv 80) the execution of Germanicus did not take place for nearly a year after the death of his father, the execution being ordered by Mucianus, Vespasian's general, who had made himself all-powerful at Rome: Isdem diebus Mucianus Vitellii filium interfici iubet, mansuram discordiam obtendens (''alleging'"), ni semina belli restinxisset.
: so Tac. iii 86, septimum et quinquagesimum aetatis annum explebat: Eutrop. vii 18, periit aetatis

: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 8, vixit annos quinquaginta septem. This, however, is irreconcilable with the date of his birth as given by Suetonius in c. 3, 2, viz. Sept. 24, 15 A.D. If he was born then and slain on Dec. 22 (?), 69 A.D., he was only aged 54 years and 89 days at his death, which is what is stated in Dio lxv 22 (Zonar. xi 16). Such chronological discrepancies with regard to the age, etc., of the emperors are frequent in Suetonius (see on Galb. 23; Oth. 11, 2; Tit. 11). No satisfactory explanation of them has been suggested: Reimar (on Dio l.c.) assumes that Suetonius took the dates of birth and the ages of the emperors at death from different authorities and did not trouble to consider whether they were consistent. Suetonius does not state the length of Vitellius' reign, which is variously given by other authors; e.g. by Dio (Zonar.) as 1 year all but 10 days (Vitellius was first saluted as Imperator by the army in Germany on Jan. 3); by Aur. Vict. as 8 months (the day of his accession being Apr. 19, see on Oth. 11, 2); by Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 11, 4) as 8 months and 5 days; by Eutropius as 8 months and 1 day; by Tertullian (adv. Iud. 8) as 8 months and 27 days. See Dessau, Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 450.
: see c. 9.

: the adj. Gallicanus was specially used with reference to the provinces of Gallia Cisalpina and Gallia Narbonensis. In Suet. Ner. 43, 1 “Gallicani homines” are the inhabitants of Cisalpine Gaul, and in Cic. Cat. ii 3, 5 "Gallicanae legiones" are the troops stationed in that province. In Cic. Quinct. 25, 80 ‘‘fundus Gallicanus" is used of an estate held by a Roman in Narbonese Gaul, and it is to this province that Suet. is referring here. See also R. Ellis on Catull. 42, 9, catuli Gallicani.

: born in Gaul, he became a senator at Rome, but was banished under Nero for forgery: he was restored by Galba and given command of the 7th legion (Galbiana) in Pannonia: he offered his services to Otho but was rejected: he induced the legions in Pannonia and Moesia to declare for Vespasian: he defeated the Vitellian forces at Betriacum, stormed Cremona, and entered Rome at the head of his victorious army: for a brief time he exercised an almost autocratic power at Rome, but on the arrival of Mucianus he was reduced to a subordinate position (Tас. Н. iv 11): incensed at this he went to Alexandria to complain to Vespasian, but was coldly received by him; later we hear of him as a friend and patron of Martial who (Epigr. x 23) mentions him as living peacefully at the age 2B2 of 75 in 98 A.D. Tacitus (H. ii 86) thus describes Antonius: Labantibus Vitellii rebus Vespasianum secutus grande momentum addidit, strenuus manu, sermone promptus, serendae in alios invidiae artifex, discordiis et seditionibus potens, raptor largitor, pace pessimus, bello non spernendus.

: mod. Toulouse, in Gallia Narbonensis, on the Garumna (Garonne); it was the capital of the Tolosani or Tolosates; captured by the Romans in 106 B.c., it afterwards became a colonia Latina. It is mentioned as the birthplace of Marcus Antonius Primus in Mart. ix 99, 3, Marcus Palladiae non infitianda Tolosae. | gloria, quem genuit Pacis alumna Quies (the epithet Palladia, applied to Tolosa also by Auson. and Sidon. Apollin., marks it as a centre of the literary culture of Gaul). .. ..

: Becco is probably dat. by attraction to cui; cf. Iul. 59, cui Salvitoni cognomen erat: Aug. 7, 1, infanti cognomen Thurino inditum est. This attraction is very frequent in Plaut.; in Cic. both nom. and dat. are used; in Caes. only nom.; in Liv. the dat. is the more usual; Tac. only uses the dat. with adjs., e.g. A. i 31, cui nomen Superiori. The name in the gen. is first found in post-Aug. writers; e.g. Suet. Calig. 60, quibus Gai praenomen fuit: Tac. A. xii 55, nationes quibus Clitarum cognomentum: Val. Max. i 8, cui nomen erat Equi. See KühnerStegmann i 420. beccus (Ital. becco, Fr. bec, Eng. beak) seems to be a Gallic word. As a proper name it occurs in C.I.L. xii 2514, deo Apollini Beccus ex voto. A derivative is Becciacus vicus (Bessay, Vendée), Greg. Tur. glor. Mart. 89. Becco is another form of the name: C.I.L. xii 5381, (Tolosae) deo Silvan(o) dom(estico) Becco v.s.l.m. (i.e. votum solvit libenter merito); also found in Greg. Tur. Iul. 16. Becca as the name of a cinaedus occurs in Anth. 321, 3.

: = significat; cf. Varr. R.R. i 31, ὠκέως valet cito: Cic. Fin. ii 4, 13, quaerimus verbum Latinum par Graeco et quod idem valeat: Quintil. x 1, 13, et “intellego” et “sentio” et “video” saepe idem valent quod “scio.” So δύνασθαι, e.g. Thucyd. vii 58, τὸ νεοδαμῶδες δύναται (valet) ἐλεύθερον εἶναι.
: see on c. 9. Suetonius does not mention the coincidence between gallus (a cock) and Gallus (a Gaul).
